News.title: Mum who vanished from Birmingham with three kids may be 117 miles away - police say
News.content:
Mum who vanished from Birmingham with three kids may be 117 miles away - police say

Police have issued an update in the search for missing Alimat and her three children who were all last seen on Saturday in the Digbeth area of central Birmingham

View 2 Images Police are looking to find Alimat and her three children

West Midlands Police have issued an update in their search for a missing mum and her three children.

‌



Alimat, 31, from Wolverhampton, was last seen on Saturday with her children in the Digbeth area of central Birmingham. As per shots taken from CCTV footage, the 31-year-old was spotted on security cameras walking with her three children and at least two suitcases.

‌



She was also pushing along a pram which, as well carrying her smallest child, appeared to be rammed full of clothes and coats.

‌



View 2 Images London Euston railway station (Image: Getty)

As per the Birmingham Live, the Wolverhampton mum and her kids have not been seen since. West Midlands Police took to social media, posting: "Have you seen Alimat?". "The 31-year-old from Wolverhampton is missing along with her three children.", Click here to 

In an update yesterday West Midlands Poice believed they could have travelled 117 miles away from New Street station to London Euston.

‌



A spokesperson said: "We are continuing to ask for your help to locate Alimat who is missing from #Wolverhampton. The 31-year-old, and her three children, were last seen in the city on Saturday before being spotted in #Birmingham city centre the following day.

"It is understood she may have travelled from New Street station to London Euston. If you can help, please call 999 quoting PID 461858."

Of the 170,000 people who go missing in the UK each year, some cases remain etched in our minds, while others fade too quickly from public attention, if they were ever known at all.

‌



Yet for the families and friends of those still missing, the need for answers and support never diminishes as hours, days, months, and years pass by.

This is why, in 2025, the Mirror is launching Missed . In partnership with Missing People, our mission is to bring awareness to every publicly listed missing person in the UK through our live, interactive map.

Article continues below

Simply zoom into your chosen area to see how many people have gone missing in that location. Zoom in further to reveal photos of missing persons plus the names, ages and length of time they’ve been missing.

Simple to use, the map allows you to report a sighting in confidence as well as share on social media.

For advice, support and options, if you or someone you love goes missing, text or call Missing People’s Helpline on 116 000 or email 116000@missingpeople.org.uk. It’s free, confidential and non-judgmental, and sightings information can also be taken. Or visit www.missingpeople.org.uk

News.title: Parents urged to check if children can get free school meals after rule change
News.content:
Parents urged to check if children can get free school meals after rule change

More than half of parents whose children will be newly eligible for free school meals do not know they will qualify, alarming research by The Child Poverty Action Group shows

View 3 Images Eight in 10 parents (80%) said they have struggled with the cost of school meals or packed lunches, research showed (Image: PA)

More than half of parents whose children will be newly eligible for free school meals do not know they will qualify, alarming research shows.

‌



The Child Poverty Action Group (CPAG) found 55% are unaware that all kids whose mums and dads receive Universal Credit will be entitled to lunches under a major expansion of the policy from next month.

‌



The group also found that eight in 10 parents (80%) said they have struggled with the cost of school meals or packed lunches, while more than a third - 34% - have or have owed dinner money debt to their child's school in the last year.

‌



And six in 10 have been spending £15 or more per child each week on food for the school day, with nearly one in five (17%) spending over £30.

Major warning over free school meal expansion as kids at risk of missing out READ MORE :

View 3 Images The Mirror has long campaigned for free school meals for all primary school children (Image: Andrew Teebay Liverpool Echo)

Former PM Keir Starmer last year announced an extension of free school meals to all children in families who receive Universal Credit, which comes into force next month, and could benefit some 500,000 kids.

‌



CPAG’s head of education policy Kate Anstey said: "Our survey shows wider eligibility for free school meals will give hard-up families some badly- needed breathing space.

"But September is only weeks away and our new analysis shows the DWP (Department for Work and Pensions) and DfE (Department for Education) have left the job half done. With so many families struggling, it’s on government to ensure the country’s children get what little help is available."

To receive a free school meal, children must be registered but schools don't automatically know which families are newly eligible because they don't hold information on which parents receive benefits.

‌



Following its polling, CPAG is calling on the Government to do more ahead of September to ensure that every child gets the meal they are entitled to from day one.

It argues that the DWP and DfE have the data and the means of informing parents and must utilise these to make sure that all eligible parents know that they qualify and know what they need to do to register.

Other experts and campaigners have long warned that children who are eligible for free school meals must be automatically registered for the support to avoid hungry kids missing out.

‌



In a report last October, the Education Policy Institute (EPI) called for a major review of the system to ensure the Government’s expansion of free hot lunches is implemented as intended.

View 3 Images CPAG is calling on the Government to do more ahead of September to ensure that every child gets the meal they are entitled to from day one. (Image: Getty Images )

In a series of recommendations, the EPI called for a national system of centralised auto-enrolment for free school meals to reduce the number of entitled children missing out on free lunches and other associated support.

Article continues below

The Mirror has long campaigned for free school meals for all primary school children.

A Department for Education spokesperson said: "We're working closely with schools and councils to make sure every eligible family knows about it. So if you're a parent and you're not sure whether your child qualifies - just ask the school."

::: Survation surveyed 201 parents in England on Universal Credit whose children are currently ineligible for free school meals but will qualify for them from September between June 26 and August 6.

News.title: Thousands to get money off electricity bills for living near pylons
News.content:
Thousands to get money off electricity bills for living near pylons

The first wave of projects include National Grid transmission infrastructure from Bramford to Twinstead in East Anglia, the North London Reinforcement project and the Emmock substation in north east Scotland

View 2 Images Thousands could be set for cheaper bills (Image: Getty)

Thousands of households living near new or upgraded pylons will be the first to get money off their electricity bills, the government has announced.

‌



Payments will start from next year, as the first projects expected to qualify for a new bill discount scheme are unveiled.

‌



Communities in over 40 locations will get direct benefits for hosting vital infrastructure that will provide cheaper, clean electricity to the whole country. Those living within 500 metres of the projects could get get £2,500 off their electricity bills over 10 years.

‌



The first wave of projects include National Grid transmission infrastructure from Bramford to Twinstead in East Anglia, the North London Reinforcement project and the Emmock substation in north east Scotland.

How to save water and money with more than two-thirds of England now in drought READ MORE :

View 2 Images Energy Minister Michael Shanks said upgrading Britain's electricity grid was 'vital' (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

Energy Minister Michael Shanks said: “Upgrading Britain’s electricity grid is a vital part of how we deliver secure, homegrown energy and unlock economic growth across the country.

‌



“It is a moment of national renewal – upgrading what was built largely in the 1960s for the modern age and is our route to bringing down electricity bills for households across the country.

“It’s vital we build again as a country and we are determined those communities which host pylons should benefit, which is why we’re bringing down the energy bills of those hosting this vital national infrastructure.”

A Government impact assessment earlier this year found that more than 100,000 households could benefit from the scheme in the coming decades as further projects follow.

‌



Most households that qualify for the scheme will receive the discount automatically on their electricity bill every six months via their energy supplier, officials said, although some may need to apply, such as those on commercial meters.

Ministers said they will be directly contacted by their energy supplier or Ofgem with further information in the first half of 2027.

Neil Lawrence, Ofgem executive director for delivery and schemes, said: “Communities that host new electricity transmission infrastructure are playing a vital role in delivering the cleaner, more secure energy system Britain needs.

Article continues below

“The bill discount scheme will help ensure eligible households living near these projects see a direct benefit through discounts on their energy bills. As the scheme administrator, Ofgem’s role is to make sure payments are delivered effectively, fairly and transparently to eligible customers.”

News.title: Tributes pour in for woman, 23, who dies at scene of crash which claimed two lives
News.content:
Tributes pour in for woman, 23, who dies at scene of crash which claimed two lives

Natasha Denman, 23, was one of two people in their 20s who sadly died at the scene of a serious crash as her family express their 'heartbreak' over her 'sudden' passing

View 2 Images Natasha Denman, 23, died in the crash in Gorton (Image: GMP)

Tributes are pouring in for a 'funny' and 'caring' 23-year-old who lost her life alongside a 24-year-old man in a horrific crash in Manchester last week.

Natasha Denman, 23, was one of two people in their 20s who sadly died at the scene of a collision on Hyde Road in Gorton on Wednesday evening (August 5).

Her family have been left 'heartbroken' following her 'sudden' passing after the car she was travelling in collided with a stationary digger near the junction with Clumber Road at around 9:30pm.

Greater Manchester Police said that four people were in the car, with Natasha and Jack Cartwright, 24, passing away at the scene.

Ms Denman's family paid tribute to their 'loving and caring' Tasha on August 11, expressing their 'heartbreak'.

View 2 Images A Greater Manchester Police vehicle (Image: Kenny Brown | Manchester Evening News)

Her family said: “Tasha was a much-loved daughter, sister, granddaughter, niece and cousin. We, as a family, will never recover from her sudden and unexpected passing at such a young age.

“Our hearts are forever broken. We would like her to be remembered as the naturally funny, loving and caring person she was.

“She can rest peacefully knowing she will always be cherished. We would politely ask people to accept our request for privacy at this time.”

Apollo Simms, 26, of Tealby Road, Manchester, has been charged with two counts of death by dangerous driving and failing to provide a sample for analysis in relation to the incident. He was due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on August 11.

Police confirmed another man who was arrested has been released on bail.

The force are appealing for any witnesses who may have seen the moments prior to the collision or anyone who has mobile phone, ring doorbell or dash cam footage to get in contact with them to assist the investigation.

Article continues below

Anyone with information can contact police on 0161 856 4741 quoting the log number 3717 of 05/08/2026. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Ferry capsizes leaving 15 dead and more missing on world's largest man-made lake in Zimbabwe
News.content:
Ferry capsizes leaving 15 dead and more missing on world's largest man-made lake in Zimbabwe

Search and rescue operations were deployed on the huge lake which is teeming with Nile crocodiles and hippopotamuses - there were 114 adult passengers onboard at the time

View 3 Images A ferry has capsized in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba (Image: Mutsa Murombedzi/X)

A ferry has capsized in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba, leaving 15 people dead and 27 other missing.

The country's national disaster management agency said 77 people were rescued after the incident on Tuesday, August 11 and made it to a small island on the lake, with boats now being dispatched to bring the survivors back.

The boat has a carrying capacity of 90 people. Zimbabwe's Civil Protection Unit said it could only confirm through registered ticket sales that there were 114 adult passengers onboard, with five crew members.

There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were not accounted for.

Zimbabwean state broadcaster ZBC published video of speedboats making their way to what appeared to be an overturned boat on the lake as a helicopter hovered overhead.

View 3 Images The boat had a carrying capacity of 90 people (Image: ZBC News)

An underwater team for search and rescue operations was deployed on the lake, which forms part of the border between Zimbabwe and neighbouring Zambia.

Lake Kariba is the largest man-made lake in the world by volume. It was created by building a dam wall to block the Zambezi River, resulting in a valley slowly filling with water to form a huge lake.

The lake is teeming with Nile crocodiles and hippopotamuses.

View 3 Images There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were on board (Image: Mutsa Murombedzi/X)

Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of Parliament, said rural communities use the boat to travel along the lake to the town of Kariba, a journey that usually takes about five hours.

Ms Murombedzi posted a video of what she said were people on shore waving off what appeared to be the ageing ferry at the start of its journey.

Article continues below

Some people standing on the shore were worried the ferry would not survive strong waves on the lake, according to the video.

News.title: 'Small boat crisis 'must be fixed once and for all' after horror 230-people mega dinghy'
News.content:
'Small boat crisis 'must be fixed once and for all' after horror 230-people mega dinghy'

EXCLUSIVE: Newly-appointed borders minister Anna Turley told the Mirror she was horrified when a record 230 people reached the UK in a single boat - but admitted Brexit has made fixing the problem harder

View 6 Images A 15-metre mega dinghy carried 230 people to the UK (Image: PA Wire)

Labour's border security chief has said the Channel migrant crisis must be fixed "once and for all" after a huge mega dinghy carried 230 people to the UK - as Andy Burnham said he would keep going until crossings stop.

‌



Anna Turley voiced her horror after a 15-metre boat transported the record number of asylum seekers from France on Sunday. The newly-appointed Home Office minister said Britain was working with intelligence services from around the world to smash smuggling gangs - but admitted Brexit is making it harder.

‌



Ms Turley told The Mirror that mega dinghies landing on UK shores must not become the norm. She said: "I won't accept that. We cannot become used to seeing that. That cannot be the norm."

‌



There is growing alarm about the size of the larger dinghies making the perilous journey, with at least 13 people believed to have died so far this year alone. Last week a boat carrying 173 people capsized after catching fire, sparking a rescue operation in the Channel.

Andy Burnham confident release of PC Harper's killers will be blocked READ MORE :

Dangerous mega dinghy with record 230 people on board crosses Channel to UK READ MORE :

View 6 Images Border Security and Asylum minister Anna Turley in Blackpool, where an asylum hotel in a landmark venue has closed

Ms Turley said: "We've already had a fire last week in a huge vessel, and I'm really concerned that we're going to see a really serious incident. Not a single boat, if I had my way, would be leaving French soil to make its way to the UK. We've got to end this once and for all."

‌



Asked if the record-breaking crossing on Sunday night was a turning point, she said: "That was horrifying. We've seen a couple of those large boats in the last couple of weeks, and that's just not acceptable.

"It shows the lengths that these people will go to and the risks to human life that they will do to push people into these boats and get them across the Channel, and the levels of exploitation that they are undertaking."

It came as Andy Burnham said the government "will keep going at this issue" until small boat crossings are stopped. He told GB News: "People will say to me, 'we don't want any crossings'. I understand that concern.

‌



"There are further things that we are doing and we will keep going at this issue until we deliver that eradication that people are looking for." But pressed on whether he could promise small boat crossings would end by the next general election he said: "It would be wrong, I think, for me to make a prediction now based on a timeline."

Arrivals have dropped by more than 40% compared to last year, and earlier this month were at their lowest level since 2021. Ms Turley pointed to successes denting the supply of small boat parts in recent months. This has included a haul of 25 boats on their way to Germany from China capable of transporting over 2,000 people last month.

View 6 Images Andy Burnham has said the government will not stop until small boats crossings end (Image: WPA Pool, Getty Images)

‌



She said: "While I'm pleased we've made huge progress and huge strides, we've been working at pace across the world, right from the supply of where these boats are coming from to where they're being assembled, to where they're getting onto the French shores.

"We're working with intelligence across the world to tackle that supply. We're smashing the gangs, we've had great success in doing that."

Britain has long pushed for access to key European intelligence databases like the Schengen Information System and Eurodac, which it cannot access since leaving the EU. Asked how much she wanted access to more European-held intelligence, Ms Turley said: "I think it's really important. One of the things my first two-and-a-half weeks has taught me is just how important international cooperation is.

‌



"We can't solve the boats problem without working with the French, we can't do this without tracking the gangs that are crossing multiple countries' boundaries. So, we have to work together with our European partners and others.

"So, using that data, using that intelligence, sharing that is critical." Pressed on whether Brexit had made it more difficult to tackle small boat crossings, Ms Turley said: "The facts are clear that immigration has quadrupled since, you know, since Brexit. That is a challenge that we face, we're now outside the Dublin Convention (which allowed Britain to return migrants to countries they had passed through). These things do make things more difficult."

View 6 Images 230 people crossed the channel in a 'mega-dinghy' (Image: Facebook /Station SNSM Berck sur Mer)

‌



It comes as the government today announces that a further 13 asylum hotels will close, bringing the number in operation down to below 160. Ms Turley insisted it is realistic to get the remainder closed by 2029 - pointing out there were over 400 in operation under the Tories.

Standing outside the Metropole Hotel in Blackpool - one of the latest to be shut and returned to its operators after housing hundreds of migrants - the minister said her department's focus is on moving people to large sites such as military bases.

She said: "The priority is large sites, and those former military bases are important because we can contain people in one place for their safety, for their security.

‌



"We can provide services at a much cheaper cost, and it relieves the pressure on local communities and results in fewer sort of flashpoints than we've seen with situations like hotels."

Ms Turley stated: "Under the Tories in 2023 there were 400 asylum hotels in use. We're now down to less than 160. So, we're working through them at pace.

"And it's such an important day today because a hotel like the Metropole behind me here in Blackpool is so iconic. And it's the message it sends to the people of Blackpool that we care about your community, we care about this town. We want this town to flourish.

‌



"And we want hotels like this to be where people come and spend their weekends, spend their money in the town, go up the tower, see the illuminations, and and help get this town back on its feet and be a brilliant, thriving seaside town."

View 6 Images The boat arrived in the UK on Monday morning (Image: Facebook /Station SNSM Berck sur Mer)

Asked whether it is realistic that the remainder can close within three years, Ms Turley said: "Definitely. We're already making huge progress. I think, you know, we're over half now, so we are well on our way."

‌



Last week The Mirror followed migrants, including mums and babies, making the dangerous journey from France to the UK. We saw French police, including armed gendarmes, follow the group throughout a four-hour journey to the coastline, including walking with them into a forest, but making no attempt to stop them.

Ms Turley voiced her frustration, stating: "The reality is, of course there's more that can be done. Not every French officer has the same legal powers as others do, so often people, when they see a French officer standing by, they literally don't have the powers to intervene, but other specialised trained officers do.

"Our priority is to make sure those officers know where these gangs are, they are able, they have the powers and the resources to intervene. And as we're seeing now, the stretch of of space along the French coast that they are now using is a sign that we are having an effect, but it's dispersing.

‌



"We've got to make sure that, working with the French, we're flexible, we're finding out where they are, and we're making sure that this is not kind of stretching across across the the entirety of the coast."

View 6 Images The size of dinghies has increased significantly (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

A National Crime Agency spokesperson said: “People smuggling gangs are constantly trying to adapt and we are working internationally to tackle their business models, end-to-end.

Article continues below

"We are proactively targeting and degrading the supply chain of boats and engines, the social media they use to advertise crossings, their finances, and the controlling minds coordinating the crossings, in the fight against organised immigration crime.

“The ability of facilitators to bring engines, migrants and boats together simultaneously has been degraded. What has not changed is the callous disregard that people smugglers have for human life, and their willingness to employ substandard and dangerous equipment for these illegal crossings.”

News.title: Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’
News.content:
Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’

Craig Fox, 22, miraculously walked away from a head-on collision on the M50 after he was hit by what is believed to be a stolen Toyota Yaris carrying eight underage teens as travelling 100mph.

View 2 Images The scene of the crash near junction 12 of the M50 (Image: © 2026 COLLINS PHOTO AGENCY)

A shocked mum has spoken of the moment she arrived at the scene of a crash involving her innocent son and a car allegedly carrying eight underage teenagers.

‌



The devastating collision took place as Sarah Jane Fox's son, Craig, 22, was driving on the M50 in Dublin when a reportedly stolen Toyota Yaris crashed into his Skoda Fabia head-on. The Toyota was travelling the wrong way down an off-ramp near junction 12 of the motorway at Firhouse around 5.30am on Sunday.

‌



It has been reported that eight teenagers, all under 16, were in the Toyota, including a 13-year-old boy who suffered critical, life-threatening injuries. Craig and the other seven teenagers were also taken to hospital, with the 22-year-old suffering internal bleeding.

‌



Still, he stepped out of his car to check on the teenagers in the other vehicle, with Ms Fox saying "there were guardian angels" watching over her son, who remains in shock in hospital after the crash.

"There were guardian angels with my child on Sunday morning," Ms Fox told the Neil Prendeville Show. "It's the only thing I can tell you how he walked out of that car."

She said Craig managed to get out of the wreckage before sitting down around 10 feet away. "But he walked out of that car and checked on the other kids. He was asking how they were."

‌



Ms Fox said Craig suffered internal bleeding following the crash but was able to avoid surgery. "Craig is doing well at the moment. He's stable," she said. "He had some internal bleeding yesterday, but it stopped without surgery, which was a relief.

"He's sitting up, talking, but he is sore all over, which is expected. He was hit head-on at 100 kilometres an hour so he's in shock as well."

View 2 Images Sarah Jane Fox believes 'guardian angels' were responsible for her son's survival (Image: Image: Mick O'Neill/Daily Mirror/Irish Daily Star.)

‌



Craig called his mother from a police officer's phone just after 5.30am to inform her of the incident. This was due to his own phone being thrown from the car during the crash, the Irish Mirror reports.

Ms Fox said: "Craig rang me at 5:32 from a police officer's phone. He couldn't find his phone. We realised then it had flown out of the car when it was spinning.

"He rang me from the police officer's phone, and I got into my car and was across the M50 as quickly as I could." Emergency services were on the scene within minutes, the mother said.

‌



"Craig said it was no more than two minutes before the police were jumping the barrier on the M50 because they came down the correct side of the road and came across to him," she said. The mother said she was particularly distressed after learning that those in the other vehicle were under 16.

"I'm not going to get into that part of it, but I have a feeling that another word isn't being used," she said. Asked about the ages, she confirmed: "Yeah, under 16."

Ms Fox said she had seen TikTok videos involving the young people and struggled with the circumstances surrounding the crash. "The TikTok videos show children in that car, and I keep saying the word children because that's all they are," she said.

‌



She said she had heard that the group had allegedly been in a stolen car for several hours before the collision, but stressed that this information was second-hand and that she could not confirm it. "Apparently, this is what I'm hearing, and again, it's I'm hearing it second-hand, so I can't confirm it," she said. "But they were out prior to hitting my child for a number of hours in a robbed car."

Despite her anger and heartbreak, Ms Fox repeatedly stressed that she was not looking to blame the children. "I don't blame the children for this. I'm not going to place blame on anyone," she said.

"It's after happening. My child is alive and he's lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what's happened."

‌



She added: "What they've done is wrong. I'm not taking or minimising what they've done is wrong. What I'm saying is, I'm not going to start placing hate and anger after the families. I hope they make it up for the justice system."

The crash has also left Craig without the car he relies on for his electrical apprenticeship. "My child has no car now. He's a third-year electrician, and he's no car for work now," Ms Fox said.

"And he's not going to have a car for a while." She said she was also worried about whether her son would be able to get behind the wheel again.

‌



"And the other thing is, is my child going to get back in a car after what's happened?" she said. Craig remembers the crash, according to his mother.

"Every bit of it,” she said when asked if he could recall what happened. "That's why, at the moment, he's still in shock. It's going to cause issues, I think."

Ms Fox described her son as a hard-working 22-year-old who secured his electrical apprenticeship himself and had been working since before he left school. "He's a good kid. He's a kind, caring, loving young fella that's gone out. He's been working since before he left school," she said.

‌



"He got his apprenticeship off his own back. He used his initiative. He got it all off his own back." She said Craig had been looking forward to finishing his apprenticeship and travelling.

"He goes to his gym. He has his girlfriend. He has his pals there - normal 22-year-old young fella," she said. "And his dream is that when he finishes electrical apprenticeship, that he goes travelling." For Ms Fox, however, the memory of the crash scene remains deeply distressing.

"Once I knew my child was okay, I could look at something else," she said. "But if you were at that crash site and you'd seen what I saw at that crash site - it was like a clown car with eight children coming out of it."

‌



She said emergency crews were treating those involved as the young people emerged from the vehicle. "Those kids that came out of it, were on the ground. Ambulance men everywhere," she said. "And that's, I think, why I have this reaction, because I saw the crash site."

For now, her focus is on Craig's recovery and the lasting impact the collision may have on his life. She is grateful her son survived, but believes what happened cannot simply be left without consequences.

"My child is alive and he’s lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what’s happened."

Article continues below

The State’s policing watchdog has launched an independent investigation into the incident. In a statement on Monday, Fiosrú, which investigates incidents involving contact with Gardaí where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured, confirmed it received a referral regarding the incident.

It said a team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.

"A referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaí have been accused of wrongdoing. Instead, it means that Fiosrú should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaí may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it said.

News.title: Woman assaulted by double murderer says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again
News.content:
A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on to kill and attack more women.

Laura, whose surname we are not using, said she had been trying to protect other women by reporting Levy in 2018, but feels betrayed by what he was later allowed to do after being released from jail.

Levy was convicted on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins and raping another woman in London in 2025. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.

He was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the Tube in London between 2023 and 2025.

Police, prosecutors and the courts made a series of disastrous decisions that left Levy free. He attacked 14 more women before being taken off the streets, despite being a sex offender who was monitored by the Met Police.

Levy was a registered sex offender because he sexually assaulted Laura â and a separate victim - in summer 2018.

Laura says that Levy is "evil" and that his attack "completely changed my life".

But she now realises that what she would "think about, dream about, have nightmares about was actually happening - he was actually still out preying on vulnerable women".

Waiving her anonymity, she said she had been trying to protect other women by ensuring that Levy was jailed.

"I feel like when I reported it, I was doing the right thing and I thought I was doing it to protect other women.

"I feel absolutely devastated for all of those women that have been affected by him â and the families."

Laura says she feels let down by the whole criminal justice system including the Met Police, the courts and judges who bailed Levy, as well as the Crown Prosecution Service.

"They're all as guilty for allowing him to continue to do what he was doing", she says.

"They could have prevented so many women from being hurt.

"They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."

News.title: More weather records as UK heat set to spike again
News.content:
The record for the number of days reaching 30C in any year has been broken, according to the Met Office.

After several locations exceeded 30C on Sunday, it has now confirmed that there have been a total of 35 days where the maximum daily temperature has exceeded this threshold - beating the 34 days set in 1995.

This tally is widely expected to be topped again on Wednesday and Thursday with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England.

A rare amber extreme heat warning has been issued by the Met Office, external for Thursday.

News.title: Police chiefs call for PM to prevent early release of PC Harper's killers
News.content:
The police chiefs from Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland also called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered - such as with the government's early release scheme, which was designed to reduce prison overcrowding.

Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, will become eligible for release from custody after serving half of their sentences.

In the letter, released on Tuesday evening, police chiefs said the early release of PC Harper's killers, and that of anyone involved in the death of an officer, could cast doubt over the "value placed on their service and sacrifice when they put themselves in harm's way to protect others".

They outlined three requests of the prime minister, beginning with pursuing "every lawful option to determine whether the earlier release of those responsible for PC Andrew Harper's death can be prevented" - which Burnham has already pledged to do.

Second, they called on the government to put greater consideration into the crimes committed by prisoners when altering their sentences.

They wrote: "Where an offender has caused a death, committed exceptionally serious violence, or presents an ongoing risk to individuals or communities, there should be explicit consideration of public protection, victim impact and community safety before release arrangements are amended.

"This is not simply a question of punishment. It is a question of ensuring that public protection, victim confidence and community safety remain central to decisions that may substantially reduce the time an offender spends in custody."

Lastly, the letter called for victims and bereaved families to be "properly considered whenever significant changes are made to sentencing or release arrangements".

Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the early release scheme, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.

News.title: UK to get best eclipse since 1999 as Moon blocks out Sun across Europe
News.content:
But when it comes to the weather, fortunes will be mixed. In much of the UK, clear skies should give many a good view of the eclipse. However, across some parts of north Wales, northern England and especially Scotland and Northern Ireland, areas of cloud could move in between 18:00 and 19:00.

Across some parts of western Scotland and in towards the north and west of Northern Ireland, cloud could bring outbreaks of rain.

For those lucky enough to be in Spain, there will be clear skies for people to see a total eclipse in Bilbao, Valencia and Palma, Mallorca, while both Barcelona and Madrid will see more than 99% coverage.

Depending on the location, the total eclipse will peak between 20:26 and 20:33 local time (19:26 to 19:33 BST).

Crowds have been flocking from all over the world to northern Spain for the event with half a million visitors expected, according to the finance ministry.

Julie who travelled with her family from Brest, France, to the Spanish city of Burgos, said she was "very excited".

"We came from very far to see it in totality. I have seen [it] once and it was beautiful and amazing - I am so happy to have the chance to see one again."

Leonor Aguilar from JaÃ©n, Spain, said: "During that minute and a half, what I hope to see is the grandeur of nature and to experience it with my family.

"We often spend money on trivial things instead of investing in something as beautiful as witnessing such a marvellous sight."

Martin Griffith, the director of Brecon Beacons Observatory, in Wales, described the eclipse as "one of the great phenomena of nature".

"It is going to be a fantastic eclipse in Spain, we are right on the path of totality," he said. "What they will see is about a minute and 40 seconds of totality. It will be dark, the Moon will completely cover the Sun.

"Although we know they happen quite often we're not always in the path of totality - they could be over the Pacific Ocean, but to have it over land is just incredible," he said.

The next time the Moon obscures as much of the Sun on the British Isles will be in 2081, and the next total solar eclipse in the UK will be in 2090.

News.title: Watch: Was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?
News.content:
Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported.

The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said.

He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US.

Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane.

The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams explains.

News.title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
News.content:
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.

Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.

Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.

Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.

Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.

Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.

The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.

Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.

The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.

"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.

To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.

"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

News.title: The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer
News.content:
She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn't bother getting it checked. So I guess I'm saying don't ignore anything â get everything checked out.

"As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there's a lot I have learned from it, and I'm grateful for that."

She continued: "I'm not scared of whatever comes next. I'm at peace with it. I'll see my [late dog] Gracie sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it's far harder for them than for me."

Davis added: " I still would like to keep working. I'm perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life."

Following her post to Instagram, Davis received an outpouring of support from fans and well-wishers.

The Office US star Jenna Fischer wrote: "Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let's spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort!"

Fischer played receptionist Pam Beesly on the American version of the show, with Davis playing the character's UK counterpart.

News.title: Wealthier areas must play their part in housing asylum seekers, Burnham suggests
News.content:
Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics, external showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.

He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.

Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.

The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution.

News.title: Summer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met Office
News.content:
This summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, according to the Met Office.

Only average conditions are needed for the remainder of August to surpass the record set just last year.

Provisional Met Office statistics show that the UK's mean temperature for meteorological summer so far (1 June to 10 August) currently stands at 16.48C (61.66F), which is 1.88C above the 1991-2020 average.

In summer 2025, the mean temperature across the country - which includes overnight lows as well as daytime highs - was 16.10C (60.98F).

It is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

News.title: Eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
News.content:
At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves.

"I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.

They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.

Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.

But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.

Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders.

Meanwhile, eclipse glasses have been turning up for sale in unexpected places as retailers try to capitalise on the demand.

"I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme.

"People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.

News.title: Criticism as thousands of seats empty at Europeans Athletics Championships
News.content:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost Â£150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost Â£110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (Â£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

News.title: Man guilty of harassing MP Stella Creasy on Tube train
News.content:
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP for Walthamstow after preventing her from leaving a Tube carriage and behaving in an "abusive and aggressive" manner.

Clifford Wilby, from east London, targeted Stella Creasy on a Victoria line train between Walthamstow Central and Finsbury Park on 15 July last year.

Westminster Magistrates' Court heard how Wilby spoke to Creasy about knife crime and her "failings as a Member of Parliament" before filming her, leading to members of the public intervening.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Wilby and Creasy first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 as part of her role as an MP.

She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else's case.

Creasy said he had "made a series of very serious allegations", became abusive and "referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath".

The meeting was stopped because of Wilby's behaviour.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to block new betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and for many people, the high streets they grew up with are "unrecognisable".

He said the plans were "shaped" by a series of BBC News investigations which exposed organised crime on high streets, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes, vapes, cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco for up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham told the BBC that the changes would make it "easier for police to close a vape shop and have it closed for longer".

He said: "At the same time we're changing the planning regime... which should stop the proliferation of vape shops on our high streets."

The prime minister added that Operation Vulcan in Cheetham Hill, Greater Manchester, cleared the area of counterfeits and crime and "proved" what could be achieved.

"When I look at police reform across England, I will be asking for a similar approach to be taken," he said. "I want the strongest possible neighbourhood policing, with all agencies involved, to rip out criminal behaviour that is pulling places down."

Burnham said he did not accept the decline of the high street as "inevitable".

"I don't see why anywhere should have to accept they have empty shops, vape shops and the challenges that come with that."

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday that many people were frustrated at vape and gambling outlets "popping up even near schools and some of them are linked to illegal activity and crime".

News.title: Man dies after punch from security guard in Turkey bar, inquest hears
News.content:
A rugby player was punched in the head by a security guard while on holiday in Turkey and died after he returned home, an inquest has heard.

Scot James, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, had been in hospital since he suffered head and brain injuries in an alleged bar assault on 5 July.

He fell and hit his head during a "verbal exchange", Pontypridd Coroner's Court was told on Tuesday.

The 34-year-old was repatriated to the UK and died on 26 July at the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant, Rhondda Cynon Taf.

A provisional cause of death was given as blunt head injury.

James' family described him as a "loving father, son, grandson and partner" in tributes following his death.

Maesteg Celtic RFC said he was an "outstanding player and a great character".

Coroner Rachel Knight said a full inquest was necessary as there was reason to suspect the death may have been unnatural.

She said that as police in Turkey would potentially be investigating James' death, the next inquest hearing would be scheduled for later this year.

Knight said it may be necessary to pause inquest proceedings pending the outcome of any criminal investigation and confirmed the court would liaise with Turkish authorities.

Police in Turkey are understood to be investigating the death, with assistance from the Foreign Office.

In a statement, James' family said he "had a warm heart, a great sense of humour, and a natural ability to bring people together".

"We are heartbroken by his loss," they said.

"No words can truly express the pain we are experiencing or the void his passing has left in our lives."

Maesteg Celtic RFC said: "Everyone at the club is devastated by this news and our thoughts go out to his family and friends at this difficult time."

News.title: England set to be one of the first countries to eliminate hepatitis C
News.content:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit, external without needing to speak to a GP.

News.title: YouTube couple's donkey sanctuary plans approved
News.content:
A famous YouTube couple have been allowed to build a donkey sanctuary behind their West Sussex home.

Earlier this year, Zoella - real name Zoe Sugg - and her fiancÃ© Alfie Deyes applied for permission to develop a five-acre field they had bought next to their property near Hassocks.

They were warned by Mid Sussex District Council (MSDC) that there could be potential Roman, Anglo-Saxon or even prehistoric remains buried there.

MSDC approved their application at a planning meeting on Friday, having recommended that work cannot begin until archaeologists conduct an investigation.

Zoella, 36, who made her name with make-up videos before moving on to books and her own range of products, applied for planning back in May.

Included were proposals to create an enclosure for the animals, stables, three shepherd huts, parking for tractors and a pond.

However, an earlier excavation across the road had uncovered items from the Roman period, with MSDC's archaeological adviser previously stipulating that no groundwork should take place until a programme of archaeological monitoring was approved.

Locals also voiced concerns about how the development might impact the views of the surrounding area, increase traffic and impede access to nearby bridleways and public footpaths.

They complained that a gate and fences have already gone up at the site.

"We also don't like the gates and would rather they were not there," said one resident, who did not want to be named.

"Once you have gates up, it's not the same.

"There are paths and bridal ways all around here and people use them for walks all the time."

On the gate is a poster from Sugg and Deynes which reads: "We've lived here for nine years with our garden backing onto this field, and we have always worried about it one day being developed into new houses.

"After many years of trying to purchase it, last year we managed to do so.

"This means not only is the view from our house and many others nearby protected, it also helps keep this area the lovely walking spot it is for so many people each day.

"If you live in this area and are also keen to keep as much green space thriving as possible, please head over to the council's planning website and leave a positive comment to help encourage the approval of other projects like ours - thank you."

Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez quietly split from her longtime fiancé Riley Roberts months before she started freezing her eggs, according to a new report.

The progressive New York Democrat announced on Instagram over the weekend that she decided to start the egg-freezing process, giving the 36-year-old the option to get pregnant later in life.

“I want to share this because I was weighing it for a very long time, and I think that, you know, I was saving for it for a very long time, and there just isn’t a ton out there, I feel, and sometimes it can feel very daunting,” Ocasio-Cortez said during a live video on her Instagram story Saturday.

As the congresswoman opened up about this very personal experience, Leigh Ann Caldwell, Puck News’ chief Washington correspondent, revealed that a “reputable Democratic source” told her about 18 months ago that Ocasio-Cortez and her partner Riley Roberts had ended their engagement.

“AOC stopped wearing her engagement ring several months before that,” Caldwell wrote on X Tuesday. “There have been no public photos of her and Riley together in recent history.”

open image in gallery Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez quietly split from her longtime fiancé Riley Roberts months before she started freezing her eggs, according to a new report ( Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez via Instagram )

The Independent has reached out to the congresswoman’s office for comment.

Ocasio-Cortez and Roberts were last photographed together at the 2021 Met Gala, according to TMZ. Months later, in May 2022, the congresswoman confirmed that she and Roberts were engaged.

The two had always kept a rather private relationship, so it’s not shocking that the news of their breakup went under the radar.

Ocasio-Cortez and Roberts met at Boston University when they were both 19, according to a September 2022 GQ profile on the congresswoman. They started dating in their 20s, and more than a decade later, Roberts popped the question while on vacation in Puerto Rico.

open image in gallery The progressive New York Democrat reportedly stopped wearing her engagement ring more than 18 months ago. Roberts popped the question in 2022 after more than a decade of dating ( Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez via Facebook )

“I feel like I won the men lottery in my life,” Ocasio-Cortez told GQ when talking about her relationships, including the good examples her father and cousins set.

Ocasio-Cortez also mentioned her French bulldog, Deco, in the 2022 profile, who has appeared in her vlogs about her egg freezing process.

“Dogs have a way of evening out the lows. It’s kind of like a hard floor, and I definitely felt like my lows would be lower before him,” she told GQ at the time.

open image in gallery Ocasio-Cortez announced over the weekend that she decided to start the egg-freezing process, giving the 36-year-old the option to get pregnant later in life ( Getty Images )

Now, as the House of Representatives is on its August recess, Ocasio-Cortez is embarking on a new journey, and she’s taking her Instagram followers with her.

In her latest vlog about her egg freezing posted Tuesday, the congresswoman explained what’s happening to her body during the process, including the side effects she’s had.

While she said the side effects have been “pretty minimal so far,” she listed bloating, tenderness and issues with her sleep.

“No mood issues quite yet,” she added.

News.content:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel may soon be equipped with specialized gloves that deliver painful electric shocks designed to force compliance from combative individuals.

ICE aims to spend up to $20 million to obtain thousands of the "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices" for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

Known as the G.L.O.V.E., an acronym for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, the items are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC in Lexington, Kentucky, and have been utilized by select police departments and jails in recent years.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode ( AP Photo/Ryan Murphy )

DHS said Tuesday that it was working on a response to an Associated Press inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email, “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”

The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.

Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone's skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”

Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

“For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage” because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.

Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.

To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy told caregiver she had ‘intrusive thoughts’ before killing her children
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Lindsay Clancy messaged one of her caregivers less than two months before she killed her three young children in 2023, saying she was experiencing “intrusive thoughts I never had before,” feeling “completely hopeless” and worried about becoming addicted to certain medications.

Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner with South Shore Health’s Perinatal Behavioral Health Program, testified Tuesday that she regularly exchanged messages with Clancy through a patient portal in late November and December 2022. Much of their communication focused on Clancy’s difficulty sleeping, depressive symptoms and efforts to find the right combination of medications to manage them. The two also had both in-person and virtual appointments.

At several points, Clancy told Jollotta she had not taken the full dose of a prescribed medication or wanted to reduce her dosage or switch prescriptions because of what she described as intolerable side effects. She also expressed concerns about becoming dependent on medications such as Ativan, though Jollotta testified that she did not believe Clancy was addicted.

open image in gallery Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague questions Dr. Jennifer Tufts about medication that Lindsay Clancy was prescribed ( Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP )

Struggle to find the right medications

“I really don’t like the way I feel on the Remeron and I know that I can’t stick with taking it,” Clancy said in a December message asking to switch from the antidepressant, which also is used to treat anxiety and insomnia, to a previous prescription mix. “I started having very intrusive thoughts that I never had before.”

Jollotta tried to assure Clancy that having intrusive thoughts is common with someone diagnosed with postpartum depression and anxiety and encouraged her to give the Remeron more time to work since she had only been on it a few days.

“This could be some postpartum anxiety. And I wanted to familiarize her with the symptoms, so that she had them written down and she could report them to me,” Jollotta said.

Jollotta, who is among several providers that Lindsay and her former husband Patrick Clancy have sued over her care, repeatedly came up with alternative treatment plans for Clancy including a range of different medications, behavioral therapy, support groups and meditation. But she acknowledged that it was up to Clancy whether she chose to follow her advice.

“I’m only making recommendations based on my education experience, training and what I’m seeing in terms of symptoms,” Jollotta said. “The patient has the autonomy.”

During their virtual and in-person visits, Jollotta said, Clancy never talked of having a plan to harm herself or her children. She also never showed signs of psychosis or mania.

But Jollotta acknowledged that Clancy did report having thoughts of suicide. She also suggested that Clancy might have underlying bipolar disorder — due to her days of going without sleep. But Patrick Clancy denied that was the case.

Suicidal thoughts

In mid-December, Jollotta had a call with the couple and was told Clancy had her “worst day” and was “having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide.” Jollotta suggested she consider a higher level of care such as that offered by Massachusetts General Hospital. She settled on the Women and Infants Hospital postpartum program in Rhode Island but was soon discharged — with advice to stop taking one of her antipsychotic medication.

open image in gallery In mid-December, Jollotta had a call with the couple and was told Clancy had her ‘worst day’ and was ‘having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide’ ( Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via AP )

Jollotta, who was going on vacation, said she was concerned that Clancy had been discharged from the hospital, telling her in a message that she could “could benefit from the groups and added support separate even from medication changes.”

She was worried the hospital wanted Clancy to go off Seroquel, the antipsychotic medications. Clancy was advised this could lead to “worsening of mood, worsening of sleep,” but she insisted on going off the medication. Jollotta agreed to slowly reduce the dosage.

During cross-examination Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued that Jollotta was not familiar with the care Clancy received elsewhere.

Jollotta never talked to one of Clancy’s psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, nor did she access Tuft’s medical records. She did not know how many times Clancy saw Tufts, noting that she only thought Tufts treated Clancy in September.

“Would it surprise you if I told you that she saw Dr. Tufts 14 times” during a four-month period ending in January, Reddington said.

Jollotta never talked to anyone from the Rhode Island hospital that admitted Clancy, nor did she have access to the records of McLean Hospital, a psychiatric facility that Clancy admitted herself into on New Year’s Eve.

“If you're treating a person through all of this stuff that we've talked about and it’s now apparent that things have decompensated so bad that they have voluntarily admitted her to a locked ward in a mental institution, is it important to Rebecca Jollotta to find out what the diagnosis and treatment was of their patient?” Reddington said.

Jollotta agreed it was but acknowledged that she never did find out.

Killer, or someone who was mentally ill

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old. They were found in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, where their mother was lying in the yard. She had jumped from a second-story window, and she remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors argue that the former labor and delivery nurse was an intentional killer who contrived to get her husband out of the house and then strangled the children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as “a public debate about women’s mental health and how the medical system treats women.”

Clancy’s attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children. But they say she should not be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill, believing she heard voices ordering her to take their lives and her own.

The defense says she was in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare postpregnancy condition that can alter a woman’s sense of reality. A forensic psychiatrist diagnosed Clancy with those conditions after the killings.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

A cable TV polling expert claims that numbers from two surveys conducted two years apart show just how deeply President Donald Trump has disappointed America's voters when it comes to Iran.

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said Tuesday that a July 2024 poll of people who were extremely motivated to vote in that year’s presidential election found that 53 percent were confident Trump would be able to handle the situation in Iran, according to a video clip posted online.

But a July poll of people extremely motivated to vote in November's midterm elections shows that just 29 percent now approve of how Trump is actually handling Iran, Enten said.

"We're talking about a 24-point fall in just two years," he said. "What was an advantage for President Trump going into the 2024 election amongst those who really wanted to turn out and vote has turned into a tremendous disadvantage this time around."

Enten added: "Promises were made and promises were not kept. They were broken as far as those voters were concerned."

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s approval rating on Iran among extremely motivated voters has taken a nosedive over the past two years ( Reuters )

In a prepared statement, White House spokesperson David Ingle told The Independent, "What matters most to the American people is having a Commander-in-Chief who takes decisive action to eliminate threats and keep them safe, which is exactly what President Trump is doing."

"The President does not make these incredibly important national security decisions based on fluid opinion polls or political pundits, but on the best interests of the American people," he added.

It's been more than five months since Trump started his war against Iran on February 28, without congressional approval, leading to 18 U.S. military deaths and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, which increased global oil prices.

The newly-named secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Moshen Rezaei, vowed Tuesday that the strait would remain closed until the U.S. ends the war, releases frozen Iranian assets and stops all conflicts in the region, "including in Lebanon and Gaza," according to Reuters.

Rezaei announced the demands one day after Trump said that he wanted Iran to pay compensation for all of "the damage ​they've done over a 50-year period," and that he was considering letting Iran's economy collapse or hitting the country "really, really hard."

open image in gallery Ships are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz as it remains closed due to Trump’s war against Iran ( Getty )

Polling on which political party is more trusted to deal with wars, conflicts and terrorism also spells trouble for Republicans, who were ahead of Democrats by 18 percentage points in January 2025, Enten said.

"That advantage, because of President Trump, has turned into a disadvantage on a core, key question that almost always favors Republicans. Now, Democrats have a two-point edge," he said.

Enten also said that "perhaps the most shocking thing" was the question of whether the U.S. would "ultimately reach a good deal with Iran."

"Just 27 percent of all voters believe that, and get this: just 41 percent of Republicans believe it," he said. "We are seeing below 50 percent across the board on this issue, and this is the reason I think, more than any other, that folks disagree with Trump on Iran because they, simply put, don't see what the point of it is. They don't see a way out of it."

As of Tuesday, the Real Clear Polling website gave Democrats an average edge of 7.1 percentage points over Republicans in a generic congressional contest, 48.6-41.5.
