World.title: In Gaza’s tents, widows face war’s harshest realities alone
World.content:
Widows in Gaza struggle alone under displacement, burdened by loss, insecurity, and daily battles for survival.

Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Under the scorching heat inside a displacement tent in northern Gaza, Mona al-Masri tries to plan for each day as it comes.

Mona is a widow, and the mother of four children, ranging in age from nine to two. Her husband, Mohammed, was killed in an Israeli strike in September 2024.

Between fabric walls that provide little protection, Mona carries the responsibilities of a family burdened by displacement brought on by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying loss of security.

Mona begins each morning trying to secure her family’s basic needs, searching for water, arranging food, and attempting to protect her children from a reality that no longer resembles the life they knew before the war began in 2023. She says that what hurts her most is not only the harshness of their living conditions, but also the feeling that she has been forced to confront every detail of daily life alone.

“There is no normal life inside the tent. Every day begins with the same questions: how will we secure our needs, and how will we get through another day surrounded by this exhaustion?” Mona says. “The war did not only take away our homes; it took away our sense of safety and stability and made even the simplest things require enormous effort.”

Rising numbers

Mona is one of thousands of women in the Gaza Strip who have found themselves facing new roles imposed by the war, taking care of their families by themselves.



According to data from the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the total number of widows in the Gaza Strip has risen to more than 50,000. The figure includes 28,224 women who became widows as a result of the war, in addition to more than 22,500 widows who were already registered with the ministry before the war.

Aziza al-Kahlout, spokesperson for the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, says the number is expected to rise further because not all widows have yet been registered.

“The war has left these women facing a difficult reality, including the responsibility of supporting their families without a provider, amid widespread destruction and the collapse of the basic conditions needed for a decent life,” al-Kahlout says.

“This requires effective programmes for economic empowerment, job creation and strengthening self-reliance to help lift them out of poverty and deprivation,” she says.

Al-Kahlout stresses that widows’ needs extend beyond financial assistance. They also require psychological and social support, healthcare, and legal assistance related to guardianship, custody, financial rights and inheritance.

“Protecting and empowering widows in the Gaza Strip has become a shared national and humanitarian responsibility that requires an urgent and sustainable response,” al-Kahlout says.

She explains that widows need regular financial assistance, emergency relief, psychosocial and healthcare services, legal support and educational opportunities, in addition to vocational training and support for small and family businesses.

Psychological support

The loss of a husband during the war has not only deprived thousands of women of their life partners, but has also been accompanied by displacement, the destruction of homes, and the loss of stability.

Aseel Abu Shaweesh, a psychologist, explains that losing a husband during war represents a traumatic experience with profound psychological and social impacts on widows and their children. She notes that many women who lost their husbands have found themselves facing new and increasing responsibilities while simultaneously dealing with their other troubles.

“A widow in Gaza faces the pain of losing her husband, the responsibility of supporting her family, and caring for her children in an environment filled with fear and instability,” Abu Shaweesh says.

She adds: “Many women are forced to hide their grief and emotional collapse so they can carry on in front of their children, while the accumulation of daily pressures and the lack of space to express their pain increase levels of anxiety and psychological exhaustion.”



Abu Shaweesh explains that children in families who have lost one parent are also deeply affected, especially when the loss of the father is accompanied by displacement and deteriorating living conditions.

“A child loses their father and their sense of safety and stability. They may show signs of constant fear, sleep disturbances, and behavioural changes as a result of the difficult experiences they have endured,” Abu Shaweesh says.

The psychologist emphasises that widows’ needs include financial assistance as well as psychological and social support services to help them adapt to the new roles imposed by the war.

“These women need continuous support that helps them regain a sense of safety and the ability to manage their lives and their families under these difficult circumstances,” she says.

World.title: Fishermen face deadly dangers as Yemen’s Red Sea becomes a warzone
World.content:
Many Yemeni fishermen have abandoned the trade, seeking safer livelihoods as Red Sea becomes too dangerous.

Al-Makha, Yemen – Mazhar works on a sea that has long been a front line in Yemen’s conflict.

The fisherman, based in the city of al-Makha (also known as Mocha) on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, has long struggled to make a living since war arrived in the region in 2015.

Fuel is expensive, and so is renting a boat. But Mazhar, who is in his 40s and has a family that solely relies on the income from his fishing, has a bigger problem: whenever he sets out for the sea, he might not return home.

“Recently, a fishing boat in al-Khawkhah was fired on, and we lost two colleagues,” Mazhar said. “No one knows why, and the authorities haven’t announced the cause of the incident.”

Venturing beyond the shoreline is a dangerous gamble since the sea turned into a battlefield – Mazhar knows fishermen who have gone missing without a trace. But when there’s no food left at home, he decides to risk it anyway.

Red Sea restrictions

Yemen’s Red Sea coast is one of the main hubs of the country’s fishing industry, which before the war was the country’s second-largest source of export earnings after oil.

The Red Sea fishing industry has been impacted since the early years of the war, with fish exports from the region falling by about 70 percent, according to a 2018 study.

The region is strategically important for other reasons, too. Yemen’s principal port of Hodeidah sits about 160 kilometres (100 miles) up the coast from al-Makha, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait lies at its southern entrance, controlling entry into one of the world’s most vital waterways. All of that means that the coastline has been heavily contested since the early days of the war.



Currently, the Houthi rebels control most of the territory from Yemen’s border with Saudi Arabia down to Hodeidah, with pro-government forces, largely the Guardians of the Republic force, operating south of the port city. The front line had been quiet in recent years, but recent Houthi attacks against pro-government forces across the country have also targeted al-Makha.

But it is events in the waters of the Red Sea that have drawn the most attention internationally. The Houthis began regularly striking shipping passing through the region after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, and have also recently attacked Saudi shipping. The attacks have prompted the United States, the United Kingdom, Israel and Saudi Arabia to strike Houthi targets in Yemen at various times, including on the Red Sea.

Mazhar explained that fishermen now face strict boundaries at sea that they cannot cross. That is not only the case in al-Makha, but also in neighbouring al-Khawkhah district and large parts of the entire Red Sea coast.

“We pay money to buy scrap barrels and car bodies to dump into the sea to form artificial reefs. However, with every escalation in the Red Sea, we are denied access to our reefs for military reasons and are forced to fish near the shore,” Mazhar said.

Threats

“I cannot name the party restricting us right now because I am a fisherman, and speaking out could put me at risk,” Mazhar said. “But both warring sides have prevented us from sailing at different times. We are the victims of every faction fighting in our area.”

Before 2018, local fishermen say that the National Resistance Force (which the Guardians of the Republic forces later emerged out of) prevented fishermen from venturing into deep waters and reaching their reefs. Although restrictions were later eased, the fishermen say that both the Houthis and pro-government forces have placed restrictions on sailing since 2023.

“In the end, it is the fishermen who suffer to provide for their families,” Mazhar said. “We have no hand in this war, yet we bear its worst consequences.”

He added that several of his fellow fishermen have been arrested after being accused of smuggling or aiding one faction against another – claims he says are completely unfounded.

Akram, who also works as a fisherman in al-Makha, describes another danger: sea mines.

“Last year, I left home alongside two of my neighbours, and a sea mine exploded under their boat near the shore in al-Khawkhah,” he recalled. “It’s a sea mine; how can we avoid it? I can say with certainty that the Red Sea is no longer safe, and we have to move elsewhere.”



“We are witnessing the worst days in the Red Sea,” Akram added. “To be a fisherman in the Red Sea, you must carry your shroud on your shoulders.”

Fouad Doubla, head of the Fishermen’s Association in al-Khawkhah, told Al Jazeera that more than 30,000 fishermen have been affected by the conditions on the Red Sea coast and are struggling to provide basic necessities for their families, as fishing is their sole source of income.

Doubla noted that 113 fishermen have gone missing in the Red Sea since 2023, with their families receiving no information about their whereabouts. He added that the presence of sea mines is a direct consequence of the war that continuously threatens fishermen’s lives.

“Sea mines have killed 264 fishermen and maimed 215 others, forcing many to stop fishing and look for alternative work,” Doubla said, adding fishermen had also been detained by pirates in the Red Sea.

Alternative choices

Doubla explained that the difficulties and dangers encountered by fishermen have many looking for a different way to make money.

“When fishermen realised they could no longer sail safely and that their families lacked food, they were left with no choice but to either risk their lives at sea or find another job – and many chose the latter to stay safe,” Doubla said.

For Akram, that means relocating to Aden, where he believes fishing on Yemen’s southern coastline will be safer.

“Nothing is worth risking our lives for. The families of those who were lost are now struggling just to find enough food. I encourage my colleagues to join me and move to a safe area.”

Ismail, a 48-year-old who comes from a long line of fishermen, decided to leave the profession behind entirely last year, selling the gear he had collected over 20 years and using the proceeds to buy a minibus instead.

“Danger surrounds fishermen from every direction, and we never know when we will meet our fate at sea,” Ismail told Al Jazeera while holding the steering wheel of his minibus. “I don’t think any wise man would continue fishing amid such danger.”

Ismail’s wife supported his decision to quit fishing and sold some of her jewellery to help him start his new business, relieved to end the constant anxiety she and their five children felt whenever he went out to sea.

“Sometimes we stayed at sea for four days, which was completely normal under regular circumstances,” Ismail said. “But nowadays, it isn’t safe. When I stayed out for more than a day, my family would panic, and I think they had every right to be worried.”

Today, Ismail earns a modest income driving his minibus, but he is content knowing he is safe and able to share every meal with his family without constant fear.

Mazhar, who continues to fish close to their shore, believes those who transitioned to new jobs have made the right choice.

“I’ve thought more than once about leaving this dangerous profession, but I have no alternative,” he said. “As soon as I find one, I won’t hesitate for a second.”

World.title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
World.content:
Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake.

More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira.

The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday.

While the official death toll remains 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella.

Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing.

He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged.

Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses.

Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed.

World.title: Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war
World.content:
"I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."

That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in February

An Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders â and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years.

Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view.

"Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes.

These comments hint at the personal nature of this war â and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety.

Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy.

World.title: US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade
World.content:
The US military says one of its helicopters has fired missiles to disable "the steering gear" of a cargo ship attempting to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports.

In a statement, US Central Command (Centcom) says its MH-60 aircraft on Tuesday fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova vessel, as it attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman.

Centcom said it acted after "the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces". The vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran", it added.

Iran has not commented. The US has been enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, following failed attempts to end the war it and Israel started on 28 February.

Tehran retaliated by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states across the Gulf. It has also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - a key oil shipping waterway.

A fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the strait before the war and prices have fluctuated wildly since then.

Mediators have so far failed to bring the sides to an agreement on reopening the strait - and, since the latest ceasefire collapsed in June, both the US and Iran have exchanged fire intermittently.

In its statement on X, Centcom said M/V Vela attempted to sail to an Iranian port without naming it. It also did not say whether there were any casualties or injuries.

It says the US blockade "remains in full effect", adding that as of 11 August Centcom has "redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled 3 non-compliant vessels, and boarded 2".

In a separate development on Tuesday, Yemen's internationally recognised government said six people were killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they hit a vessel carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a ship since the war began.

World.title: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
World.content:
From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.

When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.

Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust.

"In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties.

"If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."

As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people â and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.

In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people âand seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (Â£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.

From these two call centre hubs â one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows â cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.

Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations.

The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response.

Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg â and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising.

World.title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
World.content:
Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally.

In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.

The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea".

"The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world.

He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments.

It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea.

Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces.

Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024.

In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months.

In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military.

He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary".

Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs.

All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations.

One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires.

Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering.

Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko.

He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon.

Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages.

Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted.

It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors.

Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region.

Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated.

In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses.

Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.

The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery.

Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.

The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez
World.content:
Football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo has married his longtime partner - model and influencer Georgina RodrÃ­guez - in a civil ceremony in Portugal.

The Portuguese striker posted an image on his Instagram account , externalshowing two hands - presumed to be his on top of his wife's - both wearing wedding rings.

Calling it the wedding of the year, Portuguese media say the couple tied the knot on 11 August in the coastal town of Cascais near Lisbon - and that their five children attended.

The Instagram entry had more than 3m likes within 30 minutes of being posted.

World.title: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
World.content:
France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry.

From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions.

Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing.

"It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement.

"This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine StÃ©venin added.

She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer."

"This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said.

But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market.

One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin.

The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the FÃ©dÃ©ration de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses.

"You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," FrÃ©dÃ©ric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times.

According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France".

The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day.

Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls.

In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls.

World.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
World.content:
Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment.

A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it.

The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure.

Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row.

Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced.

Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity.

The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law.

"We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC.

As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon.

"We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said.

Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004.

Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security.

Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008.

Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East.

Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017.

In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed.

Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023.

Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent".

In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said earlier this month.

World.title: 2027 Elections: Police, experts to address emerging security threats at Owerri conference
World.content:
Lenders Consult International says it will deepen its partnership with the Nigeria Police Force as the country prepares for the 2027 general elections, backing a strategic conference aimed at improving the management of electoral security.

The company’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Shina Philips, made this known on Tuesday at a press conference at the Force Headquarters, Abuja, ahead of the sixth Conference and Retreat for Senior Police Officers (CARSPO).

The three-day conference, scheduled for 21 to 23 September in Owerri, Imo State, will focus on “Developing a Nigerian Police Roadmap for Effective Management of Security During Elections.”

The Nigeria Police Force is organising the event in conjunction with Lenders Consult International.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Philips said the partnership, which began in 2019, was aimed at supporting the police as the lead internal security agency, particularly as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

“As a private organisation, Lenders Consult International is committed to strengthening our strategic partnership with the Nigeria Police as they prepare to provide adequate security during the 2027 General Elections across the country.”

He said the company’s position aligned with that of the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, on the Force’s importance to the electoral process.

Mr Philips quoted the police chief as saying, “Stability of the electoral process largely depends on the Police as the lead agency in internal democracy.”

Police to devise 2027 election security plan

According to a statement by the Force Public Relations Officer, Ani Iniedu, the conference will bring together senior police officers, policing experts and other relevant stakeholders to examine emerging electoral security challenges.

The discussions will cover intelligence-led policing, police-community partnerships, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, among other contemporary approaches to policing.

The conference will primarily involve officers of the rank of Commissioner of Police and above, with deliberations expected to produce practical measures to strengthen the Force’s capacity before, during, and after the 2027 elections.

The Police said the proposed strategies would focus on protecting voters, electoral personnel, candidates, electoral materials and the wider public.

Lenders Consult seeks broader support for the Police

Mr Philips said his organisation had secured sponsorship for every edition of the conference since it received approval to organise the event, describing the initiative as part of its contribution to supporting the police.

“Since inception, when we first got approval to organise the Conference and Retreat for Senior Police Officers, we have worked to secure sponsorship for every single edition. We consider this our contribution to support the selfless and patriotic work of the Nigeria Police. While commending the government’s efforts, we emphasise that Nigerians need to support the police in fulfilling their constitutional mandate to secure our society and maintain public order.”

He said the conference had evolved beyond a domestic gathering, with international participants now attending, and pledged to maintain its focus on contemporary policing approaches.

“Our vision for the Conference and Retreat has emerged as the Conference and Retreat continues to attract international participants. As the giant of Africa, Nigeria is leading the drive to adopt modern policing methods. We will continue to partner with the Nigerian Police authorities to ensure the event remains focused on delivering cutting-edge policing solutions.”

The Imo State Government will host the 2026 edition. Mr Philips expressed appreciation to Governor Hope Uzodimma for agreeing to host the conference for the third time.

“We also express our appreciation to the Governor of Imo State, His Excellency, Senator Hope Uzodimma CON, for agreeing to host this important event for the third time.”

The opening ceremony is scheduled for 10 a.m. on 21 September in Owerri.

The Police said the conference is part of efforts to strengthen strategic leadership, professionalism and operational preparedness ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Africa’s tech boom starts at home, By Sally Wentworth
World.content:
The continent is on the move: there are more than 70 Internet exchange points across Africa; Internet penetration across the continent has grown from less than 10 per cent in 2010 to over 38 per cent today; and Africa hosts some of the world’s best technical leadership, within a thriving ecosystem rooted in civil society.

21 years’ ago, if someone in Lagos wanted to send an email to someone in Abuja – a distance of about seven hundred and sixty kilometres – that email would first travel thousands of kilometres to Europe or North America before returning to Nigeria. African Internet traffic was taking a detour around the world to reach its neighbours.

This detour was expensive and slow – burdening local businesses with high transit costs and leaving African Internet users with sluggish and unreliable connections.

In response to that challenge, the African Peering and Interconnection Forum was born in 2010. The goal was simple: to solve this fundamental connectivity problem. Together, network operators, technical experts and policymakers have successfully created much of the infrastructure to keep local Internet traffic local.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Driven in no small part by Nigerian commitment, collaboration and energy, a significant amount of African Internet traffic now stays in Africa.

The continent is on the move: there are more than 70 Internet exchange points across Africa; Internet penetration across the continent has grown from less than 10 per cent in 2010 to over 38 per cent today; and Africa hosts some of the world’s best technical leadership, within a thriving ecosystem rooted in civil society.

…we must continue to build a strong, united African technical community. This is why the Forum in Kigali matters: It brings together everyone who powers our digital ecosystem – from data centre operators and fibre providers to hardware builders. We need to fortify these connections and develop this precious community, both within African countries and across borders.

Last year, the African Peering and Interconnection Forum met in Lagos to promote the development of national and cross-border interconnection. Next week, the momentum generated in Nigeria carries over directly to East-Central Africa, where the Forum convenes again in Kigali.

It comes at a crucial time. Africa is poised to harness the advantages of the global digital economy. But to realise this opportunity, three things are crucial.

First, we must continue to build a strong, united African technical community. This is why the Forum in Kigali matters: It brings together everyone who powers our digital ecosystem – from data centre operators and fibre providers to hardware builders. We need to fortify these connections and develop this precious community, both within African countries and across borders. Ultimately, this group of people is laying the groundwork for Africa’s future economic success.

Second, we must all stay true to the goal of ensuring that people everywhere have access to affordable, reliable, and resilient Internet. About a third of the world, including many people in Africa, still do not have access to the Internet. It does no good to create the infrastructure if people cannot afford to pay for the connectivity. According to the International Telecommunication Union, a smartphone can cost up to 40 per cent of the average monthly income in some countries. And mobile Internet is 14 times more expensive in Africa than in Europe. We must do what it takes to bring down these costs.

We must vigorously defend the Internet, leveraging the great power of the ecosystem that helped build the Internet in the first place – the nonprofits, researchers, standards bodies, civil society groups, and public-interest institutions who believe the network should work for everyone.

Finally, people everywhere must have an Internet experience that is safe, secure, and protects them online. We see threats show up in numerous ways – in phishing scams that steal identities, empty accounts, and compromise organisations with a single click. And, at another extreme, we see some governments use technology to target people beyond their borders through surveillance, intimidation, and physical threats.

In February, our Nigeria Chapter delivered one of its largest national campaigns to date, equipping over 2,500 Nigerians with vital skills in cybersecurity, online scam identification, and social media safety.

We must vigorously defend the Internet, leveraging the great power of the ecosystem that helped build the Internet in the first place – the nonprofits, researchers, standards bodies, civil society groups, and public-interest institutions who believe the network should work for everyone.

This unseen ‘global army for good’ draws much of its strength and inspiration from the work done by its network in Africa.

Africa’s 1.5 billion people deserve the full benefits of a truly connected continent. Powered by a young, dynamic population ready to lead the next wave of global innovation, Africa holds its digital future firmly in its own hands.

Sally Wentworth is the President and CEO of the Internet Society.

World.title: Airport operations will continue amid aviation unions’ strike – FAAN
World.content:
The Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) has assured passengers that airport operations will continue despite the ongoing industrial action by aviation unions.

FAAN, in a statement issued on Tuesday, said it was working with aviation agencies, airlines, security agencies and other stakeholders to minimise the impact of the industrial action and ensure that airport operations were not disrupted.

The authority said it was closely monitoring developments and remained committed to maintaining safe, secure and orderly operations at Nigeria’s airports.

The assurance comes after the industrial action disrupted flight operations earlier on Tuesday, with some airlines suspending or rescheduling services following restrictions on access to airport terminals in Lagos and Abuja.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Air Peace, Enugu Air, and United Nigeria Airlines announced operational disruptions, affecting some passengers with flights suspended or rescheduled.

The action followed grievances by aviation unions over the alleged restriction of workers’ freedom to unionise and the alleged non-remittance of the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge (TSC) collected from passengers.

The unions include the National Union of Air Transport Employees, Air Transport Services Senior Staff Association of Nigeria, and the National Association of Aircraft Pilots and Engineers, with the Nigeria Labour Congress and the Trade Union Congress backing the action.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) Director-General, Chris Najomo, urged the unions to suspend the industrial action pending the return of the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, who the regulator said was working to resolve the dispute.

The NCAA appealed to all parties to embrace dialogue and cooperation, expressing confidence that the matter would be resolved and that normal flight operations would be restored as soon as practicable. The regulator also assured passengers that flight safety had not been compromised and that it continued to discharge its statutory safety oversight responsibilities.

FAAN moves to minimise disruption

FAAN said it recognised the legitimate role of organised labour and supported efforts by Mr Keyamo and other stakeholders towards an amicable resolution of the dispute.

“In the interim, FAAN is working closely with the relevant aviation agencies, airlines, security agencies and other stakeholders to minimise the impact of the industrial action and ensure that airport operations are not disrupted,” the authority said.

The authority also said earlier operational challenges affecting the movement of some flights within the airside environment had been addressed through ongoing inter-agency coordination.

It said measures were being sustained to support the orderly continuation of flight operations.

“FAAN remains committed to ensuring that Nigeria’s airports remain safe, secure, functional and accessible to passengers and other airport users,” it said.

FAAN advised passengers to remain calm and maintain contact with their respective airlines for real-time information about their flights.

The authority said it remained confident that ongoing engagements under the minister’s leadership would lead to a speedy and mutually acceptable resolution of the dispute.

It also appreciated passengers for their understanding and patience amid the disruption.

The latest assurance comes as airlines continue to adjust their operations in response to the industrial action, with passengers advised to confirm their flight status with their respective airlines before travelling to the airport.

FAAN said its priority remained maintaining safe, secure and functional airports while efforts to resolve the dispute between the unions, airlines and government continue.

World.title: Afrilition: Why the African diaspora matters for attaining a future of excellence, By Adéwálé Àjàdí
World.content:
It is absolutely critical that the opportunity to build synergies and leverage capacity across the African world is forged towards as a future alternative to the exploitation, colonialism and brutal hegemony that is currently the global approach. The wider diaspora, coordinated with a continental focus of 54 countries, can become the engine for a future that is inclusive and interdependent. The next two generations of Africans need this systemic change, and Afrlition lays it out starkly and hopefully with clarity.

The African expression of identity and character in the 21st century has to be transcontinental. It has forever been so: in the DNA of human beings, both the mitochondrial and Y chromosomes go back to African origins. Afrilition, thankfully, offers Africanness based on self-identification, not genetic or even official origins. As a book or manifesto, the focus is the engagement of the willing or remnants, as there are many born on the continent who are white supremacist in orientation and mental model. This is nothing shocking, since their formal socialisation offers Africa as a foil to perceived European or Western excellence. Afrilition targets those who choose African identity worldwide.

Across the Americas, there are many remnants – especially in the Caribbean, South America, and North America — as there are in Europe and increasingly in Asia. Africans across the globe, whose understanding and experience vary but whose commitment is unwavering towards an authentic and disciplined Afrocentric tomorrow. Often we forget to highlight the newer African world that existed, even when the world formally ended the Trans-Atlantic enslavement and trade in African people — including the return of formerly enslaved people who fought on the side of the British against the US colonialists.

Many of these people ended up in Nova Scotia, Canada; especially in Halifax. They were joined by the Maroons, who had fought the British to a standstill in Jamaica, and some of them were then sent to Sierra Leone as part of an unprepared return effort, and possibly as a colonial prototype. There was the return or exile from Bahia of those alleged champions and participants of the Imale uprising to the West Coast of Africa in their multitudes and interspersed with returned formerly enslaved Cubans.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The stories of the African American support for Abyssinia in the First World War, including helping to form the Air Force then. Some fighting aside, for raising money to support the defence of Abyssinia. Many Caribbean people came out of enslavement only to be sent to West African outposts to replace failed European missionaries, many of whom were just left to survive and sometimes die without support. All these, as Edward Wilmot Blyden was crafting his pioneering work on the African Character as the first Pan-African ideal. He was from St Thomas in the Caribbean, but got educated in Freetown, Sierra Leone, the centre of African schooling. The critical input of the African Diaspora has continued for generations, in the face of popular scepticism on the relevance, importance, or even alleged complicity of Africans in the enslavement decimation of its population.

In the past few weeks, the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to integrate Caribbean economies into the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), laying the foundation to engage a 1.4 billion strong African market predicted to be soon over three billion! The African Union has formally recognised the Caribbean as the ‘Seventh Region’ of Africa, with a consultative seat in the AU.

One of the interesting stories that the Diaspora holds is that of literacy and how much the African world has engaged with the narrative that literacy, as defined in the Western education system, is critical to transformation. Two of the countries that are at the top of world literacy are the creations of the brutal trans-Atlantic enslavement of Africans — Cuba and Barbados — which both have 100 per cent literacy. The example of Barbados is quite distinct, as it is a majority African descendant country. At full emancipation in 1838, literacy was estimated to be below 10 per cent.

The brutality of the enslavement of Afro-Barbadians was quite notorious in a very diabolical system, as its exceptionally brutal approach was imported into the Southern United States of America to destroy the spirit of rebellion. The vast majority of the emancipated population were field labourers who were denied formal education to the point of death. Even at emancipation, the white plantation owners strongly and widely resisted widespread literacy. Today their descendants are number one in the world, along with others.

The African descendants of the US faced even more ongoing resistance from the first Reconstruction, and in the face of a more recalcitrant government and people, they built over 100 private universities and thousands of schools, fighting daily stereotypes that, in paradox, suggested they did not desire education and were somehow of less intelligence or capacity. These were all allegations that are not borne out by objective data or analysis. In later articles and exploration of Afrilition, we will look at this foundation and the often ignored incredible transformation of Nigerian literacy.

Afrilition offers the African world a route that will inspire our better angels and coordinate the pursuit of our dreams. It most certainly offers us the clarity of purpose to avoid the constant triggers that are distracting our productive energies and leverage our varied capabilities.

In the past few weeks, the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to integrate Caribbean economies into the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), laying the foundation to engage a 1.4 billion strong African market predicted to be soon over three billion! The African Union has formally recognised the Caribbean as the ‘Seventh Region’ of Africa, with a consultative seat in the AU. The African Diaspora, which includes everyone who affirms the African identity, is across the world.

It is absolutely critical that the opportunity to build synergies and leverage capacity across the African world is forged towards as a future alternative to the exploitation, colonialism and brutal hegemony that is currently the global approach. The wider diaspora, coordinated with a continental focus of 54 countries, can become the engine for a future that is inclusive and interdependent. The next two generations of Africans need this systemic change, and Afrlition lays it out starkly and hopefully with clarity.

Afrilition offers the African world a route that will inspire our better angels and coordinate the pursuit of our dreams. It most certainly offers us the clarity of purpose to avoid the constant triggers that are distracting our productive energies and leverage our varied capabilities. What the willing African Diaspora shows us in their rise from enslavement and progress towards a world-class presence, is that they are key partners in Afrilition’s promise of African excellence.

Adéwálé Àjàdí, a lawyer, creative consultant and leadership expert, is author of the newly released Afrilition: 21st Century African Manifesto, and Omoluwabi 2.0: A Code of Transformation in 21st Century Nigeria.

World.title: Army rescues nine more kidnap victims in Kogi
World.content:
Troops of the Nigerian Army have rescued nine more people kidnapped along the Ajaokuta-Itobe road in Ofu Local Government Area of Kogi State.

The Nigerian Army said in a post on its official social media handle that the victims were rescued after troops from Patrol Base Itobe pursued the kidnappers to the outskirts of Adumu in Dekina Local Government Area and engaged them in a gun battle.

The incident occurred after the kidnappers ambushed commuters along the route, taking several passengers into the surrounding bush.

When the troops arrived at the scene, they found an abandoned Toyota Hiace bus and Toyota Sienna vehicle, with the passengers missing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The soldiers subsequently followed the route taken by the fleeing kidnappers and made contact with them near Adumu.

During the ensuing gun battle, the troops overpowered the criminals, forcing them to abandon the captives and flee into the bush with suspected gunshot wounds.

The nine rescued victims comprised two elderly men, two elderly women, four other adult males and an infant.

They were evacuated to safety and handed over to the police, Itobe Area Command, for further necessary action and reunification with their families.

The army said troops were continuing to search the area for other possible victims and to apprehend the fleeing kidnappers.

The latest rescue is the second major rescue operation reported in the Ofu-Dekina axis within two days.

On Monday, the army said a joint team of soldiers, naval personnel, police officers, local vigilantes and hunters rescued 16 people abducted from the Ojuwo-Ajengo-Memarebo and Ojiwo-Itobe roads in Ofu Local Government Area.

The army said the 16 victims, comprising six adult males, six adult females and four children, were abandoned by their abductors after security forces engaged the criminals in a gun battle near Adumu.

One hunter was killed during that operation, while a police officer sustained injuries.

The latest incident occurred along the same general corridor where security agencies have intensified operations following repeated attacks on commuters.

On 9 August, the Kogi Police Command also reported that its operatives had rescued 15 kidnap victims after a gun battle with their abductors along the Itobe-Anyigba Highway in Ofu Local Government Area.

The police said the incident occurred around 4 p.m. between Ojuwo Ajengo and Mamerebo, which it identified as a kidnapping flashpoint.

The reports have highlighted the security challenge along the road network linking Ofu, Dekina and other parts of Kogi, where suspected kidnappers have repeatedly used surrounding forests to abduct travellers and evade security forces.

The army urged residents to continue providing credible information to security agencies to support operations against criminal groups in the area.

World.title: Trump secretly switched planes in Turkey over Iranian threat – Report
World.content:
US President Donald Trump’s trip from Turkey last month involved an elaborate ruse to evade a potential Iranian assassination threat.

Mr Trump, on his trip from Turkey, secretly swapped planes, switching from Air Force One, which the White House said he was aboard, to an alternate military aircraft.

The Washington Post reports that the US president was secretly transferred to a military aircraft with a catering truck after he boarded Air Force One.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the NATO summit in July, where he lashed out at Spain for declining the request to allow the US to use the joint military bases on its territory for operations against Iran.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This clandestine manoeuvre to change aircraft was attributed to the potential threat of an Iranian attack on the US leader.

Mr Trump’s trip from Ankara also came a day after the US began its 13-day military strikes on Iran.

He had earlier said he was Iran’s “number one target” during the summit in Ankara.

This paper reports that Iran’s supreme leader has also previously vowed revenge for the elimination of his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, who was killed by a US-Israeli joint strike in February.

Mr Trump had arrived in Turkey in a Boeing 747-8 jumbo jet donated by Qatar last year.

Hours before his departure on 8 July, Mr Trump announced he would leave Ankara aboard the old Air Force One rather than the new jet he had taken to the NATO summit.

Mr Trump said he was switching planes “for old time’s sake,” and that American forces stationed at a UK refuelling stop would be able to check out the new plane.

Footage captured by the press showed the president walking into the old Air Force One. CBS News reported that the footage also showed a catering truck visible on the other side of the jet.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also boarded the smaller military aircraft using external stairs to make the trip appear normal.

However, several minutes later, the truck pulled away and drove off to another US government plane, which the Washington Post reported was an Air Force C-32A.

The Post reported that Mr Trump then flew from Ankara to a refuelling stop in the United Kingdom on that military aircraft, unbeknownst to the journalists and White House officials who were travelling with him and were aboard Air Force One.

The BBC reports that the officials and press members believed they were on board the same aircraft as the president.

The New York Times and CBS News previously reported that intelligence officials flagged a specific threat of an attack on the president or his jet, which triggered additional precautions.

The journalists and some White House staff aboard Air Force One were told to keep their window shades shut. It was an unusual request.

Meanwhile, the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft has been called into question.

The US spent months retrofitting the $400 million Boeing 747-8 to prepare it for the president, according to the BBC.

In a statement to CBS News, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said, “The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the president’s travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall, which will take approximately one month to complete.”

World.title: Jos bishop disowns ex-employee implicated in alleged plot to kidnap his wife, another
World.content:
A former worker of the Anglican Diocese of Jos and two security operatives (names withheld) are helping the police over an alleged plot to kidnap the wives of the incumbent and immediate-past bishops, the diocese has revealed in a statement.

The diocese announced that security agencies had intervened before the suspects executed the plot.

It rejected reports portraying the principal suspect as a serving clergyman under the current Bishop of Jos, Ephraim Gongden.

The church said the suspect worked with the diocese but had been dismissed in 2022 by the former bishop and had never been reinstated by Mr Gongden.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The clarification was contained in a statement issued on Tuesday by the Registrar of the Anglican Diocese of Jos, Harrison Ugwuala.

The statement followed the circulation of reports and photographs on social media, which, according to the church, linked the suspect to the current diocesan administration and portrayed Mr Gongden as being connected to the alleged crime.

Suspect no longer with the Anglican Diocese

According to the diocese, the principal suspect presents himself as a clergyman and had previously worked within the diocese.

“He was NOT reinstated by the present Bishop of the Anglican Diocese of Jos,” the statement said.

“The individual is NOT a clergyman in the employment, authority, or jurisdiction of the Anglican Diocese of Jos,” it said.

“The Anglican Diocese of Jos has no working relationship whatsoever with this individual.”

Reports of the alleged kidnapping plot had identified the suspect as a clergyman, creating the impression that he was still affiliated with the Anglican Church.

The diocese said that the description was inaccurate and could wrongly associate the current church leadership with the alleged criminal activity.

Two bishops’ wives allegedly targeted

The alleged plot involved the wives of both bishops.

The diocese did not disclose how the alleged plot was uncovered or how the suspects were arrested.

It confirmed the kidnap attempt and commended the security agencies for their intervention.

The diocese also did not comment on the alleged roles of the two security operatives or disclose whether they were serving members of any particular security agency.

The matter is expected to be clarified as investigations by the security agencies progress.

Complaint over alleged cyber-bullying

The diocese said it had reported what it described as misinformation and cyber-bullying arising from the incident to relevant security and legal authorities.

It urged members of the church and the wider public to remain calm while investigations continue.

“Evil will not have the last word,” the church said.

The police have yet to disclose the names of the suspects.

World.title: CIBN urges banks to deploy fresh capital to MSMEs as Nigeria targets $1 trillion economy
World.content:
The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN) has called on Nigerian banks to deploy their recently raised capital towards financing micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), saying increased lending to the sector is critical to achieving stronger economic growth and Nigeria’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy.

The President and Chairman of the Council of the CIBN, Dele Alabi, made the call at the world press conference on the institute’s 19th Annual Banking and Finance Conference, scheduled for 8-9 September at the Congress Hall, Transcorp Hilton, Abuja.

The conference, themed “Building a Resilient Economy in an Era of Disruptions: Strategic Imperatives for the Banking and Financial Services Industry,” will bring together policymakers, regulators, financial institutions, development partners, technology innovators, academics and business leaders to deliberate on the future of the banking and financial services industry.

$1 trillion economy

Speaking during the question-and-answer session, Mr Alabi said the recent recapitalisation of banks had provided stronger buffers for their balance sheets. Still, he argued that the additional capital should now be deployed towards productive sectors of the economy rather than remaining concentrated in government securities and large corporate borrowers.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Capitalisation provides a buffer for shocks. It insulates banks’ balance sheets, but it does not stop there,” he said.

According to him, the banking landscape has changed significantly, particularly as declining interest rates and tighter borrowing margins among top-tier companies reduce the attractiveness of the traditional approach to deploying bank funds.

“Smart bankers, smart bank CEOs have to think of a more ingenious way of utilising this capital. Capital is not cheap. Capital is the most expensive source of funds. It’s more expensive than debt. Equity capital is more expensive than debt capital,” Mr Alabi said.

The CIBN president said banks should therefore look further down the economic ladder by increasing financing to MSMEs, which he described as critical drivers of economic growth, particularly in emerging markets.

Mr Alabi said the shift would also advance the CIBN’s impact vision, under which inclusion is one of the Institute’s key priorities.

He explained that financial inclusion should go beyond access to basic financial services and ensure that critical participants in the economy, particularly small businesses, have access to finance.

“MSMEs represent the critical growth source for the engine of the growth of the economy. Not only in Nigeria, globally for emerging markets, but MSMEs are also the ones that drive the economy,” he said.

He argued that increased SME financing would provide benefits beyond the banking industry by creating employment, improving business activity and supporting economic development.

The CIBN president also linked the banking industry’s role in supporting productive businesses to Nigeria’s ambition to expand its economy significantly.

He said the financial services sector would remain critical to achieving the government’s long-term economic objectives because of its role in mobilising savings and allocating capital to productive activities.

“It can be widely accepted, and there is empirical evidence to support the fact that an economy cannot grow to a $1 trillion mark without the support of the financial services sector,” Mr Alabi said.

Mr Alabi added that the banking industry was prepared to support the Federal Government in achieving the objective of significantly expanding the Nigerian economy.

“As a group in the financial services industry, we are really ready to support the federal government in achieving this objective of growing the economy of Nigeria significantly in the foreseeable future,” he added.

September Conference

Meanwhile, at the institute’s two-day conference in September, Mr Alabi described it as timely amid technological disruption, geopolitical uncertainties, evolving customer expectations, cybersecurity risks, and climate-related challenges confronting the global economy.

According to Mr Alabi, resilience has become a defining attribute of successful financial systems. At the same time, the conference is expected to provide a platform for policymakers, regulators, financial institutions, and technology innovators to deliberate on issues shaping the future of banking, finance and the broader economy.

He said the conference aligns with the strategic direction of his administration under the Institute’s IMPACT vision, which focuses on Inclusion, Membership Economy, Professionalism and Ethical Conduct, Accountability and Enhanced Financial Performance, Competencies and Skills Development, and Technology, Automation and Innovation.

Through the Conference, we seek to equip industry practitioners with forward-looking insights, strengthen institutional capabilities, and stimulate conversations that will accelerate innovation while reinforcing the professionalism and ethical standards upon which sustainable banking must be built. In doing so, we also advance our broader objective of positioning Nigeria’s banking profession to compete confidently on the global stage,” Mr Alabi said.

The CIBN president said more than 10,000 delegates from Nigeria and across the world are expected to participate in the conference.

He said the expected participants would include banking executives, regulators, government officials, development partners, academics, fintech leaders, investors and other stakeholders in the financial ecosystem.

Also speaking at the briefing, Moruf Oseni, Chairman of the Consultative Committee for the 19th Annual Banking and Finance Conference and Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Wema Bank Plc, who was represented by the Director, Southwest and Specialised Business, Wema Bank, said the conference would provide practical insights and actionable recommendations for strengthening institutions and positioning the Nigerian banking industry for sustained growth.

Mr Oseni said the conference would serve as a knowledge-sharing and solution-driven platform where stakeholders would exchange ideas, share experiences, and develop practical solutions to challenges affecting the financial services sector and the broader economy.

“As customary, the resolutions reached at the Conference will be documented and forwarded to relevant stakeholders and policymakers in the form of a communique, to support informed decision-making, policy formulation, and strategic alignment with global best practices,” Mr Oseni said.

The organisers said President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Vice President Kashim Shettima, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, and Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Olayemi Cardoso, are among the dignitaries expected at the event.

According to Mr Oseni, other participants will include leaders from government, regulatory institutions, development organisations and the private sector.

Conference sessions

The conference will feature three business sessions focused on major challenges and opportunities facing the financial services industry.

The first session, titled “Shaping the New Financial System for Nigeria’s Prosperity: The Role of Recapitalisation, AI and Geopolitical Dynamics,” will examine the implications of bank recapitalisation, artificial intelligence and geopolitical developments for Nigeria’s financial system.

The second session, a women-focused engagement, is titled “Inclusive Leadership, Stronger Systems: The Strategic Role of Women in Building Resilient Financial Ecosystems.”

The third session, titled “Navigating Cyber and Systemic Risks in the AI-Driven Future of Banking: Implications for Financial Stability and Business Resilience,” will focus on cybersecurity, systemic risks, financial stability and business resilience in an increasingly AI-driven banking environment.

Mr Oseni said the sessions were designed to address the most pressing issues facing the banking and financial services industry, while exploring strategies to strengthen financial stability, improve cybersecurity and risk management, and accelerate innovation to support sustainable economic growth.

World.title: Social Media, much more than fines, by Okoh Aihe
World.content:
Okoh Aihe

The hefty fine of $940m placed on Meta in New Mexico has retained Social Media in the centre of unwanted discourse and concerned efforts by jurisdictional authorities to deal with a menace that threatens today as well as the future of nations since the young ones are mostly affected in a world that seems to be laced with social poison. Although Social Media has become the nexus of human interactions, including work, communications, entertainment and other social relationships, the well-being of teens who virtually live on Social Medial platforms has been a cardinal concern to several nations. While some are taking proactive measures to restrict access, including placing age restrictions, quite a number have gone beyond the confines of what is possible from their end, to look at the activities of platform providers who are able to hide some sneaky details that could become harmful to young minds.

For instance, a jury ordered Meta to pay a $375m penalty for misleading the public after it found out that the organisation hid internal research about teen mental health harms and child safety risks. In what has now come to be known as Public Nuisance Ruling, a judge ordered Meta to shell out another $567m abatement fund, declaring the organisation’s negative impact on youth mental health a “public nuisance” in the level of industrial pollution. Nigeria has had its can of troubles with Meta. On July 19, 2024, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Council (FCCPC) issued a Final Order imposing a $220m administrative penalty on Meta, saying the company engaged in discriminatory and exploitative practices against Nigerians after a 38-month joint investigation with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). Not satisfied with the processes leading to the fine, Meta appealed. April 25, 2025, the Competition and Consumer Protection Tribunal delivered its judgment which affirmed that the FCCPC was painstaking in their investigations and awarded the $220m fine with an administrative penalty of $35,000.

Another $32.8m by NDPC on Meta was settled out of court. There have been other penalties however. For running unapproved and unvalidated s on its platforms, the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) imposed a fine of $37.5m on Meta. While TikTok got a wack of $5m also from NDPC for failure to take care of data concerning minors, and unauthorised cross-border data transfers. Meta, which is a behemoth in the Social Media ecosystem and, its sheer presence is intimidating and frustrating in most jurisdictions, is responsible for a number of Social Media and communication apps which include: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Threads. It is a lead player in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Virtual and Mixed Reality (Reality Labs). Meta has a suite of other operations and its activities cast a troubling shadow over human activities and corporate operations globally. Meta is nearly ubiquitous and its presence in the lives of young people has attracted a palpable harmful hue in some instances. There may be somebody somewhere who may be of the mind that some nations are hitting Meta for cash as the organisation seems to have a huge pile. For such persons, I will advise that they open a Facebook or Instagram account without stating preference of materials. The materials that will be dumped on you in the first few minutes are enough to wreck a matured mind, especially the one that has tried to remain on the good side of sanity.

There is a reason to worry about teen operations in the Social Media space as the New Mexico case has demonstrated and as the Nigerian Government also demonstrated from 2024 to 2025. It is not just about Meta but all the Social Media platforms which seem to prey on young minds to build business fortunes. While fines could be a reasonable deterrent to the Social Media big-heads like Meta, Google, ByteDance, Tencent and Microsoft, among others, some jurisdictions are embarking on alternative actions to clip the wings of the platform providers; put them away permanently from the lives of the young ones. But is that ever possible? Australia was the first country to take such a bold step, damning criticisms from the business community and other stray minds. The Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act is to protect youth mental health, stop exposure to dangerous online content, and reduce addictive screen habits. That decision didn’t come from the void. A commissioned research revealed that seven out of eight children aged 10 to 15 encountered disturbing materials in the Social Media while some youngsters faced widespread exposure to cyber bullying, eating disorder promotion, suicide instructions, and misogynistic or violent media. The Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, said the goal was to “give kids back their childhood and parents their peace of mind.”

To me, there couldn’t be a better response to what seems like the monstrosity of Social Media. The age of innocence is fast receding into a world that exceeds the descriptive confines of ordinary words. If the Australian parents couldn’t help themselves or even the family, the state has provided an answer that looked harsh on the surface but really deserving in the long run. Already, a number of nations are rallying to join Australia in what may turn out to be an elite group of the Social Media ban for teens. They include: Indonesia – implementing phased restrictions, France – which passed landmark legislation restricting social media access for children under 15, Malaysia – which approved and announced an under-16 account registration ban, and Brazil – which implemented the ECA Digital (Digital Statute for Children and Adolescent), a modified ban which enforces strict parental controls, design limits like infinite scroll and auto play for minors. So many other countries are revving up and at different levels of implementation. They include: the United Kingdom, Canada, Norway, Spain, Austria, Germany and the United States, just to list a few. For instance, in America, some states have passed laws requiring age checks or parental consent, while some federal lawmakers are debating algorithm and account restrictions. But polls show generally that roughly two-thirds of US adults are in support of strict minor access bans.

But Nigeria is not missing in the line of duty concerning Social Media. The harmful nature of Social Media to children is not fable but reality; clear and present danger. In Nigeria, the Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, alongside the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), conducted a survey which shows that 83 percent of surveyed Nigerians support some form of Social Media regulation for minors. There will always be critics and advocates who see things from a different perspective, far from the troubling content some of us see daily including those that lead very young people to take terrible decisions and actions that ruin their lives, destroy homes and wreck communities. They are advocates and want freedom without limits. But the responsibility of the state is to impose limits on human excesses including businesses that feed fat on the weaknesses of humanity and frailties of children to make profit that pose more danger than expected good to the society. One expects Nigeria to take stricter actions rather than fines which hardly diminish the wealth of these octopal Social Media platforms.

Let me state here that it remains a classic case of irony that the children whose Social Media status is being targeted in the various jurisdictions for their good, will do everything to sidestep whatever restrictions are being put in place. I do not expect them to understand why they need to be protected from themselves. It is the way of children. One day, they will understand. Like we did when we left the shelter of our parents only to find out that with all the good things in the world, there is much evil lurking in the dark and waiting for who to destroy. Social Media carries so much beauty but the beast is not so far awake.

World.title: A fight to the finish in Osun, by Rotimi Fasan
World.content:
In concluding my piece here two weeks ago on the Osun State governorship election that is scheduled to hold on Saturday this week, I had suggested that Governor Ademola Nurudeen Jackson Adeleke had successfully skirted around the political landmine represented by the federal might that could have been deployed against him to threaten his chances in the election by President Bola Tinubu. I was not being prematurely sanguine in reaching that conclusion about the attitude of President Bola Tinubu to the Osun State election. My conclusion was based on the pragmatism of Governor Ademola Adeleke’s decision to support the re-election bid of President Bola Tinubu against the backdrop of his thwarted attempt to decamp from the Peoples Democratic Party to the All Progressives Congress, from where he had decamped to the PDP in 2017.

President Bola Tinubu had up to the last couple of weeks assumed what would seem a neutral position in who becomes the next governor of the State of the Living Spring between the two leading contenders, the incumbent Ademola Adeleke, and the APC candidate, Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, aka AMBO, the former finance commissioner in the administration of Governor Gboyega Oyetola, the former chief of staff in the Rauf Aregbesola administration that I had in my earlier intervention on this subject erroneously referred to as a former deputy governor. While Abuja had since February 2025 seized Osun State local governments’ allocation following the disputed control of the local governments between the Oyetola-led APC and its successor PDP government at the LGA level, the decision had been portrayed as a local issue that would be determined on entirely legal principle between the APC and the PDP in Osun State. This was the case even if the fund seizure was at the behest of the Bola Tinubu-led federal government through the office of the Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Chief Lateef Fagbemi.
