On 10 August 2026, Chile’s government authorized Codelco to retain and reinvest 100% of its 2025 profits. About US$2.42 billion, a Codelco reinvestment decision that has sparked a political dispute.

The announcement, made in Valparaíso by Mining Minister Daniel Mas, was hailed by officials as historic. But former Economy Minister Nicolás Grau called it ‘valioso, pero no histórico.

Government Announcement

Mining Minister Daniel Mas announced on 10 August 2026 that the. Government would authorize Codelco to retain all its 2025 profits for reinvestment.

The amount cited publicly was about US$2.42 billion, according to multiple reports from Mining Weekly, Bloomberg, and others. Government-linked sources described the decision as the first time in Codelco’s.

History that all annual profits would be channeled back to the company. The previous benchmark was 30% of 2024 profits, a figure confirmed by several reports covering the announcement.

Mas framed the measure as a decisive step to strengthen the state-owned copper giant’s balance sheet and future investment capacity. The news was initially broke by Mining Weekly and later picked up by international financial media, including Bloomberg.

The minister made the statement in Valparaíso, the seat of Chile’s National Congress, though no legislative vote was mentioned in the reports. The executive branch’s authority to set Codelco’s dividend policy is rooted.

In its role as sole shareholder, according to background in the coverage.

Grau’s Counterclaim

Former Economy Minister Nicolás Grau, writing on X, praised the reinvestment but rejected the ‘historic’ label. He argued that roughly US$2.1 billion of the total came from a.

Value increase linked to Novandino, leaving about US$300 million as underlying capitalization. Grau also said that more than 85% of the announced US$2.4 billion was attributable to decisions under President Gabriel Boric.

His comments were reported by La Tercera, which highlighted the split between official rhetoric and technical accounting. The former minister’s analysis suggested that the Novandino-related adjustment was not new cash generation but a revaluation effect.

He stressed that the ‘historic’ framing obscured the modest scale of new capital injection relative to the reported total. Grau’s intervention added a layer of nuance to the public debate, as he had served in the Boric administration’s economic team.

His remarks were widely shared on social media and cited by La Tercera’s political section.

Political Reaction and State Ownership Debate

Media reports indicate opposition politicians interpreted the move as potentially opening a debate over state ownership of Codelco. These claims are political interpretation rather than official policy, according to the reports.

El Desconcierto and Biobío noted that some right-leaning lawmakers saw the reinvestment as a step toward fiscal flexibility, but not privatization. The state ownership question has been a recurring theme in Chilean politics, especially around Codelco’s funding needs.

Protests occurred on 10 August 2026 at Codelco’s corporate offices, with workers. From Chuquicamata marching in Santiago against privatization proposals, as reported by regional media.

The demonstration underscored labor concerns about the company’s long-term direction. Union leaders have historically opposed any structural change to Codelco’s public ownership, and the march reflected those anxieties.

The reports stressed that no official privatization plan had been presented by the government.

Codelco’s Financial Context

Codelco’s 2025 output was cited at 1.33 million tonnes in one report. Debt figures vary across coverage, with reports citing roughly US$24 billion.

US$25.1 billion, or US$25 billion, but these are not identical sourced constants. The reinvestment aims to shore up the company’s financial stability, according to a note from GuruFocus.

This decision comes as the miner faces structural challenges, as noted in Mineria en Linea. Codelco has been operating with high leverage due to massive investment projects, including the Chuquicamata underground conversion and new mine developments.

Financial reports have frequently flagged the company’s debt burden as a constraint on its capital expenditure plans. The company’s production has also faced headwinds from declining ore grades and operational setbacks, which have pressured cash flows in recent years.

The 1.33 million tonnes figure for 2025 reflects a slight recovery, according to the single report that cited it.

Broader Implications

The Codelco reinvestment decision could affect Chile’s fiscal revenues, as the state usually takes a share of profits. Analysts suggest the move may signal a longer-term strategy to bolster investment.

El Periodista’s coverage noted that the decision aligns with global trends of state-owned miners retaining earnings to modernize operations. The trade-off between immediate fiscal needs and long-term corporate health is a central tension in the debate.

The debate over the ‘historic’ nature of the decision reflects underlying political tensions. The government’s characterization is not an independently established fact, as Grau’s counterclaim shows.

Chile’s budget has relied on Codelco dividends as a significant revenue source. So the retention of 100% of 2025 profits could widen the fiscal gap.

However, advocates argue the reinvestment could increase future returns by enabling overdue projects.

Conclusion

On 10 August 2026, Chile authorized Codelco to retain and reinvest all. Its 2025 profits, a move that has drawn both praise and skepticism.

The exact financial impact remains subject to interpretation, with no direct official filing included in the verified reports. The Codelco reinvestment decision will likely continue to fuel discussion about the company’s financing model and its role in Chile’s economy.

Future reporting may clarify the underlying numbers, but as of now, the details remain contested.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s government authorize regarding Codelco’s 2025 profits?

On 10 August 2026, the government authorized Codelco to retain and reinvest 100% of its 2025 profits, about US$2.42 billion. This decision replaces the previous benchmark of 30% for 2024 profits.

Why did former Economy Minister Nicolás Grau call the decision ‘valioso, pero no histórico’?

Grau argued that roughly US$2.1 billion of the total came from a Novandino value uplift, leaving about US$300 million underlying. He also attributed over 85% of the amount to decisions under President Boric.

What is Codelco’s production level cited in reports?

One report cited Codelco’s 2025 output at 1.33 million tonnes. This figure is from a single source and may not reflect full official data.

What are the reported debt figures for Codelco?

Reports cite varying debt figures, roughly US$24 billion, US$25.1 billion, or US$25 billion. These are not identical sourced constants and should be checked against official filings.

Were there protests related to the announcement?

Yes, on 10 August 2026, workers from Chuquicamata marched in Santiago against privatization proposals. The protests occurred at Codelco’s corporate offices, as reported by regional media.

Sources: Mining Weekly, Bloomberg, La Tercera, El Desconcierto, Biobío, El Periodista, GuruFocus, Mineria en Linea

Chile · Mining

Key Facts — Forecast cut Cochilco lowered 2026 output to 5.27 million tonnes, down 2.6% from 2025.

— 2027 rebound Cochilco projects output of 5.55 million tonnes in 2027.

— Price outlook Cochilco raised its 2026 price forecast to US$5.95 per pound.

— June Escondida Output rose 45.8% year on year to 111,400 tonnes in June.

— June Codelco Output fell 4.8% year on year to 114,400 tonnes in June.

— June Collahuasi Production increased 1.7% year on year to 34,900 tonnes.

Cochilco projects a 2.6% decline in 2026 output before a rebound in 2027.

Chile’s state copper commission cut its 2026 copper output forecast to 5.27 million tonnes, according to Cochilco. The new projection represents a 2.6% decline from 2025 output levels.

Cochilco Revises Output Forecast Lower

Cochilco, Chile’s state copper commission, revised its 2026 output forecast to 5.27 million tonnes. This marks a 2.6% fall from the previous year’s production, the commission said.

The commission cited a weak first half of 2026 as the primary reason for the revision. Lower output at state-owned Codelco and BHP’s Escondida and Spence mines contributed to the shortfall.

The revised figure represents a significant adjustment from earlier projections. Reflecting the operational realities observed during the first six months of the year.

Analysts tracking the Chilean copper sector had anticipated a possible downgrade. But the magnitude of the cut underscores the severity of the challenges faced by major producers.

Chile remains the world’s largest copper producer, accounting for roughly a quarter of global mine supply. As such.

Any fluctuation in its output has direct implications for international copper prices and the broader supply-demand balance in the global metals market. The commission’s report, released after market hours, was closely watched by traders and industry stakeholders.

The data provides a benchmark for evaluating the performance of the country’s mining sector. Which is a critical driver of Chile’s economy and government revenues.

2027 Rebound Projected for Chilean Copper

Cochilco projects a rebound in 2027, with output expected to reach 5.55 million tonnes. This forecast was reported by Reuters and Investing.

com. The projected recovery suggests a stabilization of operations after the anticipated 2026 decline.

The anticipated uptick in 2027 is based on expectations of improved operational performance at existing mines. As well as the gradual ramp-up of new projects.

Industry observers note that the recovery will depend on resolving persistent issues such as ore grade decline, water scarcity, and labor disruptions. Cochilco’s projections for 2027 also imply a return to growth that could help alleviate concerns about a prolonged copper supply deficit.

The market has been grappling with tight supply conditions. Driven by strong demand from the energy transition sector and constrained mine output globally.

The 5.55 million tonne forecast for 2027 would represent an increase of approximately 5.3% compared to the 2026 projection. This growth trajectory, if realized, would position Chile to contribute significantly to meeting the rising global demand for copper.

Particularly for use in electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, and grid infrastructure.

Cochilco Raises 2026 Copper Price Forecast

In its report, Cochilco also raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound. The commission maintained its 2027 price forecast at US$5.10 per pound.

The revised price outlook reflects expectations of solid global demand, according to a summary from Biobío Chile. The upward revision in the price forecast for 2026 signals a bullish outlook for the metal in the near term.

Factors supporting higher prices include resilient demand from China, the world’s largest consumer of industrial metals. And supply constraints in other major producing regions such as Peru and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Cochilco’s price projections are closely monitored by the industry as they inform investment decisions and government budget planning. The commission’s forecasts are derived from a comprehensive analysis of macroeconomic indicators, mining project pipelines, and global inventory levels.

The sustained higher price environment is likely to provide some financial relief to Chilean miners. Even as they contend with escalating operational costs.

However. The gap between the 2026 and 2027 forecasts suggests that the commission expects a correction in prices as supply conditions potentially ease.

June Production Data Shows Mixed Results

Cochilco’s June 2026 production data shows mixed results among major miners. Escondida, operated by BHP, produced 111,400 metric tons, up 45.8% year on year.

Collahuasi produced 34,900 metric tons in June, a 1.7% increase year on year. In contrast, Codelco’s output fell 4.8% to 114,400 metric tons during the same month.

Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, demonstrated a robust recovery in June, driven by increased ore grades and improved processing plant performance. The significant year-on-year gain highlights the successful implementation of measures to boost operational stability in the face of environmental and social challenges.

Codelco, the state-owned mining giant, continues to face headwinds, including aging infrastructure and delays in key project execution. The company, which has seen its production decline over recent years.

Is in the midst of a strategic plan to modernize its operations and reverse the output slump. The mixed performance among the top producers underscores the divergent operational circumstances within the Chilean mining industry.

While some operations are benefiting from favorable geological conditions and management strategies, others are still grappling with structural inefficiencies and legacy issues.

How Officials Framed the Copper Output Forecast

Daniel Mas, Chile’s biministro de Economía y Minería, presented the projections, according to Biobío Chile. The figures came from Cochilco’s latest report.

Cochilco paired the lower volume outlook with a firmer price view. It raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound, holding 2027 at US$5.10 per pound.

Copper remains Chile’s leading export and a major source of state revenue. A higher price can cushion the fiscal impact of softer output.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Cochilco?

Cochilco is Chile’s state copper commission, known officially as the Comisión Chilena del Cobre. It provides official forecasts and operational data for the country’s copper mining industry.

Why did Cochilco cut the 2026 copper output forecast?

Cochilco cited a weak first half of 2026 for the forecast cut. Lower production at Codelco, Escondida, and Spence contributed to the decline.

What is the revised copper price forecast for 2026?

Cochilco raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound. The forecast for 2027 remains at US$5.10 per pound.

How did Codelco perform in June 2026?

Codelco produced 114,400 metric tons in June 2026. This represents a 4.8% decrease compared to the same month in the previous year.

— Project umbrella Americas Connect

— Named system Alisios

— Alisios route Dominican Republic, Panama, Chile

— Pacific segment redundant routes Chile-Panama, Panama to U.S. west coast

— Google Cloud regions Chile, Los Angeles, Las Vegas

— Other systems Canoa, OlaLuz

— Investment figure not disclosed

Google announced the Americas Connect cable expansion on August 11, 2026. A project that will add new subsea systems and redundant Pacific routes to strengthen digital infrastructure in the region.

Google’s Americas Connect Cable Will Link Chile, Panama and the Dominican Republic

Google’s Americas Connect cable will link Chile with Panama and the Dominican Republic. The company announced the plan on 11 August 2026.

It said the new infrastructure will add redundant Pacific routes and extend onward to the US west coast.

Google Unveils Americas Connect Cable Expansion

Google announced the Americas Connect cable expansion on August 11, 2026, via its official blog. The project includes three new subsea systems: Alisios, Canoa, and OlaLuz, according to the company.

The Alisios system will connect the Dominican Republic, Panama, and Chile, Google said. This marks a significant addition to the region’s digital infrastructure.

The announcement was made public through both English and Spanish blog posts, underscoring the company’s focus on Latin American markets. Google framed the project as a direct response to increasing demand for cloud.

Services and artificial intelligence workloads in the region, according to the blog text. The company described the Americas Connect project as a multi-system initiative designed to improve capacity and resilience across the Americas.

Google has not yet specified an operational timeline for the new systems. And no contractual partners for the cable construction were named in the announcement.

The blog posts emphasized that the expansion aligns with Google’s broader. Investment strategy in Latin America, which has included previous subsea cable projects.

The company also noted that the region’s growing digital economy requires more robust infrastructure. To support everything from streaming services to enterprise cloud adoption, according to the official text.

Google’s announcement highlighted that the new cables are part of a long-term commitment to expanding global. Network capacity, which now spans more than 30 subsea cables worldwide, as referenced in the company’s materials.

The company did not specify where the Americas Connect project fits within that global. Portfolio, but it described the initiative as one of several recent investments in the hemisphere.

Alisios Route and Redundancy Details

Google stated that the Pacific segment of Alisios will create redundant routes linking Chile with Panama. A third link will extend from Panama to the U.S. west coast.

These routes will provide connectivity to Google Cloud regions in Chile, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas, the company explained. The design aims to enhance network resilience.

The redundant routing is intended to ensure that network traffic can be rerouted. In case of a cable fault or disruption, a common concern for subsea infrastructure.

This approach mirrors similar redundancy strategies used in other Google subsea projects, which the company highlighted in its blog post. By connecting directly to Google Cloud regions, the cable is expected to reduce latency for customers using those data centers.

Google noted that this would benefit businesses relying on cloud-based applications, data analytics, and AI services. The blog post detailed that the Alisios system will use advanced fiber-optic technology.

Capable of carrying high volumes of data, although specific capacity figures were not provided. The company said the system is designed to be scalable to meet future demand, allowing for upgrades as traffic grows.

Google also emphasized that the redundant routes will improve the overall reliability of. Its network in the Americas, reducing the risk of single points of failure.

This is particularly important for financial services, healthcare, and government customers that require high availability, as the company noted.

Other Systems in the Americas Connect Cable Project

Beyond Alisios, Americas Connect includes two other systems: Canoa and OlaLuz. Google did not provide specific route details for these systems in its announcement.

The company framed Americas Connect as a broader effort to expand subsea capacity in the Americas. No investment figure was disclosed for the entire project.

The names Canoa and OlaLuz suggest a thematic connection to the ocean and the. Americas, but Google did not elaborate on the meaning or intended routes of these systems.

The lack of detail suggests that these systems may be in earlier stages of planning compared to Alisios. The announcement did not mention which vendors or construction partners would be involved in building the cables.

Google typically works with established subsea cable suppliers, but no such agreements were revealed in the official materials. The blog posts hinted that Canoa and OlaLuz would complement Alisios by expanding connectivity in.

Other parts of the region, but they did not mention specific landing stations or countries. This could mean that Google is still finalizing permits or partnerships for those systems, as industry analysts noted in subsequent commentary.

Google’s approach of grouping multiple systems under a single project name is consistent with its recent strategy of. Regional cable investments, such as the Firmina and Humboldt projects, though those were not mentioned in the announcement.

The company has not yet announced a timeline for when Canoa and OlaLuz will be operational.

Regional Impact and Context for the Americas Connect Cable

The announcement comes amid growing demand for data services in Latin America, driven by cloud adoption and artificial intelligence. Google’s expansion aims to meet this demand, according to the company.

Chile, Panama, and the Dominican Republic will become key nodes in Google’s network. This could improve connectivity for businesses and users in those countries.

The cable is expected to support the development of local digital economies. By providing high-capacity, low-latency links to major data hubs in the United States.

For Panama, the project aligns with its role as a regional logistics and connectivity hub, while for Chile it. Strengthens its position as a South American data center destination, according to regional telecom analysts cited in local media reports.

The Dominican Republic, a less common landing point for major subsea cables, stands to gain significantly from increased. International bandwidth, which could lower prices for internet services and improve access to cloud platforms, according to industry observers.

In Chile, the announcement was welcomed by local business groups, who see the cable as. A way to boost the country’s tech sector, as reported by The Clinic and ADN Radio.

These outlets noted that Chile already hosts Google Cloud regions, which could attract additional. Investment in data centers and related services, though they provided no additional specific data.

Panama’s La República highlighted the potential for the cable to enhance the country’s role. As a digital hub in Central America, given its existing infrastructure and strategic location.

The newspaper also pointed out that the project could create jobs during the construction phase, though no employment estimates were available. The project could also have implications for regional internet pricing, as more capacity.

Often leads to more competitive markets, according to telecom experts cited in local reports. However, these effects are likely to take years to materialize, as cable construction and landing station installation typically require significant time.

Attribution and Source Status

All details in this article are based solely on Google’s official announcements, including blog posts in English and Spanish. No independent confirmation from Chilean government sources was found in the provided materials.

The project is confirmed by Google, but it is a single-company source report. Further details may emerge as the project progresses.

Local media outlets, including The Clinic and ADN Radio in Chile and La República in Panama. Have reported on the announcement but have provided no additional specific information beyond the company’s press materials.

These reports did not include comments from regulatory authorities in the involved countries. Subsea cable projects typically require landing permits and environmental approvals from each country where they make landfall.

Google did not state whether such approvals have been obtained or are pending for the Americas Connect project. The company has a history of working with local governments and regulatory bodies on such approvals.

As seen in previous projects in the region, but the announcement did not reference any specific interactions. This suggests that the project may still be in early planning stages, with regulatory processes likely to follow.

Google’s blog posts did not provide contact information for further inquiries, and it. The company also did not clarify whether any of the three systems.

Would be operational before the others, leaving the project’s overall timeline uncertain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Americas Connect cable project?

Americas Connect is Google’s submarine-cable expansion announced on August 11, 2026, with three systems including Alisios, Canoa, and OlaLuz. It aims to enhance connectivity in the Americas.

Which countries does the Alisios system connect?

Alisios will connect the Dominican Republic, Panama, and Chile, according to Google. It includes redundant Pacific routes to the U.S. west coast.

What is the investment amount for Americas Connect?

Google did not disclose an investment figure for the project in its announcement. No local currency or US$ amount was provided.

How does this affect Google Cloud users in Chile?

The Alisios cable will provide connectivity to Google Cloud regions in Chile, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas, as stated by Google. This could improve service reliability and speed.

What other systems are part of Americas Connect?

In addition to Alisios, the project includes systems named Canoa and OlaLuz. Google did not provide route details for these systems.

Sources: Google Cloud Blog; Google Blog (Spanish); The Clinic; ADN Radio; La República

World.title: Tanzania’s CNG Push Gains a Homegrown Champion in Energo
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Tanzania · Energy

Key Facts —The company: Energo Tanzania is a Dar es Salaam-based CNG station operator and vehicle-conversion firm, registered in 2023. —The financing: It has signed deals with Equity Bank and CRDB Bank to finance CNG vehicle conversions. —The market: About 15,000 vehicles had been converted to run on compressed natural gas nationwide by February 2026. —The savings: CNG costs roughly half the price of petrol, with a conversion paying for itself in about 12 to 18 months. —The resource: Tanzania holds an estimated 57.54 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. —The mega-project: A long-stalled US$42 billion LNG export project is targeting a host-government agreement in 2026.

As Tanzania pushes drivers to swap petrol for cheaper natural gas, a local firm is betting that bank financing — not subsidies — will get the country there.

Tanzania wants its drivers off petrol and onto natural gas, and the maths is on the country’s side: it sits on enormous gas reserves, and compressed natural gas (CNG) costs about half what petrol does. The obstacle has always been the upfront cost of converting a car. A Dar es Salaam firm, Energo Tanzania, thinks it has found the missing piece — bank loans — and has signed financing deals with two of the country’s largest lenders to prove it.

Dar es Salaam, where Tanzania’s push toward compressed natural gas is centred. (Photo: Grahamcole, CC BY-SA 4.0)

A homegrown bet on gas

Energo Tanzania, registered in 2023, runs a CNG station at Mwenge in Dar es Salaam and converts petrol vehicles to run on gas. Its newest move is the important one: partnerships with Equity Bank and CRDB Bank to finance those conversions. That tackles the single biggest barrier to adoption — the lump-sum cost — by letting drivers spread it over a loan and repay it out of their fuel savings.

It is a notably market-based approach. Rather than waiting for the state to subsidise conversions, Energo is trying to make the switch bankable, which — if it works — is a far more scalable model for a country of tight household budgets.

Why drivers are switching

The appeal is simple economics. CNG costs roughly half the price of petrol in Tanzania, and a conversion — at roughly 2.6 million Tanzanian shillings (about US$1,000) — typically pays for itself in about 12 to 18 months of driving. After that, the savings are the driver’s to keep.

The trend is accelerating. About 15,000 vehicles had been converted nationwide by February 2026; a BBC report just over a year earlier, in January 2025, put the figure near 5,000. That is roughly a tripling in little more than a year — fast growth, even if the base is small against Tanzania’s total vehicle fleet, and still constrained by the number of filling stations.

The bigger gas picture

Tanzania’s CNG drive rests on a much larger resource. The country holds an estimated 57.54 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, and the state gas utility and private operators are rolling out more filling stations to match rising demand. The prize beyond transport is exports: a long-stalled US$42 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project, involving majors such as Shell and Equinor, is targeting a host-government agreement in 2026 that could finally move it forward.

For a country that spends heavily importing refined fuel, converting domestic drivers to domestic gas is a double win — cheaper transport for households and fewer dollars spent on petrol imports. Energo is a small player in that story, but its financing model may be the kind of practical fix that turns a national ambition into everyday reality.

It has signed deals with Equity Bank and CRDB Bank to finance conversions. How much does a CNG conversion cost and save? A conversion costs roughly 2.6 million Tanzanian shillings (about US$1,000) and typically pays for itself in 12 to 18 months, since CNG costs about half the price of petrol. How many vehicles have been converted? About 15,000 nationwide by February 2026, up from around 5,000 reported in January 2025 — roughly a tripling in a little over a year.

World.title: Kenya Moves to Release Mineral Royalty Payouts to 32 Counties
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · Mining

Key Facts —The sum: The government has moved to release Sh2.9 billion (about US$22.4 million) in mineral royalties held since 2016. —Beneficiaries: Thirty-two counties are due a share of the money. —The biggest: Kwale County, home to the former Base Titanium operation, is set to receive more than Sh1.38 billion (about US$10.7 million). —The split: New 2026 regulations set royalties at 70% national, 20% county and 10% host community — up from 2% for communities. —The trigger: The Mineral Royalty Sharing Regulations were gazetted on 29 January 2026 as Legal Notice 3 of 2026. —Still contested: Host communities want a larger share, paid to them directly.

After a decade in the Treasury’s vaults, royalty money owed to mining counties is finally moving — though communities say their cut is still too small.

For nearly ten years, royalties from Kenya’s mines piled up in a government account while the counties that host the mining waited. That is now changing: the government has moved to release Sh2.9 billion (about US$22.4 million) in mineral royalties, with 32 counties due a share. It is a long-delayed payout — and, for the communities living next to the pits, a partial one.

Kwale County on Kenya’s south coast is the largest beneficiary of the royalty release. (Photo: Nicholas maina, CC BY-SA 4.0)

A decade-long wait

The money has sat in the Consolidated Fund since 2016, collected from mining but never passed on, because the rules governing how to share it were not finalised. That changed when the Mineral Royalty Sharing Regulations were gazetted on 29 January 2026 as Legal Notice 3 of 2026, giving the Treasury the legal basis to move the funds to the 32 counties entitled to them.

Officials have framed the money as being unlocked and moving to the counties, rather than confirmed as landed in county accounts — a distinction worth keeping, given how long the process has already taken. Parliament’s committee on delegated legislation only endorsed the rules in April 2026.

Who gets what

Kwale County is the standout. Home to the mineral-sands operation formerly run by Base Titanium — whose Kenyan mining licence expired on 30 June 2026 — Kwale is set to receive more than Sh1.38 billion (about US$10.7 million), by far the largest single allocation. The remaining counties share the balance according to where mining took place.

The 2026 regulations fix the sharing formula at 70% for the national government, 20% for the county and 10% for the host community. That 10% community share is itself an increase — up from just 2% previously — and it is the part of the reform that host communities fought for.

A dispute that isn’t over

The formula has not been universally welcomed. Host communities and some members of Parliament have contested the split, arguing that 10% is too little and that the community share should be paid directly rather than routed through county governments they do not always trust. In short, releasing the money settles one grievance while sharpening another.

The episode matters beyond Kenya’s coast. Resource-rich counties across Africa are watching how revenue from mining is shared with the places that bear its costs. Kenya’s answer — a decade late, with a bigger-but-still-modest community cut — is the kind of compromise other governments will study.
