World.title: As Lake Maggiore runs low, Switzerland steps in as Italy faces growing water shortage
World.content:
Switzerland is opening the taps on Lake Lugano to help prop up Lake Maggiore. It is an emergency solution that, more than any set of figures, shows how sensitive the water situation in northern Italy has become: more water will be released from the Ceresio towards Ponte Tresa, with the aim of supporting the level of Lake Maggiore and, above all, guaranteeing supplies for the rice fields on the plain.

 

The discharge will rise from the current 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. The two lakes are connected and a significant share of the extra water will flow into Lake Maggiore.

The measure was discussed within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Consultation Body on the regulation of Lake Maggiore's levels and the management of water resources in its basin, convened urgently by the Ministry of the Environment on the basis of data from the Po River Basin Authority. The Italian delegation, made up of representatives of the ministry and the Lombardy and Piedmont regional authorities, accepted the Swiss proposal, which could be implemented as early as today.

Switzerland's help and the 'short blanket' problem

The decision taken by Canton Ticino is temporary and will be reassessed in the coming days, but its significance goes well beyond this one-off intervention. The underlying problem is that the available water is no longer sufficient to meet all needs at the same time.

On the one hand are the rice paddies of Piedmont and Lombardy, which at this stage of the season need large volumes of water. On the other are the water supply networks, rivers, lakes and ecosystems, all having to cope with ever lower flows.

It is the classic "short blanket" situation: if you increase the provision for one sector, you have to check what is left for the others. And when the overall resource shrinks, even a seemingly technical decision on how to regulate a lake becomes a strategic issue.

The case of Lake Maggiore is particularly telling. Back in July, the Po River Basin Authority was already warning that the lake was close to its minimum operating level, while agriculture in Piedmont was among the sectors under greatest strain.

The problem is not confined to irrigation water for farmland. In several parts of Italy, scarcity has also started to affect drinking water supplies.

Lake Maggiore, who is in charge?

Lake Maggiore is a transboundary basin, shared between Italy and Switzerland, but its regulation is not by joint management in the strict sense. The lake level is controlled by the Miorina dam at Sesto Calende, on Italian territory, and day-to-day management is entrusted to the Ticino Consortium.

Italy and Switzerland nevertheless discuss and coordinate decisions within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Body, because changes in the lake's level have consequences on both sides of the border.

The picture is even more complex because the Lake Lugano, also shared between the two countries, is linked to Lake Maggiore via the River Tresa: it is through this system that Switzerland is now providing support, by temporarily increasing flows from 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. So Lake Maggiore is regulated in Italy, but managing the water resource cannot be done without coordination with Switzerland.

Water tankers fill supply gaps

In Piedmont the situation is especially sensitive. By mid-July, the regional authorities reported that around 100 municipalities had already adopted ordinances to curb water use, above all in mountain areas and more isolated hamlets. In around 50 municipalities, with a combined population of 25,000, water tankers were already being used to top up reservoirs serving the water supply networks.

Figures from Arpa Piemonte painted an equally worrying picture: surface water resources were 37 per cent below the seasonal average, while in the first ten days of July many gauging stations were showing deficits of more than 40 per cent. At Isola Sant'Antonio, the Po had an average flow of just 62 cubic metres per second, 75 per cent below its historical reference value.

The heat has made matters worse. June 2026 in Piedmont was marked by temperatures far above the average, with a regional anomaly of about +3.5 °C. Higher temperatures increased evapotranspiration, causing soil and vegetation to lose water more quickly.

The crisis spreads across the Po basin

Piedmont, however, is not an isolated case. The problem affects a far wider area.

At the end of July, the permanent observatory on water use in the Po River District raised its assessment of water stress from "medium" to "high". Flows in the Po had progressively fallen to values below those typical of low-water conditions, and the drought index was indicating severe conditions across most monitored sections, with an "extreme" situation recorded at Cremona.

As early as 21 July, the Basin Authority was reporting problems not only for agriculture but also for water destined for households. In Lombardy, 50 municipalities were struggling, 17 of them supplied by tankers; in the Marche region there were 32. Critical situations were also reported in Veneto and Piedmont.

The picture also includes the Po Delta, where reduced river flows increase the risk of saltwater intrusion from the sea. When the river carries less freshwater, saltwater can push further inland, putting ecosystems, farming activities and water supply installations under strain.

Rice fields, drinking water, rivers: who comes first?

This is where the real issue emerges. The emergency is not just about "how much water there is", but how to distribute it when there is not enough.

Agriculture needs irrigation precisely during the hottest phases of the year. The rice fields of Piedmont and Lombardy are among the most exposed sectors, and Piedmont is one of the areas where the region has most clearly flagged the risk of crop losses linked to limited water availability.

But that same water is needed for water supply networks, to maintain minimum flows in rivers, for ecosystems, for certain industrial uses and, in some areas, for energy production.

Hence the growing need for increasingly sophisticated interventions and agreements between regions and countries. The release from Lake Lugano towards Lake Maggiore is a concrete example: a resource available in one basin is temporarily used to support another water system in difficulty.

And in the South the problem has not gone away

The water crisis, however, is not confined to the North. Conditions vary from region to region and not all of Italy faces the same situation at the same time, but vulnerability remains high, especially in Mediterranean areas and in regions that depend heavily on reservoirs.

ISPRA monitors the severity of water stress in the various Italian districts and defines the "high" scenario as a situation in which, despite preventive measures, the resource may not be sufficient to avoid damage to the system.

It is a snapshot that helps explain why water is becoming one of the most sensitive issues in land management: it is no longer enough to wait for rain. Reservoirs are needed, along with more efficient networks, reduced losses in water supply systems, reuse of treated wastewater, less wasteful irrigation systems and planning that takes account of increasingly variable water availability.

World.title: Russia frees former US Marine Robert Gilman after more than four years in prison
World.content:
Former United States Marine Robert Gilman is on his way back to the US after being freed from prison in Russia.

 

US President Donald Trump said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had approved Gilman's release on humanitarian grounds. Gilman is said to be in poor health and was reportedly being held in a psychiatric ward of a hospital.

Trump added that Moscow did not ask for a prisoner swap and that Gilman was set to land at Andrews Air Force Base near Washington, D.C on Tuesday evening.

"I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Gilman was arrested and detained in Russia in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer following an incident on a train in Voronezh, to the south of Moscow. He was sentenced to four and a half years in prison over the incident, but his sentence was later extended to 10 years after he was alleged to have attacked prison staff.

This photo provided by the family shows Robert Gilman and his sister, Lexie Hudson, in Lilburn, Ga., in 2019. Gilman family

According to US Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Gilman was diagnosed with a "dissociative stupor" around 50 days ago and became "non-responsive."

"He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia," he said.

In a post on X, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio thanked Russia for working with special envoy Steve Witkoff to secure Gilman's release, which he said would allow him "to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States."

But Rubio made it clear that while Washington was grateful for the "positive step," the Trump administration would still be pushing for the "immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans."

"The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he added.

Gilman was one of a number of Americans detained in Russia. Others being held in the country include Stephen Hubbard, who the State Department has labelled a "wrongful detainee," and Army Staff Sergeant Gordon Black.

World.title: Heatwaves in France: is thermal comfort becoming a new property criterion?
World.content:
The heat is now a factor even during property viewings. As heatwaves multiply this summer, French buyers are paying increasing attention to the thermal comfort of their future homes.

 

In Paris, a man in his thirties viewing a 14-square-metre studio flat under the eaves wonders: "Between May and September-October, will I be able to use this flat and still live comfortably? Or will I also have to flee like everyone else because it's too hot?".

Long seen as an asset, a property's orientation is now assessed according to how cool it helps keep a home, and in the capital a full southern exposure is losing its appeal.

"South-facing properties are no longer as much in demand as before, because people are realising now that when you're facing south, the sun beats down very hard," notes estate agent Joseph Denke from FredéLion.

At viewings, buyers now pay close attention to anything that can help keep a property cool: a through-layout, the possibility of airing the place at night, shutters, a terrace or shaded outdoor space. Some even factor in the presence of trees in the neighbourhood.

Air conditioning, a serious selling point

Air conditioning, until now rarely highlighted in listings, is itself becoming a real selling point. Owners no longer hesitate to promote this feature when putting their property on the market.

"In the past, owners did not necessarily think about highlighting the fact that they had shutters or air conditioning. Today, these are things that are very clearly pushed to the fore," says Laetitia Caron, managing director of PAP (Particulier à particulier).

The shift in buying criteria is weighing on the sale of certain properties. In the 5th arrondissement of Paris, a 66-square-metre flat, despite its large windows, is struggling to find a buyer. The property is not dual-aspect and air circulates poorly.

"People feel as if they are stifling in there, and there is no other option than to install air conditioning," says estate agent Christian Tokoto from Guy Hoquet.

One in three French people could consider moving house

According to the Leboncoin study "Canicule & Immobilier 2026", conducted among 1,752 respondents, 81% of French people say they feel discomfort linked to high temperatures in their homes, and one in three could consider moving because of heatwaves.

Heatwaves are no longer seen as isolated phenomena but are now being factored into residential choices, explains Sophie Bourg, marketing director at Leboncoin Immobilier.

"Coolness and summer comfort have become a property criterion in their own right," she says.

World.title: Solar eclipse: protective glasses in short supply across France
World.content:
In recent days, special eclipse glasses have been flying off the shelves in pharmacies and specialist shops in France. Faced with ever-rising demand, some outlets are already out of stock, while others are placing repeated orders in an effort to meet customers' needs.

 

"We didn't have any for three days, but this morning we received a good stock that should see us through to Wednesday evening," explains Aurélie Letavi, a pharmacy assistant, speaking to AFP.

Demand is so strong because these protective glasses are absolutely essential.

To watch the eclipse – that moment when the moon passes between the Earth and the sun – you must wear special glasses that comply with the ISO 12312-2 standard and carry the CE mark, which are vital to protect your eyes.

They are sold in pharmacies, at opticians and in certain specialist chains, with prices ranging from €1.50 to €4 per pair.

Related How to protect your eyes while watching the solar eclipse

Retinal burns and irreversible eye damage

Experts all agree: looking at this solar eclipse with the naked eye can have long-term consequences. In just a few seconds, the sun’s rays can burn the retina and cause irreversible eye damage.

"The danger lies in retinal burns. And because we tend to stare at the sun’s disc, the burn will occur at the level of the macula or just next to it. This area is very small, about 500 microns in diameter. It is where the cones and rods are located. This is the zone that allows you to see colours and to have sharp, detailed vision. So if you burn this area, you lose your precise vision. And that damage is irreversible," warns Dr Eric Frau, an ophthalmologist and retina specialist.

The last total solar eclipse visible in Europe dates back to August 1999. At the time, 1,024 people consulted a doctor after the eclipse in mainland France. Among them, around 300 showed a retinal abnormality, according to the Institut de veille sanitaire (InVS) (source in French). One hundred and forty-seven patients (14%) had retinal damage and 106 (10%) had damage to the cornea.

Watching the solar eclipse: a few rules to follow

In France, the Ministry for the Economy and the Ministry of Health have launched an awareness campaign (source in French) in the run-up to the event.

A few basic rules have been set out so that as many people as possible can enjoy the spectacle without taking unnecessary risks.

Before the eclipse -For buying protective glasses, opt for recognised retailers (opticians, specialist chains, pharmacies, reputable associations);-Check for the CE mark (glasses certified to ISO 12312-2) ;

-For buying protective glasses, opt for recognised retailers (opticians, specialist chains, pharmacies, reputable associations);-Check for the ; During the eclipse

-Do not look at the sun for more than three consecutive minutes;

-Take breaks between viewing periods to rest your eyes;-Pay particular attention to children, who are often less aware of the danger."It is not more dangerous for a child. It is simply that children are harder to keep under control. And if they do suffer a burn, they will be affected for the rest of their life," explains Dr Frau.

The solar eclipse on Wednesday 12 August will also be visible from northern Spain, Iceland and Greenland. It will then be necessary to wait until 2081 for such a spectacle to cross mainland France again.

World.title: Bulgaria lights up its Black Sea coast with digital art festival
World.content:
Installations and projection shows illuminated buildings, fields, beaches and the sea in Tsarevo, Varvara, Ahtopol and Sinemorets. Artists from eight countries took part, combining contemporary art with the coastal landscape after sunset. The programme ran each evening from 9 p.m. to midnight and was free to the public, with video mapping, interactive installations, lasers and large‑scale light compositions transforming familiar urban and natural sites into a continuous night‑time route.bnrnews+3

 

In Varvara, MP‑STUDIO projected its “Time Harvest” installation onto hay bales in the meadow above the beach, while Latvian artists Those Guys Lighting presented “Divine Geometry” and other works in the same open field, turning the grassy slope into a luminous landscape.

In Ahtopol, “Endless Currents” used the shoreline and the changing surface of the sea as a projection surface, with waves and tides becoming part of the moving image.bnrnews+1

Tsarevo hosted several works, including “Gifts of the Sea”, a video mapping show on the façade of the Georgi Kondolov Community Hall, and “The Moon”, the festival’s symbol, displayed as a light installation near the Ship Fountain. Mayor Marin Kirov said the first seaside edition had drawn a record number of visitors and that the 2026 event had been expanded with more locations and installations, including the new stop in Varvara.

In Sinemorets, the light installation “For Peace” by Slovak artist sedemminut was presented in a meadow overlooking the beach, featuring glowing human figures that appeared to run through the darkness in a message of peace, freedom and artistic expression.

Organisers said the festival aims to connect people with nature while attracting visitors interested in contemporary art, building on the success of the original LUNAR festival in Sofia, which has attracted hundreds of thousands of spectators since its launch in 2022.

World.title: Drone attack hits Libya's largest oil refinery
World.content:
Fires broke out at the Zawiya oil complex after explosives-laden drones struck the site. Hours later, fresh violence in Benghazi highlighted Libya's persistent security challenges.

Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Tuesday that fires at a fuel storage facility had been quickly brought under control after a drone attack.

The Zawiya oil complex west of Tripoli is home to the country's largest refinery and has been the scene of repeated armed clashes between warring factions fighting for primacy in the country since the fall of former strongman leader Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.

What happened in the drone attack on Libya's Zawiya oil refinery?

Monday's attack by an as yet undeclared actor targeted the Zawiya Oil Refining Company with explosives-laden drones, causing a tank containing about 4.5 million liters (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline to collapse after a fire.

Owner Brega Petroleum Marketing said the fires had been brought under control far faster than expected, with engineers telling Reuters news agency that damage had been limited, though operations were interrupted.

In a statement on X, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, Libya's internationally recognized prime minister, wrote that the crime of targeting civilian infrastructure would "not go unanswered."

Libya's UN-recognized Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah condemned the drone attack on the Zawiya oil complex, saying the targeting of civilian infrastructure would "not go unanswered" [FILE: October 13, 2022] Image: Yousef Murad/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The use of drones to strike vital facilities," wrote Dbeibah, "is not a random incident, but rather an organized and dangerous act that requires a firm response to protect the state and its institutions and prevent its recurrence."

Officials from Libya's electricity provider said two further drones targeted the Zawiya power plant early Tuesday morning, with one hitting the fire-fighting system but causing no damage.

What is the security situation in divided Libya?

Libya has remained divided since the 2011 uprising that toppled Gadhafi. Dbeibah's UN-recognized government is based in Tripoli in the west, while eastern and parts of southern Libya are controlled by the Libyan National Army (LNA), a military force led by commander Khalifa Haftar.

Amid those tensions, the LNA said its head of military intelligence, Fawzi al-Mansouri, was killed in a car bombing in Benghazi on Monday night.

According to the LNA, an explosive device attached to al-Mansouri's vehicle detonated as he left a mosque. Authorities have not identified those responsible.

Khalifa Haftar commands the Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls eastern Libya and parts of the country’s south [FILE: September 5, 2024] Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

Khaled Haftar, one of Khalifa Haftar's sons, said an investigation had been opened, adding that initial "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic," according to AFP news agency.

His office later said authorities had arrested a "terrorist cell" in Benghazi that was allegedly preparing acts of sabotage, but did not say whether it was linked to al-Mansouri's killing.

Al-Mansouri was a prominent military figure close to the Haftar family and had played a key role in fighting jihadist groups in eastern Libya.

How has Libya's political division affected oil production?

The split between dueling administrations has stunted the country's oil producing progress and kept foreign investors wary as rival sides clash over control of the oil revenues that pour into the Central Bank of Libya.

In 2024, a standoff over control of the bank slashed the country's oil exports by more than half.

Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, yet has struggled to return to pre-2011 production levels of 1.6 million barrels per day. June production hit 1.44 million barrels per day, the highest output levels since 2013, but far short of its target of 2 million barrels per day.

World.title: UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
World.content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power, millions of Afghan girls remain excluded from secondary education. UNESCO warns of lasting social and economic consequences.

Around 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan have been denied access to secondary education since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, UNESCO said Tuesday.

The figure has risen by about 200,000 since last year and could reach nearly four million by 2030 if the ban remains in place.

"Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are formally banned from secondary and higher education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO’s program coordinator for education in emergencies, said.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child’s education. It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

Why are Afghan girls banned from secondary schools and universities?

The Taliban seized power on August 15, 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew after two decades of war.

They initially assured the international community that women would be allowed to continue studying.

Taliban fighters took control of Afghanistan's presidential palace in Kabul after President Ashraf Ghani fled the country [FILE: August 15, 2021] Image: Zabi Karim/AP/picture alliance

But secondary schools were closed to girls in March 2022. Women were barred from universities in December that year.

The Taliban described both measures as temporary, but they remain in force.

The authorities say they respect women's rights in line with their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have also insisted the issue is a domestic matter.

Restrictions extend beyond education. Women face limits on employment and movement and have been barred from public parks, gyms and beauty salons.

The UN has described the broader system of restrictions as “gender apartheid.” Russia is the only country to formally recognize the Taliban administration.

What has happened to girls' education since the Taliban takeover?

UNESCO says the restrictions have reversed two decades of progress.

Girls had very limited access to schooling in 2001. By 2021, nearly one million were enrolled in secondary education.

"Afghanistan had made really major progress in expanding girls’ access to education," Jaberian said. "But unfortunately, much of that progress now has been completely reversed."

UNESCO has called for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls' and women's right to secondary and higher education.

The agency continues to support community-based education as well as literacy and skills programs, often held in community spaces or facilitators' homes.

How is the Taliban ban affecting Afghanistan's economy?

UNESCO estimates that excluding women from secondary and higher education could push around 600,000 women out of the workforce by 2066.

The restrictions could also cause cumulative income losses of 9.6 billion US dollars and increase the risk of early marriage.

The ban is also worsening a shortage of female teachers. UNESCO expects Afghanistan to face a deficit of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.

"Many teachers have left the country and those who were in the system are banned from continuing teaching," Jaberian said.

She added that restrictions on women teaching boys had left some pupils with unqualified male teachers or no teachers at all.

How severe is Afghanistan's wider education crisis?

Afghanistan's education system is facing problems far beyond the ban on girls.

More than two million primary school children are already out of school for other reasons. More than 90% of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, while the national literacy rate stands at 37%.

Many schools are overcrowded and poorly equipped. Nearly half lack water, sanitation or heating.

Natural disasters, including earthquakes and floods, have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, adding further pressure to the country's education system [FILE: November 5, 2025] Image: Sayed Hassib/REUTERS

The system is also under pressure from people returning to Afghanistan.

Three million people returned in 2025 alone, either voluntarily or forcibly. More than seven million have returned or been forced back since 2023.

Natural disasters have added to the crisis. Earthquakes, floods and other disasters have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, UNESCO said.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
World.content:
Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists have also said the outbreak may have started earlier than previously thought.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.

In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.

The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."

Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.

The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 4,000 cases To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.

The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.

The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.

'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister

Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.

Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.

"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.

Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.

Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.

On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."

WHO, DRC officials appeal to Congolese as Ebola spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?

Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.

Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.

Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.

Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.

Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.

Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.

Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

World.title: Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
World.content:
A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.

Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials.

US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia.

Who is Robert Gilman?

The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance.

He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years.

Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed.

What did Trump and the State Department say about the release?

Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place."

He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US.

The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard."

The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home."

Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release

Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today."

She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress."

"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"

According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison.

He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said.

Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him.

"It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today."

Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

World.title: Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?

One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps.

Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process.

According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP

PKK law divides society and parliament

Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament.

She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation.

The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives.

Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran. Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors.

According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy.

The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA

What's in the law?

The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this.

The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PKK views law as a mere first step

The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either.

They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying.

PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM

Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag.

Peace without democratization?

Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP.

For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu. He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption.

The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago.

Criticism of Erdogan's role

Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented.

This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center.

"Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK.

In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process.

Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hungary's parliament elects Orban critic as new president
World.content:
Hungary's parliament has overwhelmingly confirmed Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, to the largely ceremonial role of president. New Prime Minister Peter Magyar controversially removed his predecessor.

Hungary's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday.

The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections.

Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure.

Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban, whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role.

What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote?

The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber.

It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats.

Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment.

Baka took his oath of office and gave a short speech to the chamber after Tuesday's vote Image: Bernadett Szabo/REUTERS

Who is Andras Baka?

Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991.

He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court.

In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary.

Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance."

Baka, 73, spent almost 20 years at the European Court of Human Rights earlier in his career as a jurist Image: Zoltan Balogh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious?

Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era.

Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally.

Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end.

Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this "tyrannical" and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory.

Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president.

Magyar initially floated the notion of presidential star power, until chess phenom Judit Polgar said 'thanks, but no thanks' Image: Judit Polgar Foundation

What has Baka said about the process and his appointment?

Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat."

However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime.

"There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force."

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier
