Meanwhile, Undersecretary Angelo Tapales of the Council for the Welfare of Children mentioned that parenting in the digital age does not mean policing the technology or platforms kids use, but rather, “building trust, maintaining open communication, and creating an environment where teens feel safe to ask questions, seek guidance, and report concerns.”

TIKTOK TOWNHALL. Yves Gonzalez, Public Policy head for the Philippines at TikTok; Sheila Estabillo of Plan International Pilipinas; Amihan Abueva of Child Rights Coalition Asia; developmental and behavioral pediatrician Dr. Francis Dimalanta, veteran television host Kuya Kim Atienza; and Bea Bautista, communications lead for the Philippines, Thailand, and Malaysia at TikTok.

Addictive features, exploitative algorithms

The release of the family-focused digital guide in the Philippines comes amid a US appeals court’s ruling allowing thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet’s Google, ByteDance’s TikTok, and Snap Inc’s Snapchat over claims they designed their products to be addictive to young users.

These lawsuits, filed by US states, municipalities, school districts, and individuals, allege social media companies intentionally addicted young users.

This addiction, they say, contributed to a rise in depression, anxiety, and body-image issues — alongside a burgeoning mental health crisis — among US youth.

While the US ruling doesn’t directly impact the Philippines, it does beg the question: Why are social media companies like TikTok putting the onus of responsibly using social media on parents and individual users, rather than curbing the addictive features and algorithmic amplification of engagement-producing content themselves? – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Considers Baku-Supsa Oil Route Amid CPC Disruptions
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is considering additional oil export routes through Azerbaijan and Georgia, including Baku-Supsa, after temporary restrictions on crude intake by the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) in July prompted the diversion of some volumes to alternative routes.

During the restrictions, some Kazakh oil was redirected through the Aktau port, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline toward China and the Atyrau-Samara route, reported Kazinform, citing Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry spokesperson and adviser to the minister, Assel Serikpayeva.

“Additional export options under consideration include transportation through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan system, trans-Caspian shipments through Azerbaijan and the Baku-Supsa route,” she said.

Kazakhstan currently transports approximately 1.5 million tons of oil per year through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline. According to Serikpayeva, Azerbaijan has expressed readiness to increase its intake of Kazakh oil to 2.2 million tons annually.

Under the BTC route, Kazakh oil is shipped across the Caspian Sea from Aktau to Azerbaijan before entering the pipeline, which crosses Georgia and reaches the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in Türkiye.

Baku-Supsa provides another route through Azerbaijan and Georgia, reaching the Supsa terminal on Georgia’s Black Sea coast. Kazakhstan considered using the corridor in 2025, when the ministry said its potential use would depend on commercial terms, operational efficiency and agreements between the companies involved.

The search for additional capacity comes as Kazakhstan continues to rely heavily on CPC for crude exports. The pipeline carries oil from western Kazakhstan to a marine terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk. According to the ministry, 64.8 million tons of oil were exported through the route in 2025, out of Kazakhstan’s total oil exports of 78.7 million tons.

The route faced several disruptions in July. The Tengiz-Novorossiysk system resumed operations on July 8 following scheduled maintenance, while loading at the CPC marine terminal was later suspended after drone attacks on tankers on July 19 and 20.

Kazakhstan has previously redirected oil when CPC capacity was constrained. In December 2025, KazMunayGas rerouted approximately 300,000 tons through alternative channels, including shipments toward China and through the BTC system. Kazakhstan also exports oil through the Atyrau-Samara and Atasu-Alashankou pipelines and across the Caspian through the Aktau port.

World.title: Fewer Births, Better Chances: Kazakhstan Advances in Newborn Care
World.content:
ASTANA —Kazakhstan recorded nearly 150,000 births in the first half of 2026, down approximately 7% year on year, while neonatal mortality fell to 3.9 per 1,000 live births in 2025, the lowest rate in Central Asia, according to the Bureau of National Statistics and the Ministry of Healthcare.

The decline in births follows a broader downward trend in Kazakhstan’s total fertility rate, which measures the average number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. A demographic review by the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund (UAPF) shows the rate fell from 3.32 children per woman in 2021 to 3.06 in 2022 and 2.57 in 2025. The review described declining fertility as part of a broader global trend.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, 335,000 children were born in Kazakhstan in 2025, with boys accounting for 51.5% of births and girls for 48.5%. The country recorded 64,700 deaths from January through June, resulting in a natural population increase of 85,100 people.

While the birth rate has been declining, the ministry data show improving outcomes for newborns requiring specialized medical care, particularly premature babies and children born with severe congenital conditions.

Survival improves in complex neonatal cases

Over the past five years, mortality among newborns with severe congenital conditions has fallen more than threefold, from 22% to 6.9%, while postoperative survival has risen to 93%. Approximately 1,400 operations are performed on newborns each year, with specialized care available at perinatal centers across Kazakhstan.

The ministry attributes the improvement to the development of obstetric and neonatal services, the introduction of modern medical technologies and the work of specialized medical teams. Such treatment can be particularly demanding for premature babies, who require specialized preparation before surgery and intensive care afterward.

Neonatal and pediatric surgeon Zhenis Sakuov told The Astana Times that successful treatment depends on coordination across the entire medical team.

“Operating on newborns is difficult, and operating on premature babies is even more difficult because they require specialized preparation for surgery. (…) The operation itself is complex, the postoperative period is complex, and they need specialized care afterward. This is teamwork,” he said.

About 17,000 premature babies were born in Kazakhstan last year, with each receiving a range of specialized medical care, according to the ministry.

Earlier diagnosis expands treatment options

Advances in neonatal care increasingly begin before birth. Modern prenatal diagnostics can detect many congenital conditions between 18 and 20 weeks of pregnancy, allowing doctors to determine how the pregnancy and delivery should be managed and prepare a medical team to assist the child immediately after birth. When fetal abnormalities are identified, expectant mothers are referred to specialized perinatal centers, where doctors determine the timing and method of delivery and prepare a treatment plan in advance.

This approach has also expanded through one-day clinics at fetal health centers. According to the ministry, since their introduction in 2024, prenatal screening coverage has increased by 10%, detection of fetal abnormalities by 12%, and childhood disability has declined by 8%.

Treatment in some cases can now begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, or the intrauterine correction of certain fetal conditions, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

For some conditions, treatment can begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, which involves correcting certain fetal conditions in the womb, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

After birth, about one-third of newborn surgeries are now performed using minimally invasive techniques. Kazakhstan has also used extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) since 2022 to support patients in critical condition with severe respiratory failure.

“Intensive care is developing, as well as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, anesthesiology, and diagnostics. All of this significantly increases children’s chances of recovery and a good quality of life. And most importantly, many families today can receive high-tech medical care without leaving Kazakhstan,” Pediatric Cardiac Surgeon Tlektes Nashkenov told The Astana Times.

The ministry’s data show survival rates of 80% to 90% for children born with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, 85% to 95% for esophageal atresia and more than 90% for gastroschisis. Mortality among premature babies with necrotizing enterocolitis has fallen more than 2.5 times as diagnostic and surgical treatment has improved.

World.title: eGov GPT Expansion Advances Kazakhstan’s Digital Government Push
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand its AI-powered eGov GPT assistant so that services available through it account for approximately 70% of citizen requests by the end of 2026, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at an Aug. 11 government meeting.

The assistant currently provides access to 50 of the most frequently requested government services, which together account for approximately 30% of citizen requests. Since its launch in April, eGov GPT has been used more than 150,000 times. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministry and government agencies to increase the number of services available through the assistant to 150 by year-end.

The system allows users to describe their situation in ordinary text rather than search for the appropriate form, certificate or government agency. The assistant identifies the relevant service, prepares the required application and provides the result.

“eGov GPT should become a universal AI assistant for all matters involving interaction between the state and citizens,” said Madiyev.

The expansion is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into public services under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, approved in June.

“The year of digitalization and artificial intelligence marks the starting point for achieving this goal. In June, the nationwide Digital Qazaqstan strategy was approved, with the digitalization of public services identified as one of its key priorities,” said Bektenov.

The Aug. 11 meeting, chaired by Bektenov, focused on developing an AI-based public service ecosystem and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to accelerate digital transformation across the economy and public administration. The government is also seeking to make interactions with citizens and businesses increasingly digital and proactive.

Government agencies shift to QazTech

All government agencies are now working with QazTech, Kazakhstan’s unified platform for developing digital public services, while the migration of existing information systems continues under a two-year government plan. The platform has been operating since April 1 and is designed to shorten the development and launch of new digital services from several years to several weeks.

“This year, 39 systems are scheduled for migration, with work on 36 nearing completion. Another 25 systems are being migrated or developed outside the plan, while 10 systems are already fully operational on the platform. This means the work is progressing ahead of schedule, and today all government agencies are already working with QazTech,” said Madiyev.

A moratorium on creating new government information systems outside QazTech has also been in effect since the beginning of 2026. The move is intended to consolidate digital development within a common technological environment, reduce duplicative systems and establish shared standards across government agencies.

Kazakhstan launches eGov 3.0

The government has also launched eGov 3.0, an upgraded version of Kazakhstan’s electronic government portal built on the QazTech platform.

According to Madiyev, the previous eGov portal had reached the limits of its technological capacity, prompting the launch of eGov 3.0 on the QazTech platform. The upgraded portal simplifies services by removing unnecessary requirements and steps, with several of the most frequently requested services already available in the new format.

The modernization is aimed at simplifying access to public services while reducing pressure on government digital infrastructure as demand for online services continues to grow.

According to the latest United Nations e-government survey published in 2024, Kazakhstan ranks 24th among 193 countries in the E-Government Development Index, with a score of 0.9009, placing it in the UN’s “very high” e-government development group.

World.title: What Lies Behind Kazakhstan’s External Debt
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s external debt rose 7.5% year on year to $182.8 billion as of April 1. External liabilities of the government and state-controlled institutions jumped 39%, while private-sector debt remained virtually unchanged and intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment declined 5.5% in one year.

The National Bank defines external debt as debt obligations of Kazakhstan’s residents to nonresidents. The measure covers both public- and private-sector liabilities and includes debt regardless of the currency in which it is denominated.

From April 1, 2025 to April 1, 2026, gross external debt increased from $170 billion to $182.8 billion, up $12.8 billion, or 7.5%. Intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment fell from $92.5 billion to $87.4 billion, a decline of 5.5%. As of April, $19.2 billion was owed by banks, an increase from $14.6 billion a year earlier.

Public external debt rose from $14.7 to $18.9 billion in a year. The figures show that most of Kazakhstan’s external liabilities remain outside the government balance sheet. The latest National Bank data points to sovereign and state-controlled borrowers accounting for a growing share of the increase since the start of 2025.

Kazakhstan’s external debt is predominantly long term, with 87.1% carrying an original maturity of more than one year. According to the National Bank, that limits immediate liquidity pressure, but it does not remove longer-term risks, as refinancing and servicing costs can rise when global financial conditions tighten. Loans and borrowings from nonresidents make up 69.2% of the total, while debt securities held by foreign investors account for 13%.

By creditor jurisdiction, the Netherlands accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s external debt as of April 1, at approximately $40.8 billion, followed by the United Kingdom at $19.8 billion, Russia at $16.7 billion, China at $13.8 billion and the United States at $11 billion.

The figures should not be interpreted as direct bilateral government lending, however, as they include corporate and intercompany liabilities and may reflect the jurisdiction through which financial claims are held or administered. In the case of the Netherlands, data from the National Bank shows that of $41 billion total, government debt is only $21 million, banks – $11 million and intercompany debt – $38.23 billion, so roughly 94% of Kazakhstan’s debt recorded against the Netherlands is intercompany FDI debt.

External debt of Central Asian countries excluding Turkmenistan increased by 34.9% over the past five years, reaching nearly $290.8 billion in 2025, according to data from the CIS Statistical Committee and the Eurasian Economic Commission. Kazakhstan accounted for 62.5% of the total.

Despite having by far the largest external debt stock in Central Asia, Kazakhstan’s general government debt burden remains comparatively moderate. The International Monetary Fund data put general government gross debt at around 24.9% of GDP, compared with 27.5% in Uzbekistan and 37.4% in Kyrgyzstan.

The size of the debt, however, is only one measure of fiscal vulnerability. Economists also look at the cost of servicing it, its currency and maturity structure, and how borrowed funds are used. A country with a relatively high debt ratio can remain financially stable if investors retain confidence and debt-service costs remain manageable.

World.title: New Security Architecture: Future of Abraham Accords and  Emerging Strategic Landscape for Kazakhstan
World.content:
On July 22, Washington hosted an important hearing of the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa, titled “Building a New Regional Security Architecture: The Next Phase of the Abraham Accords.” American lawmakers, diplomats, and experts, including Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel, gathered at the Capitol to discuss the broader transformation of the framework under the auspices of the White House.

The hearing, together with the current geopolitical agenda, made one trend increasingly clear: the Abraham Accords have moved decisively beyond the confines of the Middle East and are evolving into a broader international coalition, with Kazakhstan assuming an important precedent-setting role.

The discussions in Congress provide valuable insight into the key trends likely to shape the future development of the Accords and help define Astana’s place within this emerging international architecture.

Resetting the framework: From a regional pact to a “Club of Power”

Speakers before Congress emphasized that the Abraham Accords have demonstrated their resilience even under the most difficult circumstances following the October 2023 crisis. The current strategy of the Donald Trump administration rests on two major pillars.

The U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal

The long-anticipated agreement on civilian nuclear cooperation between Washington and Riyadh has now been concluded. On July 22, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed an agreement establishing a framework for long-term cooperation on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

The significance of the agreement extends well beyond the energy sector. It represents an important element of the broader U.S. strategy to build a new regional architecture in which economic integration, advanced technology, energy cooperation, and security partnerships increasingly complement the normalization process associated with the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, the nuclear agreement should be viewed separately from the question of Saudi-Israeli normalization. While normalization remains an important strategic objective for Washington, the two tracks are not identical. The conclusion of the nuclear agreement nevertheless strengthens the broader strategic framework within which future regional arrangements may develop.

Expanding the Geographic Scope

The second pillar is the expansion of the Accords beyond their original Middle Eastern framework. Bringing influential states from outside the Arab world into the process demonstrates that the platform can serve as a broader mechanism for international cooperation, reinforcing its relevance, resilience, and legitimacy.

The Central Asian dimension: why do the Accords matter for Kazakhstan?

Kazakhstan’s formal accession to the Abraham Accords in November 2025 was highlighted at the congressional hearing as an important diplomatic precedent. Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel and a prominent American expert on the regional normalization process,emphasized in his testimony that Kazakhstan’s decision helped dispel skepticism about the framework and demonstrated its appeal beyond the Arab world, particularly among moderate Muslim-majority states.

Against the backdrop of today’s geopolitical turbulence, participation in the Accords offers Kazakhstan three strategic opportunities.

Diplomatic Balancing and Multi-Vector Foreign Policy

Positioned at the intersection of Russian and Chinese interests, Astana can use the platform as an additional instrument for diversifying its international partnerships. This allows Kazakhstan to broaden its network of strategic partners without entering into direct confrontation with regional powers or Tehran.

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s engagement with the Abraham Accords should not be interpreted as a departure from its traditional multi-vector foreign policy. Rather, it reflects an adaptation of that policy to a rapidly changing global environment.

Experts increasingly point to a shift from a largely passive model of maneuvering between major powers toward a more active model of pragmatic and sovereign balancing, in which foreign policy is increasingly anchored in the protection of national interests and economic security.

Under this approach, diversification is not an end in itself. It is a strategic instrument designed to preserve Kazakhstan’s sovereignty, expand its room for maneuver, reduce excessive dependence on any single external partner, and secure access to capital, technology, markets, and critical infrastructure.

Participation in the Abraham Accords therefore fits within the broader evolution of Kazakhstan’s foreign policy: not a rejection of multi-vector diplomacy, but its modernization in response to a more fragmented, competitive, and unpredictable international system.

A Direct Track to Washington

Demonstrating support for U.S.-backed peace and normalization initiatives can strengthen Kazakhstan’s standing in Washington. This is particularly important for safeguarding long-term American investment in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and critical minerals, while also helping the country navigate the risks created by global tariff disputes and geopolitical fragmentation.

For Astana, closer engagement with the United States through emerging regional frameworks can therefore serve both diplomatic and economic purposes. It creates an additional channel for dialogue with Washington while reinforcing Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of maintaining diversified external partnerships.

A Pragmatic Economic Foundation

The expanding framework can provide Astana with access to new sources of capital and technology. Wealthy Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, can contribute financing to major infrastructure and connectivity projects, while Israel offers advanced expertise in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, water management, agricultural technology, and resource efficiency.

For Kazakhstan, therefore, the value of the Accords lies not simply in diplomatic symbolism. Their importance increasingly rests on the possibility of connecting different pools of capital, technology, infrastructure, and political influence within a broader international framework.

At the same time, as experts at the hearing made clear, Kazakhstan retains its sovereign position. Participation in the Accords does not alter Astana’s commitment to a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or its support for humanitarian efforts. Kazakhstan can therefore participate in the emerging framework while maintaining its established position on the Palestinian issue.

The future of the Abraham Accords lies in their transformation from a primarily regional political and security framework into a broader international network encompassing security, connectivity, logistics, energy, investment, and technological cooperation under U.S. leadership.

The developments of 2026 suggest that this transformation is already underway. The expansion of the Accords beyond the Arab world, Kazakhstan’s participation, and the newly concluded U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement all point toward an emerging architecture that is considerably broader than the original normalization framework.

For Kazakhstan, the Abraham Accords are therefore becoming more than a symbolic diplomatic gesture. They represent an additional instrument of the country’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy — one that can help Astana diversify strategic partnerships, attract new investment and technology, deepen its engagement with Washington and the Gulf states, and strengthen its resilience amid growing geopolitical competition.

The strategic opportunity for Kazakhstan lies in turning its early participation into practical cooperation — transforming diplomatic positioning into tangible economic benefits, technological partnerships, and greater geopolitical resilience.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, an independent think tank based at Astana International University.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Sport’s Next Generation Won’t Choose Sides, Says Phygital International CEO
World.content:
ASTANA — Phygital sport’s future will depend on building lasting local ecosystems, developing a new generation of athletes skilled in both physical and digital competition, and establishing itself as a distinct international sporting movement, Phygital International CEO Daniel Merkley said in an exclusive interview with The Astana Times.

The Games of the Future 2026 powered by Samruk Kazyna (GOTF 2026) concluded in Astana on Aug. 9 after 12 days of competition across eight disciplines. With the event over, attention is turning to what comes next for phygital sport and how it can develop beyond major international tournaments.

Drawing on more than 20 years of experience working on Olympic and Paralympic events, Merkley said phygital sport has much to learn from established sporting institutions, particularly in governance, athlete-centered development and trust.

“One of the greatest lessons from the Olympic and Paralympic Movement is that lasting success comes from strong governance, clear values and a commitment to serving athletes first. Major sporting movements are built over decades through trust, consistency and collaboration, and those principles are just as relevant for phygital sport,” said Merkley.

“At the same time, we should not assume that because something has always been done a certain way, it is the right approach for a new generation,” he added.

For Merkley, strong governance – the rules, decision-making and accountability behind how a sport is organized – will be essential to building international credibility. However, he emphasized that the emerging movement should not simply reproduce the structures of traditional sport.

“Rather than asking young people to adapt to traditional sport, we can meet them where they already are. That means embracing technology, creating more engaging experiences for athletes and fans, and building a model that reflects how younger generations participate, compete and consume sport today,” said Merkley.

“Ultimately, our goal is not to replace traditional sport. It is to create something complementary that learns from its strengths while being confident enough to evolve in its own direction,” he said.

Astana’s legacy will be measured in years

According to Merkley, the most meaningful outcome for Kazakhstan will not be found in final scores, viewing figures or the scale of the event itself.

“The real measure of success won’t be what happens during these 12 days of competition. It will be what happens over the next three, five or even 10 years. If, in a few years’ time, Kazakhstan has more young people participating in phygital sport, a growing calendar of competitions, stronger links between sport, education and technology, and a new generation of athletes developing both physical and digital skills, then we’ll know these Games have created something that lasts,” he said.

He noted that impact could extend beyond organized competition, particularly as Kazakhstan places greater emphasis on innovation, technology and artificial intelligence. An event linking sport with digital skills can introduce young people to opportunities beyond the competition itself.

“If these Games encourage more young people to engage with technology, develop new skills and see opportunities at the intersection of sport and innovation, that is a powerful legacy in itself,” said Merkley.

He said Phygital International also works with host cities and partners to support continued development after the flagship event ends, to create local structures capable of sustaining participation and attracting future investment.

“Ultimately, success means leaving behind a stronger phygital ecosystem that continues to inspire young people, attract investment and create new opportunities long after the closing ceremony,” he said.

A new type of athlete

That distinction is also reflected in the demands placed on competitors themselves. In phygital sport, athletes compete across digital and physical stages within the same discipline. Depending on the format, a video game result can carry into football, basketball, combat sports or another physical contest, requiring competitors to perform effectively in both environments.

For Merkley, that combination is beginning to produce athletes who no longer fit neatly into the traditional distinction between gamers and sports competitors.

“What makes phygital athletes unique is that they cannot rely on excellence in just one environment. They have to combine elite gaming ability with high-level physical performance, while also being able to transition seamlessly between the two under competitive pressure. That demands technical skill, tactical intelligence, physical fitness, mental resilience and adaptability in equal measure,” said Merkley.

As competition develops, he expects training systems to become increasingly specialized around those combined demands. Coaches could prepare athletes for both stages, supported by sports science in areas such as physiology, biomechanics, psychology and performance analysis tailored specifically to phygital competition.

“I think we’re witnessing the emergence of a new type of athlete – one who develops physical excellence and digital mastery in parallel. (…) I also believe we’ll see more young athletes developing physical and digital skills side by side, rather than feeling they have to choose between traditional sport and gaming,” he said.

Becoming a category of its own

Phygital sport currently sits at the intersection of several industries, combining elements of international sport and entertainment while connecting traditional sports organizations, esports and technology companies.

“I don’t think those possibilities are mutually exclusive. Phygital sport has the potential to become a recognized international sporting movement while also delivering world-class entertainment and creating meaningful connections between traditional sport, esports and technology. What is important is that we do not define ourselves solely by comparison with existing models,” he said.

His long-term ambition is for the Games of the Future to become one of the world’s leading international sporting events while developing an identity that does not depend on resembling the Olympics, esports tournaments or any other existing model.

“Achieving that will require disciplined choices. We must protect sporting integrity, maintain high competitive standards and continue building trusted relationships with athletes, publishers, sports organizations, governments and commercial partners,” Merkley said.

“If we can balance those priorities, I believe phygital sport can become one of the defining sporting movements of the next generation,” he added.

World.title: Campaign Week in Review: Education Debate Leads Kazakhstan’s Election Race
World.content:
ASTANA – A nationally televised debate on education dominated Kazakhstan’s election campaign during the week of Aug. 3-9. Representatives of the country’s seven political parties outlined their visions for reforming the education system during the two-and-a-half-hour broadcast.

The debate consisted of four segments. Party representatives first presented their election platforms and questioned one another in an open discussion. The second segment focused on education reform, with candidates responding to questions submitted through social media. During the third round, audience members in the studio posed questions before candidates concluded the event with final appeals to voters.

Viewers also voted online for the most convincing performance. The Adilet party received 45.48% of the vote, followed by Auyl with 15.58% and Respublica with 12.01%. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) placed fourth with 9.71%, followed by the Aq Jol Democratic Party (7.98%), the People’s Party of Kazakhstan (6.96%) and Baytaq Green Party (1.58%). Another 0.7% of viewers said none of the participants had been convincing. A total of 73,628 people took part in the online poll.

Meanwhile, parties continued campaigning across the country, promoting proposals on rural development, healthcare, business support and social inclusion.

Adilet Party

The Adilet campaigned in the West Kazakhstan, Zhambyl, Kyzylorda and Kostanai regions, meeting residents in district centers as well as remote villages. The public raised concerns about road conditions, water supply, public utilities and social infrastructure. Poor mobile phone coverage and limited internet access in rural communities were recurring issues.

Party representatives said their election platform aims to provide high-quality internet access to at least 97% of Kazakhstan’s more than 6,000 rural settlements through a combination of mobile and fixed-line technologies.

Auyl Party

The Auyl party continued meetings with rural residents and agricultural workers, focusing on job creation, infrastructure development, modern farming technologies and measures to encourage young professionals to remain in rural areas.

The party representatives said all proposals and concerns raised during the meetings had been documented for follow-up.

Food security was another key topic. According to the party, ensuring national food security depends not only on agricultural production but also on efficient storage, processing, market access and affordable distribution. The representatives said strengthening every stage of the supply chain is essential for improving the country’s food security.

Aq Jol Democratic Party

The party met with manufacturing companies and logistics businesses in Almaty and the Almaty Region.

Discussions focused on creating a more favorable environment for domestic manufacturing and reducing administrative burdens on businesses. The party emphasized the need to encourage investment in the real economy and expand procurement opportunities for Kazakh producers.

The party also highlighted support for small and medium-sized businesses, job creation, investment attraction and the protection of workers’ rights.

Baytaq Green Party

In addition to its daily meetings with voters, the party organized an environmental cleanup campaign in Oskemen.

Volunteers collected household, construction and bulky waste in the Berezovaya Roshcha area along the Irtysh River and near the protected water zone in the Kulenovka neighborhood. Organizers said 140 bags of waste were removed.

Nationwide Social Democratic Party

The NSDP organized an Inclusive Forum in Astana, bringing together families, experts and advocates to discuss systemic challenges related to inclusion and the protection of the rights of people with disabilities.

The forum featured panel discussions, expert sessions and interactive workshops designed for children and adults with physical and intellectual disabilities. Participants also received free legal and social consultations from specialists and party representatives.

The event placed particular emphasis on early diagnosis, rehabilitation and social adaptation for children with autism spectrum disorder and other developmental disabilities. The NSDP also presented legislative proposals aimed at improving inclusion and quality of life.

People’s Party of Kazakhstan

Candidates from the party met with healthcare professionals in Semei to present its healthcare proposals.

The party pledged stronger labor protections for medical workers, including the creation of a national AI-powered medical quality control system designed to reduce bureaucracy and improve healthcare oversight. It also proposed higher salaries, particularly for rural doctors.

Other initiatives include targeted training programs based on regional workforce needs and expanded support for medical graduates through relocation grants, employer-provided housing and preferential mortgage programs.

For patients, the party proposed creating a unified digital health portal that would provide secure access to medical records, test results, prescriptions and treatment history. According to the party, the system would protect personal data, improve transparency and prevent unauthorized changes to medical records. It also called for greater transparency in the Social Health Insurance Fund and the expansion of palliative care services, particularly for children with severe illnesses.

Respublica Party

The Respublica held two major public forums in Shymkent on Aug. 7 and Almaty on Aug. 8, where party leaders reviewed the results of the party’s three and a half years of activity.

The party also focused its campaign on visits to manufacturing enterprises, arguing that industrial development is essential for creating jobs, increasing household incomes and strengthening the national economy.

According to the party, meetings at production facilities provide direct insight into workers’ concerns and help translate practical challenges into policy solutions.

Voting to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral parliament, is due on Aug. 23.

World.title: Kazakhstan Household Deposits Near $54 Billion as Savings Rise 20.9%
World.content:
ALMATY – Household deposits in Kazakhstan’s banks approached nearly 25 trillion tenge (US$53.5 billion) by the end of June 2026, increasing by 20.9% over the year, reported the Finprom financial and analytical agency. While the overall volume of savings continues to grow, deposits remain concentrated in several major cities and regions, revealing significant differences in household savings across the country.

Of the total, 84% or 21 trillion tenge (US$44.9 billion) was held in deposits denominated in the national currency, while foreign-currency deposits accounted for 16%. The predominance of tenge deposits is partly linked to the difference in returns. Interest rates on foreign-currency deposits cannot exceed 1%, while tenge deposits have offered comparatively high returns amid the elevated base rate.

Term deposits dominate

Term deposits accounted for 90% of all household deposits, making them by far the most common form of savings. Savings deposits represented 9.7%, while demand deposits accounted for only 0.05%. The concentration of deposits is particularly pronounced geographically.

The city of Almaty remained the country’s largest center for household savings, with 9.6 trillion tenge (US$20.5 billion) deposited in banks as of the end of June. This represented almost 40% of all household deposits in Kazakhstan. Astana followed with 3.2 trillion tenge (US$6.8 billion), while the Karagandy Region held 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3 billion). West Kazakhstan and Shymkent ranked fourth and fifth, with 1.2 trillion (US$2.6 billion) and 1.1 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion) respectively.

The smallest overall volumes of household deposits were recorded in the Ulytau, Almaty and Zhetisu Regions.

Savings gap exceeds 25 times

The regional differences become even more pronounced when deposits are calculated per resident. As of July 1, Kazakhstan had an average of 1.2 million tenge (US$2,570) in household deposits per person. However, only five regions exceeded the national average.

Almaty ranked first, with more than 4 million tenge (US$8,570) per resident, followed by Astana at 1.9 million tenge (US$4,070). West Kazakhstan recorded 1.7 million tenge (US$3,640) per resident, while the Karagandy and Kostanai Regions each recorded nearly 1.3 million tenge (US$2,780).

In contrast, average deposits per resident amounted to just 144,000 tenge (US$310) in the Almaty Region and 161,000 tenge (US$345) in the Turkistan Region.

Overall, 12 of Kazakhstan’s 20 regions had less than 1 million tenge (US$2,139) in deposits per resident. The difference between the highest and lowest regional figures therefore exceeded 25 times.

The figures point to a banking sector in which household savings are expanding, but where the ability to accumulate financial assets remains closely linked to regional economic conditions. The concentration of almost two-fifths of all household deposits in Almaty, alongside substantially lower savings in several regions, underscores the continuing gap between Kazakhstan’s major economic centers and less affluent areas.

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Mecca defence pact: new opportunities for South Caucasus and Azerbaijan
World.content:
Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

The joint defence agreement signed in Mecca on 7 August marks an important step towards shaping the region’s security architecture, establishing collective defence commitments between three leading Muslim-majority states.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement. It stipulates that an armed attack on one party will be treated as an attack on the other two.

The agreement also has the potential to influence the future security architecture of the South Caucasus.

Context of the Mecca joint defence agreement

The agreement builds on the Saudi-Pakistani Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed in September 2025. Official statements describe it as a purely defensive mechanism that does not target any country, including Iran, and has no religious or sectarian basis.

The parties stress that the agreement remains open to expansion. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that, technically, the deal resembles Article 5 of NATO. He said the parties plan to establish a ministerial-level committee and a secretariat based in Saudi Arabia. Erdogan’s vision includes expanding the initial three-member group and potentially involving other countries, including Egypt.

The strength of the agreement lies in the complementary advantages of its members. Turkey has NATO’s second-largest army and a developed defence industry, particularly in unmanned aerial vehicles. Saudi Arabia has significant financial resources, energy reserves and a unique symbolic status in the Muslim world. Pakistan, meanwhile, has a large and experienced military and is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons.

At the same time, the agreement does not establish an integrated command structure like NATO’s. The parties are still working out its operational details.

Prospects for expansion and the South Caucasus

In comments to Report on 9 August, Fidan said he did not rule out a similar joint defence agreement with South Caucasus countries.

He highlighted Turkey’s strategic role as a link between the Middle East, the Caucasus, the Mediterranean and Europe. He also said that completing the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia could open new security and economic opportunities. In the future, this could create conditions for a similar mechanism.

The statement does not amount to an official invitation. However, it opens the door to discussions about long-term scenarios for the region.

Azerbaijan’s position and the question of ties with Israel

Azerbaijan already maintains close relations with all three members of the agreement. The 2021 Shusha Declaration provides for mutual assistance with Turkey. Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan also cooperate in a trilateral format, including summits held in Lachin in 2025. Defence industry cooperation is expanding, while Saudi Arabia’s investment interest is growing. Although Baku remains outside the formal agreement, it maintains privileged relations with all three capitals.

Israel is a particularly important issue in this context. Some social media posts have claimed that Azerbaijan would supposedly “give up recognition of Israel” if it joined the agreement.

Azerbaijan’s strategic partnership with Israel – including arms supplies that played an important role in the 2020 war, oil exports, intelligence cooperation and technology – is long-standing and stable.

There is no evidence in official sources that the members of the Mecca agreement have demanded or made it a condition for Azerbaijan to sever ties with Israel or withdraw its recognition of the country. Baku has repeatedly shown that it can act as an unofficial mediator between Turkey and Israel. Formal participation in the agreement could test this balance, but Azerbaijan’s current policy prioritises a flexible, multi-vector foreign policy. Claims that “Azerbaijan must give up recognition of Israel to join the agreement” are not supported by specific evidence and remain rumours for now.

Benefits and risks in the context of multi-vector policy

Potential benefits for the South Caucasus and Azerbaijan include stronger collective deterrence, expanded defence industry and technological capabilities, an influx of Saudi capital, synergies with the Middle Corridor, stronger symbolic ties between Turkic and the broader Muslim worlds, and greater strategic autonomy amid questions surrounding external security guarantees.

Azerbaijan could benefit from closer ties among its partners without formally joining the agreement, while retaining room to manoeuvre in its relations with the West, Israel, Central Asia and other partners.

There are also risks. These include the possibility of becoming involved in Middle Eastern conflicts, including tensions involving Iran; potential pressure on relations with Israel and Azerbaijan’s image in the West; and possible negative effects on the peace process with Armenia or ties with Iran and Russia. Another risk is the new format’s institutional immaturity, particularly the absence of a clearly defined commitment to automatically deploy military forces.

Azerbaijan’s tradition of an independent, non-aligned foreign policy makes full membership in the agreement in the near future unlikely.

Likelihood of joining and the limits of Azerbaijan’s multi-vector policy

Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy does not mean automatically distancing itself from new regional initiatives. Baku seeks to balance the interests of its partners and tends to join new platforms when suitable opportunities arise. Azerbaijan’s decision in 2026 to join the Board of Peace, established at the initiative of US President Donald Trump, as a founding member provides a practical example of this approach. Close ties with Turkey and Pakistan, the trilateral Turkey-Azerbaijan-Pakistan format and the Shusha Declaration could also increase Baku’s interest in the Mecca format.

The 2026 war with Iran demonstrated the practical limits of this balance more clearly. Azerbaijan officially declared neutrality, repeatedly stressed its support for Iran’s sovereignty and said its territory was not being used against third countries. However, several international media outlets, including CNN, reported that Israeli special forces and intelligence structures were allegedly deployed on Azerbaijani territory during the war. Baku called these claims “completely unfounded”.

Several think tanks, including the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), described Azerbaijan’s position as a “carefully maintained balance between its officially declared neutrality and practical rapprochement”. Turkey’s decision not to take part in the war and its advice to Baku to maintain a cautious position also influenced this approach.

This dynamic takes on additional significance in the context of the Mecca agreement. The agreement’s principle that “an attack on one is an attack on all”, along with Saudi Arabia’s response to Iranian strikes during the war, shows how collective defence commitments can operate during periods of real tension. Azerbaijan’s deep strategic partnership with Israel, its allied relations with Turkey and Pakistan, and its expanding ties with Saudi Arabia have led some experts to believe that this rapprochement could increase Baku’s interest in formats similar to the Mecca agreement.

For Azerbaijan, therefore, the main question is not so much whether to join the agreement, but how to benefit from closer ties among its existing partners – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Israel – without taking on formal commitments. This is precisely the flexibility that its multi-vector policy provides.

Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

World.title: Number of Iranian companies in Georgia up 510% since 2012 – EPRC
World.content:
Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

According to data from the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the number of Iranian companies in Georgia has increased by around 510% since 2012, exceeding 12,800 by 2025–26.

EPRC says the figures are based on data from Geostat and the National Bank of Georgia. The organisation also notes that despite the sharp rise in the number of companies, foreign direct investment from Iran into Georgia has remained relatively low in recent years.

“Between 2013 and 2024, Iranian investment totalled $41 million. Although this is more than in the previous period, the amount per company remains quite small,” EPRC said.

According to the organisation, net foreign direct investment from Iran stood at -$0.65 million in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2025 put the figure at around $0.4 million.

EPRC estimates that Iran’s share of total foreign direct investment in Georgia remains small, according to official statistics.

The centre says Iranian companies registered in Georgia are mainly involved in small-scale trade, real estate transactions, services, construction, logistics and re-export.

“Most of this activity involves small and medium-sized businesses and is less connected to large-scale manufacturing, industrial or technology projects,” EPRC said.

The organisation notes that the activities of these companies have not led to significant job creation. It also says that dozens of companies are often registered at the same address.

According to EPRC, tourism has seen the most notable growth in economic activity linked to Iran. Between 2022 and 2024, tourism revenues from Iran rose from $91.1 million to $151.1 million, an increase of 65%. However, tourism revenues fell by 17.8% in 2025.

Why the number of Iranian companies is growing much faster than investment

The centre believes that the rapid increase in the number of companies, alongside relatively low levels of investment and official financial flows, raises questions about the true scale of their activities.

“Why is the number of Iranian companies growing much faster than investment and official financial inflows overall?” EPRC asks.

The organisation says that, given that a significant part of Iran’s financial sector operates under international sanctions, economic transactions may be taking place through alternative and potentially less transparent financial channels.

EPRC notes that if some economic activity takes place outside the traditional banking system or with limited transparency, this makes it harder for the state to effectively monitor financial flows. It also increases the risks of sanctions evasion and money laundering.

The centre also points to international practice, where such models are sometimes associated with nominal or so-called “paper” companies. These companies are officially registered, but their actual economic activity may be very limited.

According to EPRC, such companies are sometimes used for re-export operations, intermediary financial transactions, or to circumvent sanctions and regulatory requirements in different countries.

“When the number of companies grows rapidly but this is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in investment, production, exports or employment, questions arise about the real economic significance of their activities,” the organisation said.

EPRC also points to the visa-free regime between Georgia and the EU, saying that this could make the country more attractive to Iranian citizens and businesses.

According to the centre, the US sanctions imposed on Shelbit, a cryptocurrency company registered in Georgia and owned by an Iranian citizen, highlight the range of possible ways to circumvent sanctions.

EPRC believes that, in light of this case and the sharp increase in the number of companies opened in Georgia by Iranian citizens, the current figures should be viewed with additional risks in mind.

Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi’s new zoo ready to welcome visitors – video
World.content:
The new Tbilisi Zoo will open to visitors in August 2026. Construction began after the 2015 floods, and the zoo is opening in stages. Although work is still under way, visitors will soon be able to explore the new site.

One of Tbilisi Zoo’s best-known residents, Shani the lion cub, has already moved to the new zoo.

___________________________________________

___________________________________________

As David Taktakishvili, deputy director of Tbilisi Zoo, explains, the new zoo covers a large area, and the site is being developed in stages. Some animals have already been moved, but construction of the enclosures is still under way. Construction and infrastructure work will therefore continue after the zoo opens.

The zoo administration believes the public should already have the opportunity to see for themselves how a new-generation zoo is taking shape and how much better the animals will live in their new environment.

When the new zoo opens to visitors, the Caucasus biogeographical zone will be accessible to the public. In the future, the zoo will bring together spaces representing different regions of the world. At the first stage, however, the focus will be on the local flora and fauna of the Caucasus. Visitors will see red deer, bison, bears, wolves and other local species in this zone.

Construction of the African zone is currently under way. The new zoo will gradually add other biogeographical zones in the future.

In recent years, the role of zoos has also changed significantly. Today, one of their main functions is nature conservation, including protecting, breeding and caring for endangered species. The new, modern facility will serve this purpose and, in the future, will become not only a place for visitors but also an important wildlife conservation centre.

Admission prices will remain unchanged: free for children under three, 2 lari ($0.76) for children aged three to 12, and 4 lari ($1.53) for visitors aged 12 and over.

Some animals will remain at the old zoo, which will continue to operate as usual.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

New Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgian opposition figure investigated for ‘treason’ over comments on Abkhazia war
World.content:
Giorgi Baramidze case

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into comments by Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, about the war in Abkhazia. The case concerns charges of treason and actions that threaten state interests. The investigation focuses on his account of how prisoners of war were treated during the early stages of the conflict. Baramidze made the comments on a podcast, triggering a political backlash. The de facto authorities in Abkhazia have also reacted to his remarks.

What did Baramidze say?

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, discussed the war in Abkhazia on Yago Khvichia’s “Birth of Georgia” programme.

Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, he said:

“We did not take prisoners, we had no prisoners, we executed them.”

The remark prompted a strong reaction from government officials. Baramidze later clarified several times what he meant.

He said he was referring to the early stages of the war, when the Georgian side did not yet have a regular and organised army. Baramidze later explained that people enraged by the deaths of their relatives in the fighting did not take enemy fighters prisoner.

“At first, the situation was as follows: people who were enraged after their mothers, fathers and relatives had been killed did not take prisoners during the fighting but killed them instead. That is the bitter truth about the early stages of the war. I know this because I personally took part in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze said.

According to him, the situation later changed. The Georgian side began taking prisoners, which made exchanges possible. Baramidze said that around 200 Georgian prisoners were eventually brought home as a result.

“My deputy and I could not have exchanged 200 Georgian prisoners if our side had not taken any prisoners at all,” he added.

Baramidze also denies that his comments were directed against the Georgian army or the state as a whole. He insists that he was referring specifically to the situation during the early stages of the war.

At the same time, he stressed Russia’s responsibility, saying that the Russian Federation acted as an aggressor and occupier in the wars of 1992–93 and 2008.

Why has the prosecutor’s office opened an investigation?

Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office opened the investigation at the request of the State Service of Veterans Affairs.

According to the agency, prosecutors are investigating the case under Articles 307¹ and 318 of the Criminal Code. The first concerns treason, while the second covers actions that threaten Georgia’s state interests.

The prosecutor’s office said:

“The investigation began following an appeal from the State Service of Veterans Affairs concerning comments made by Giorgi Baramidze, a member of the United National Movement. The case concerns his remarks about the war in Abkhazia and the prisoner exchange process, which he made on Yago Khvichia’s programme ‘Birth of Georgia’.”

As part of the investigation, prosecutors also summoned Koba Kobaladze, head of the State Service of Veterans Affairs, for questioning.

Baramidze sees the investigation as political persecution.

“The prosecutor’s office has opened a case against me for ‘betraying Georgia’! I am not afraid of your persecution, let alone your dirty propaganda!” he wrote on social media.

What does the government say?

Members of the Georgian Dream party do not consider Baramidze’s remarks simply an unfortunate choice of words. They argue that such statements could harm Georgia’s national interests and international standing.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described Baramidze’s comments as morally unacceptable. As for the legal assessment, he said the relevant authorities should make that decision.

“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington.
