They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: Search for infant at Port MacDonnell wraps up, as police call for end to 'rubbish' chatter
World.content:
Police have stopped formal efforts to recover the body of an infant boy in SA's south east, more than a fortnight after a suspected murder-suicide.

The bodies of 36-year-old Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter Hazel were recovered on July 27, but three-month-old Lewis was not found.

Limestone Coast officer in charge Superintendent Trent Cox said efforts to recover the boy's body continued into last week.

"There were a group of seven water operations members that came down last Thursday," he said.

"They conducted three dives before weather stopped that effort. Unfortunately they were not able to find Lewis.

" The grim reality is he's unlikely now ever to be found. "

Emergency services conducted an extensive search for the missing child. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

While the formal ongoing search has ceased, Superintendent Cox said police would continue to respond to reports of washed-up material in the future.

"It doesn't mean that from time to time we won't get called to investigate something that may have washed up," he said.

"But for now there's no formal search effort underway."

SA Police confirmed in the aftermath of the incident that Ms Wright had attended the local station the day before she died. (Supplied)

Calls for end to 'rubbish' speculation

While the family has received support online, including a fundraiser that has raised more than $39,000, the tragedy has also been surrounded by speculation.

Superintendent Cox urged the community to think about the family and friends of the deceased before posting online.

"What I'd like to see happen is a lot of the community chatter that's going on social media to stop," he said.

"I know that's probably pie-in-the-sky thinking.

"Where there are gaps in information where the community's not in possession of [that information], for that to be filled with the rubbish that we're seeing out there helps nobody and it's incredibly distressing I'm sure for Mr Wright and the extended family."

Superintendent Trent Cox has called for an end to online speculation about the incident. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

He said a lot of the information being shared was "completely without basis".

"We understand the community's need for information, but we have a duty and a moral obligation and a legislative obligation to the coroner to ensure only factual information is provided," he said.

"The compilation of that information takes time."

Aerial, ground and water searches were undertaken to try and locate Lewis's body. (ABC News: Aiden McNamara)

Commissioner says actions being reviewed

SA Police have previously confirmed Ms Wright presented at the Mount Gambier police station the night before the incident.

SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens told ABC Radio Adelaide police were preparing a wide-reaching report for the coroner, but would not wait for the findings of an inquest to make changes if necessary.

"I'm not saying we did anything wrong, but we're obligated to make sure we got it right," he said.

"With all incidents like this we review our actions to ensure that we are doing what we can to best serve the community.

"Coronial inquests can take years … and if that's the case we don't want to wait that long before we make changes within South Australia Police, if there are changes that should be made."

SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens says the force will consider if it needs to make changes. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Superintendent Cox said the review was standard after any critical incident.

"We're in a constant state of review in SAPOL to see where we can improve, and if there are any gaps in our service delivery," he said.

Commissioner Stevens said it was challenging to balance welfare checks and mental health taskings with other core police work, due to a lack of resourcing.

"We know that we are the agency of last resort in a lot of cases," he said.

"We are trying to manage our workload in collaboration with those other emergency services to make sure that we're there to do our job when we need to to do it.

"We will always be there for the community; that's a non-negotiable for us."

World.title: Breaking: Bondi terror attack hero Ahmed Al Ahmed's charges dropped
World.content:
Police have dropped all charges against Bondi terror attack hero Ahmed Al Ahmed, after previously accusing him of assaulting and intimidating his father.

Mr Al Ahmed was charged in June over an incident said to have occurred at a home in Bankstown, south-west Sydney, in March.

The 44-year-old previously pleaded not guilty to domestic violence assault and intimidation.

On Wednesday, in Bankstown Local Court, the charges were withdrawn after an agreement was reached with the defence team for Mr Al Ahmed to adhere to an AVO for 12 months.

Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr told the court the AVO was being accepted without admissions.

A police prosecutor confirmed that arrangement, telling the judge the development came in light of the complainant's retracted statement.

The judge read out a list of conditions to Mr Al Ahmed, saying the AVO was a court order which governed his behaviour and the court expected it to be followed.

The order prohibits him from assaulting, threatening, stalking, harassing or intimidating his father, as well as damaging any of his property or harming any animal that belongs to him.

Mr Al Ahmed receiving a plaque earlier this year from Waverley Council Mayor Will Nemesh. (ABC News)

Mr Al Ahmed was shot multiple times during the Bondi shooting.

Videos from the scene showed him attempting to wrestle a rifle from one of the two gunmen, Sajid Akram.

Mr Al Ahmed was widely praised for his courage and was hailed a hero by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

A fundraiser to support him raised $2.6 million.

'Great outcome', Al Ahmed's lawyer says

Outside court following the decision, Mr Al Ahmed said he felt "successful".

"The law has been served," he said.

Mr Al Ahmed thanked his lawyer, and said his focus now was on recovering from his injuries sustained during the December attack.

"I'm still suffering from the pain ... so I'm still in the treatment, physiotherapy," he said.

"I still have a good team of doctors who look after me."

Mr Sakr said the past few weeks "had been a very stressful experience" for his client, and described the dropped charges as "a great outcome for all".

"My client was entitled to the presumption of innocence; that innocence is maintained," he said.

"His innocence is continued, his dignity is preserved and we look forward to what Mr Al Ahmed has next."

World.title: Zoo's attempted reunion between baby chimp and mum ends in aggression
World.content:
Keepers at a central Queensland zoo are continuing to hand-rear a baby chimpanzee after its mother showed aggression during an attempted reunion of the pair.

Chimp Sile gave birth to Cassie at the Rockhampton Zoo in June, then dropped her, breaking the baby chimp's leg.

Cassie then had to be hand-reared by keepers, until she was fully healed.

Rockhampton Zoo curator Blair Chapman nursing baby Cassie, who is receiving 24/7 care by keepers. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Zoo curator Blair Chapman said the team had facilitated interactions with Cassie and the rest of chimp troop through screens.

"We were seeing all the positive signs leading up to attempting the first introduction," Mr Chapman said.

However, things did not go as planned.

"Unfortunately, Sile did show aggression towards Cassie, so we did end up having to cease the introduction and pull Cassie back out," he said.

Keepers then separately attempted to introduce Cassie to another adult female, Mary, who gave birth to stillborn twins earlier this year.

"Because of the positive behaviour that we were seeing with Mary showing a lot of interest — Mary asking for the baby — we proceeded with that introduction," Mr Chapman said.

But Mary was also aggressive, resulting in minor injuries to Cassie.

"She did have some bruising on her belly … and a couple of bite wounds on her bottom."

Rockhampton Zoo staff have been sharing baby Cassie with the troop, with some positive reactions. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Next steps unclear

During the hand-rearing, keepers have been trying to mimic all interactions as closely as they can to chimpanzee behaviour.

"Hand-raising is an absolute last resort … Obviously, we needed to intervene because of the substantial break that she had to her femur," Mr Chapman said.

"[But] she's around the chimps all day, she vocalises to them, they vocalise to her.

"As soon as dad kicks off to do a display, she's there, it's pretty adorable to see."

Cassie is the daughter of 19-year-old alpha female Sile and the troop’s alpha male, Alon. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Cassie is fed a bottle roughly every three hours and keepers also wear a "chimp vest" when caring for her.

"They've been made in-house by one of our amazing keepers and her mum," Mr Chapman said.

"That's to encourage her to cling, because, obviously, chimpanzee females are quite hairy … so the infants usually cling to that hair, she's on that all the time."

Baby chimpanzee Cassie is being hand-reared by Rockhampton Zoo keepers. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Mr Chapman said the team was continuing to speak with primate experts from around the world to determine next steps.

"I won't speculate on anything at this stage, we are still having discussions," he said.

"Chimps are very unpredictable, so you never know how things are going to go.

"Aggression in chimps is known, and you go with what you're seeing … just, unfortunately, it's not the outcome we hoped for."

World.title: Commonwealth Bank home loan applications fall 15pc since May
World.content:
Australia's largest home lender, the Commonwealth Bank, has seen home loan applications tumble 15 per cent since May, after three interest rate hikes and the federal budget's tax changes.

CBA's net profit rose 7 per cent over the last financial year, to $10.9 billion.

But the major bank has seen the early impact of the housing market downturn, as other big banks report similar hits to home loans, with Westpac reporting a 20 per cent decline in applications since May, while NAB flagged a 15 per cent fall.

"Housing activity has softened from a high base," CBA chief executive Matt Comyn said in a statement this morning.

"Application volumes appear to have stabilised in recent weeks."

Budget changes, rate hikes hit home loans

The major lenders have highlighted the decline in the mortgage market since May, as the federal budget was handed down on May 12.

It contained sweeping changes to Australia's property taxation rules, including only allowing real estate investors to negatively gear newly built properties.

But investors who owned existing properties before the budget would still be able to deduct their net rental losses against their wages and other personal income.

Three of the big four banks have reported a significant drop in home loan applications. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

The government also abolished the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount and replaced it with a discount based on inflation indexation, as existed prior to September 1999.

It has also introduced a 30 per cent minimum tax rate on net capital gains, with the changes meaning people selling investment properties could face more tax under the new regime.

The May timing of the downturn also reflects three interest rate hikes delivered by the Reserve Bank — in February, March and May, the latter coming the week before the federal budget.

Profit climbs but CBA sees economy slowing

The Commonwealth Bank's net profit rose 7 per cent over the year, to $10.87 billion. Cash earnings closed in on $11 billion.

CBA shareholders will receive a final dividend of $2.70 per share, fully franked, taking the total payout for the year to $5.05, 4 per cent higher than last year.

Its net interest margin (NIM) was a little lower, down 0.03 percentage points compared to the previous financial year, to 2.05 per cent.

The NIM captures the difference between the interest that the bank earns from lending money and the interest it pays on deposits.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

Operating expenses rose 6 per cent to $13.76 billion, which the bank said was driven by "inflation, investment in technology, fraud scams and financial crime, partly offset by productivity initiatives and favourable foreign exchange".

Offering his economic outlook, Mr Comyn said "growth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing uneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity".

CBA said it grew at or above the level of the broader banking system across it five major divisions - home lending, business lending, consumer finance, household deposits and business deposits.

"It is the first time CBA has achieved this and the first time any major Australian bank has done so in the past 15 years," the bank said.

CBA said it is "the main financial institution for one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses".

World.title: Labor ministers stand by Albanese's 'melon' gesture, as AFP asked to step in
World.content:
Labor ministers have faced a fresh round of questions over their leader's hand gestures in front of his chest while describing a gift of two melons given to him by Japan's first female prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has resisted demands by the opposition to apologise to Ms Takaichi over what it deemed "foul-mouthed" and "classless" references to women on the Bush Deep podcast last month.

This morning, Liberal senator James Paterson said he had also asked for the Australian Federal Police to step in, after media outlets obtained an internal memo from the Japanese government that stated it would not formally seek to raise the issue.

The note sent by the Japanese government last month played down "sensationalised reporting" by Australian media and stated that Japan did not believe there was any "ill intention" in the prime minister's remarks.

But its appearance in newspapers this week reportedly caught Japanese officials by surprise.

Senator Paterson has accused the government of leaking the memo in an attempt to "exonerate the prime minister".

"[The shadow foreign affairs minister] and I have written to [the] AFP commissioner to ask that there be an investigation into the apparent unlawful disclosure of confidential correspondence from the government of Japan to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet," Senator Paterson said.

" This is a serious matter. It is important that our closest allies have confidence that when they share confidential correspondence with us that it will not find its way in the media. "

The AFP confirmed it had received the referral, but declined to comment further.

The government dismissed the Coalition's AFP referral as a "stunt".

Japan's PM gifted the Australian PM two crown melons, which can be worth hundreds of dollars each. (X: @takaichi_sanae)

'Maybe we should focus on the big issues': Plibersek

Mr Albanese's cabinet colleagues have continued to defend him as the drama drags into a new day, overshadowing the return of parliament from the winter break.

At a press conference this morning, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil expressed annoyance over what she dubbed "parlour games" while the government attempted to tackle cost-of-living concerns.

"The Liberals have completely lost the plot, referring podcast comments to the Australian Federal Police — I mean, how ridiculous," Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said.

"This is an absolute stunt and it was from the very beginning."

A frustrated Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek also dismissed questions over the remarks while at a press conference in Canberra.

"I have said all I am going to say on this on Monday. We are here talking about family and domestic violence, helping women out of homelessness. Maybe we should focus on the big issues," Ms Plibersek said.

Ms O'Neil said fresh demands by the Coalition for the AFP to intervene over leaked correspondence in relation to the melon remarks would be a waste of resources.

The pair refused to take further questions on the prime minister's gesture.

Senator Paterson said the government could not "have it both ways" on the leak of Japanese correspondence, noting Labor's "outrage" in 2022 when private text messages from French President Emmanuel Macron emerged in the media.

"In fact, in Senate estimates, Senator Katy Gallagher pursued the government about whether or not there had been an AFP referral into that apparent leaking of those messages," he said.

"It's either always wrong for confidential communications from our allies to find their way into the media, or it's wrong only when their political opponents do it."

Joyce says people would 'riot' if he made gesture

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said it had been "gruelling" to watch Ms Plibersek defend the prime minister's remarks.

"Turn the volume down and watch him … anybody would say, 'I think I know what you're talking about there, mate,'" Mr Joyce said.

"Go say the same thing about Tanya Plibersek or Penny Wong, sit them in front of you and see how you go, mate. You're going to get a slap in the face.

"Imagine if I had done that. It would be a riot."

Mr Joyce said Mr Albanese should accept he did the wrong thing, apologise, and communicate that to the Japanese prime minister.

Calls for PM to apologise to Takaichi The Australian prime minister has landed in hot water over a gesture involving two melons, which his office insists was not referring to his Japanese counterpart's body.

Mr Albanese sidestepped Coalition demands to apologise at Question Time yesterday, while also rejecting any suggestion he had made "foul-mouthed" remarks about women.

"I reject the assertion in the question," Mr Albanese said.

"Prime Minister Takaichi is a friend of Australia and a friend of mine. We're focused on working together to shape a free and open Indo-Pacific that's peaceful, stable and prosperous."

While Mr Albanese's remarks on the podcast have received significant attention domestically, they are yet to become a major issue in Japan.

Nobody in the Japanese government has publicly commented on the matter, which exploded after former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami criticised what he considered a quip about the Japanese prime minister's body.

Mr Yamagami had a fraught relationship with Labor when he was in Canberra, and was particularly angry when Foreign Minister Penny Wong urged him, while she was still in opposition, to pull back his public criticisms of China.

World.title: Biography of 'phenomenal' Australian photographer wins major $25,000 prize
World.content:
Sunbaker was undoubtedly Max Dupain's most famous photograph, but it was far from his favourite.

"He felt people made too much of it," his biographer, Helen Ennis, tells ABC Arts.

"He wished, in fact, that it didn't dominate the discussion about him. He found that quite confining and confronting.

"But photography is like that. Once a photographer has made his or her photographs, they're freed from their moorings, and the photographer doesn't have any claim on them any more.

" It's what the viewers make of them, and Sunbaker will keep resonating with different people over time. Its meaning is not fixed at all. "

The black and white photograph — taken in 1937 on a day Dupain spent at Culburra Beach with friends — depicts a man's head and shoulders as he lies in the sun.

"The composition is so monumental: that triangular shape on the sand," Ennis says.

Ennis dedicates a chapter to Sunbaker in her book, Max Dupain: A Portrait, which has won the 2026 National Biography Award, worth $25,000.

Ennis describes her book as a "joint effort", acknowledging the input from everyone from her sources to her publishers at Fourth Estate. (Supplied: HarperCollins Australia)

Also on the shortlist were Australian Gospel by Lech Blaine, Chameleon by Robert Dessaix, Groomed by Sonia Orchard, Gather Up Your World in One Long Breath by S Shakthidharan and Find Me at the Jaffa Gate: An encyclopaedia of a Palestinian family by Micaela Sahhar, which won the $5000 Michael Crouch Award for a Debut Work.

The judges described Ennis's book as "an exceptional example of the biographer's craft".

"Elegantly structured and written, it weaves Dupain's life and work into a complex whole … This biography of a major 20th-century Australian photographer will be read long into the 21st."

A complex character

Ennis, a photography curator, historian, critic and writer, came to the subject of Dupain after she published a biography of his first wife, modernist photographer Olive Cotton, in 2019.

"I realised he was such a powerful presence in her story, and I needed to turn my attention to him as well," she says.

Ennis saw that, despite his profile, Dupain had become a misunderstood figure.

"I felt that he'd become really one-dimensional and heroicised as a photographer," she says.

"He's so important in Australian culture, there's no doubt about that, but my whole motivation was to try and humanise him rather than heroicise him."

"I don't judge my subjects," Ennis says. "I want to understand them. I don't come with a fixed position."

Dupain had been typecast as an artist, thanks in part to the association of Sunbaker with ideas of Australian national identity and masculinity.

In her book, Ennis argues that the full emotional and artistic range of the photographer's work has been overlooked "because it does not align with the heroic vocabulary of modernism and conventional ideas of masculinity".

Moreover, she writes, the dominant view of Dupain is "of a hyper-masculine, quintessential Australian, an artist genius and anti-intellectual" — a description which she believes fails to recognise the contradictions of his character.

In her biography, Ennis presents a more nuanced picture of the man and the artist.

"What I was trying to do was bring in a lot of other work, lesser-known work, and put it in different contexts, so that his whole milieu looked much richer and much more complex," she says.

Ennis looks beyond Dupain as an individual and illustrates the networks of people who supported him, including the women in his life: his mother, Ena; Cotton; his second wife, Diana; and his studio manager, Jill White.

She writes: "Each of these women profoundly believed in his talent and unequivocally supported his desire to be an artist, sometimes to their own detriment."

Despite his assured veneer, Dupain's writings reveal a man plagued by self-doubt.

"Even though his photographs are so confident, they're so assertive, he personally struggled a lot with his emotions," Ennis says.

Olive Cotton at Culburra Beach, c 1938, by Dupain. Cotton and Dupain married in 1939 but separated two years later, in 1941. (Supplied: State Library of NSW)

Dupain was a teenager when he met Cotton, who came from a cultured background and shared his love of photography.

Ennis believes Cotton's early influence helps explain how a boy from a family with no great interest in the arts went on to become "such a phenomenal presence in our art and culture".

"In Australia, to become an artist is no easy thing," she says.

"It's not like he springs out of nowhere. He's got these people who know a lot about Australian life and art. They help him in his self-formation … so that he's able to function much more fully and realise his potential."

The biographer's craft

Ennis first met Dupain in the early 80s and went on to curate an exhibition of his work for the National Gallery of Australia in 1991.

While working on the NGA show, Ennis visited Dupain at his home.

"For me, when I'm working — this is my third biography — I really have to have a sense of the personal," she says.

"I'm interested in that whole art life nexus, so going to his home and sitting with him in his lounge room surrounded by things he loved, that really set me up."

Ennis recalls Dupain as "incredibly gracious" and open in his responses to her questions.

"It was only later when I realised he was actually only a few months away from death and he was being approached by so many people like me, curators and journalists and historians, and yet he gave us all this time."

New show pairs two giants of 20th-century photography Surrealist photographer Man Ray revolutionised 20th-century visual culture. In Australia, photographer Max Dupain was exploring similar territory.

Ennis says that while he was polite and welcoming, his character was reserved. "I felt that he wasn't someone who would be easy to know."

As a biographer, Ennis is more interested in exploring her subject's creative life than uncovering their secrets.

"Janet Malcolm, an American writer, speaks very famously about biographers riffling through the drawers in the bedroom of your subject," she says.

"I'm OK about leaving some drawers closed. I might gesture towards some of those private things, but … I only go as far as I feel is necessary to illuminate and elucidate the work. And I never want the subject to be abject."

The biographer never assumes she will come to know everything about her subject.

"I'm able to leave gaps," she says.

"The reader can … make their own judgements or their own assessments: Is this someone that I would have liked as a man? Is this someone whose photographs are of interest to me? How are they relevant now?

"I don't want to have answered everything. I hope that the way I write does something more dynamic with history and the past."

At home in the archives

Ennis spent five years working on the book. Unusually in a digital age, she writes and edits in longhand.

"I don't put things on the computer till later," she says.

"Writing in longhand allows me a lot more fluidity and experimentation rather than getting into a fixed position."

She spent a great deal of time trawling through the archives at the NGA and the State Library of New South Wales, which she describes as "fundamental" resources.

" I couldn't be happier than when I'm burrowing into archives of letters and papers and photographs. It's work I absolutely adore. "

Ennis also carried out field work, visiting sites Dupain had photographed, and drew on oral histories.

"I had his voice in my ear a lot of the time, which was really important," she says.

"His funny, kind of shy laugh, not a really open laugh — things like that helped me personalise him."

Dupain was interested in architecture from his mid-teens. Pictured: Sydney Opera House during construction, November 1965. (Supplied: State Library of NSW)

Accessing a subject's inner life is one of the most difficult aspects of writing a biography.

"If someone doesn't leave behind letters and diaries and people aren't prepared to give you their confidences and insights, it's really hard to bring a subject to life," Ennis says.

"With Dupain, because he gave a lot of interviews in his last years, I did get a sense of what he was struggling with … There was enough on the record that I think I could create a kind of mosaic."

Crafting a life into a narrative is another challenge.

"Making the whole life interesting is difficult, not just having that trajectory where you get a lot of activity and energy from someone's younger life and then a tailing off at the end," Ennis says.

"I really wanted to allow Dupain all his failings and experimentation but all his successes as well and it was important to me to deal with his later work in a really respectful way."

A landmark retrospective

The win comes as a major retrospective of the photographer's work, Definitive Dupain, is set to open the State Library of NSW on August 24.

The exhibition draws on Dupain's enormous archive of 250,000 negatives held at the State Library of NSW.

As a fulltime photographer, Dupain produced a large volume of commercial work, about some of which he was critical.

"Later on, he said he really didn't like doing the fashion photography and celebrity portraiture," Ennis says.

"What he liked was something more authentic. He didn't want fakery. He wanted a real connection with his subject matter — that's why landscape was important to him."

Ennis considers Dupain's "lyrical, intimate, tender" work that has been historically overlooked. Pictured: MacDonnell Ranges, Northern Territory, c 1942. (Supplied: State Library of NSW)

His documentary photography was another source of pride.

One of his favourite works was Meat Queue, 1946, "a very beautifully constructed photograph" showing a line of black-clad housewives lining up in a butcher's shop when rationing was still in place after World War II.

"[A woman] breaks into the queue and there's this little ripple of energy," Ennis says.

"He loved that; he loved the way that chance energised the photograph; it animated it for him. He was always looking for those sorts of things, where something outside his control gave the photograph some energy."

He was also drawn to architecture photography, which he described as his "long suit".

"That was what he wanted to be known for, and yet he hasn't been known for architecture as much as you would think," Ennis says.

"He definitely wanted to gesture to things other than Sunbaker as being important in his career."

Max Dupain: A Portrait is published by Fourth Estate.

Definitive Dupain is at the State Library of NSW from August 24.

World.title: Solicitor accused of manufacturing illegal 3D-printed firearms
World.content:
A solicitor from Moree, in north-west NSW, has been charged with 16 offences including manufacturing prohibited firearms.

The 32-year-old man was arrested yesterday during a police firearm prohibition order compliance check at a Sunnyside Road home.

The 32-year-old solicitor was charged with 16 offences. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The State Crime Command's Drug and Firearm squad established Strike Force Temarang to investigate the importation and manufacture of 3D-printed and prohibited firearms.

Police allegedly seized a bolt-action rifle, two pistols, a semi-automatic privately manufactured firearm, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and ammunition manufacturing equipment during the search.

Police will also allege hundreds of rounds of ammunition were seized. (Supplied: NSW Police )

Following the man's arrest, police searched a second property at Frome Street, allegedly seizing a 3D printer, blueprints to create firearms and electronic devices.

Inquiries into the manufacture of 3D printed firearms commenced in Moree in April this year. (Supplied: NSW Police )

The man will face court today.

World.title: CIT CEO receives about $445,000 as she steps down after extended leave
World.content:
The board chair of the Canberra Institute of Technology Tom Rogers says Margot McNeill received about $445,000 upon her resignation yesterday after months of controversy.

Her appointment as chief executive in June 2025 was questioned earlier this year after revelations she had failed to disclose an investigation into misconduct in her previous role at TAFE NSW.

In May, Dr McNeill came under further pressure to resign after an ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry found she "should have disclosed the information about the misconduct investigation or findings to the CIT board in a timely manner and that she did not".

Today, Mr Rogers said Dr McNeill had been awarded the settlement but would not be drawn on whether the board had asked her to step down.

"She's left, she's resigned, we've accepted the resignation and that's the main thing," he said.

"And now we need to make sure that we are moving on and providing the sort of quality education which we are doing to students."

Canberra Institute of Technology board chair Tom Rogers says they are focusing on providing quality education as they move forward. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

In a statement about her resignation, Dr McNeill said it had been a difficult decision to resign from the "much-loved Canberra institution".

"It has become clear that this decision is in the best interest of the CIT community, especially students and staff, about whom I care deeply. Equally, it is in my best interest, including that of my family."

Throughout the saga, Dr McNeill has repeatedly said she was under strict obligation not to share the existence of the investigation with her previous employer, but TAFE NSW has publicly refuted that.

Her evidence before the initial committee triggered another assembly probe exploring whether Dr McNeill had misled the assembly.

Released last week, its findings criticised her as having been "deliberately obstructive" and "combative".

Dr McNeill's legal case against TAFE NSW is ongoing in the NSW Supreme Court and she has been on extended leave throughout the controversy.

On Friday last week, Mitch Pirie was appointed acting chief executive of CIT.

CIT to focus on 'quality education': board chair

Mr Rogers told ABC Radio Canberra this morning that Dr McNeill's resignation was a "good outcome".

"It does draw a line on a lot of speculation over the last few months," he said.

He said they were looking to move forward and "rebuild the CIT's reputation".

Margot McNeill resigned on Tuesday, saying it was in the best interests of staff, students and her family. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Asked if Dr McNeill was asked by the board to step down, Mr Rogers said there had been a "process".

"There was a process and she announced her resignation and we've accepted her resignation," he said.

"That matter is now dealt with and we're able to draw a line on that and move forward."

Mr Rogers said the approximately $445,000 payout was the "figure that was agreed on after looking at a whole range of factors".

"I think the exact figure is $445,000 or something like that," he said.

He also spoke about how the board had handled Dr McNeill's recruitment prior to his appointment.

Without saying he would criticise or defend the board's approach to Dr McNeill's hiring, he said a report had found they had "gone above and beyond" during that process.

"I came in ... at the end of March, I've been dealing with a complex issue," he said.

"This is not a one-off, this is a long period of some disruption at CIT.

"What I want to try now is to steady that ship and to move it forward."

The Canberra Institute of Technology gained an acting chief executive amid investigations into the hiring of Margot McNeill. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Resignation a 'relief': Emerson

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said Ms McNeill's resignation had come as a "relief".

"I think this is an outcome that's going to be welcomed by many staff at CIT and by the broader community here in the ACT that deserves assurances our taxpayer funds are being used appropriately," he said on ABC Radio Canberra this morning.

Mr Emerson used parliamentary privilege to make claims of professional misconduct against the Electric Vehicle TAFE Centre of Excellence in May, disclosed to him by a whistleblower.

He was also a vocal advocate for Dr McNeill to stand down after it was revealed she was being investigated over allegations of "serious misconduct" at the time of her CIT hiring.

"This is something I've been calling for the last four months since it became clear that she had failed to disclose misconduct findings made against her by her former employer on a fit and proper persons declaration to the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator ASQA," he said.

"And since then we've had an assembly committee find that she actively misled her board.

"Another Assembly committee raised serious concerns about her conduct and recommend they be investigated by the Public Sector Standards Commissioner."

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson has been calling for Dr McNeill to resign for months. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The Public Sector Standards Commissioner yesterday confirmed they had "received a referral of disclosable conduct investigation" on July 30 relating to CIT's use of rental electric vehicles in the training of student mechanics.

"The matter relates to the Canberra Institute of Technology Electric Vehicle TAFE Centre of Excellence training program, and an investigation has commenced in accordance with the requirements of the PID Act," they said in a statement.

Dr McNeill had previously described the allegations as "factually incorrect" and "offensive".

Mr Emerson said that, as a public institution, CIT now needed to consider real governance reform.

"I think we need to not just tinker around the edges when it comes to governance reform, but look at a real overhaul of how things are run because current arrangements have clearly demonstrated over the last decade not to be working," he said.

World.title: After 30 years with Larry David, this was ‘the most amazing experience I’ve ever had’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Larry David’s new series Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness, which has just wrapped on HBO Max with a sketch featuring former US president Barack Obama, has provided plenty of talking points over the past couple of months. For fans of Curb Your Enthusiasm, it’s essentially been a reunion, featuring most of the show’s former stars as well as that sitcom’s unrelenting cringe comedy. Released as a “warts and all” celebration of America’s 250th birthday, it’s also been unafraid to take shots at the country’s current leadership including Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The sketch which was most critical of Trump also served as the last screen credit for legendary filmmaker Rob Reiner (a vocal critic of the president), filmed just a month before his tragic death. Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in August For David, however, this project has been 50 years in the making – born via niche gags in 1970s comedy clubs and fostered through a lifelong obsession with history. Deputy TV editor Meg Watson spoke with David’s long-time collaborator and series co-creator Jeff Schaffer about doing improv with a former president, the state of comedy in 2026 and why Larry David would “love” to be cancelled. MW: Congrats on the show! I can only imagine how fun it must have been to work on this project: some of the world’s best comedians playing dress up, hanging out with Larry. JS: That was the selling point for all the amazing people who came in! “Hey, come in for a day and play with Larry”. Every day was a new group of actors. Every day was new wardrobe, new hair and make-up, a new period – and I think that’s the real fun of the show. Each one had a surprise element. It was like historical Russian roulette. We knew we wanted to bring Jon Hamm in, for example. We had him earmarked for another part, but he couldn’t do it because he’s in 10 of the 12 television shows on the air right now. He said, “I really wanted to do something, but I can only do this one day”. So we were like, “Well OK then, you’re a Wright brother!”



Loading I’m really thrilled that we got to play with so many of the people not only in our Curb family, but our extended Curb family: Bill Hader and Jon Hamm and Sean Hayes and Lin-Manuel Miranda and Vince [Vaughn]. It was a blast to see everybody. [Note: Cheryl Hines, however, who played Larry’s wife on Curb and is now married to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr – who is openly mocked in the series – is a notable omission.] Editor's pick Logies ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again? How did you decide what events to include? I like that it’s as you’ve said, a “warts and all” history. There’s some dark stuff in there – from slavery to antisemitism, and suicide during the Great Depression. You wouldn’t look at that and think, “That’s going to make a great comedy sketch”. We started making a big list of events – and some are obvious, right? Like the Declaration of Independence. You do a little research and you realise, oh, everyone thinks Thomas Jefferson wrote it, but there was actually this group of five: Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Ben Franklin and also Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston. You’re like, “OK, that’s how we get in.” Larry is Robert Livingston. Larry gets his crack at it. Everyone hates it. He was ignored by history. And then there are other big hits where he’s not ignored by history. Instantly, we were like: Larry’s the guy who told Lincoln to go see that play. That’s Larry, right? Larry David, Bill Hader and Kathryn Hahn in Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness. HBO Max



And honestly, he knows so much about American history [it came very easily for him]. You can tell that this has been an obsession. If you look at his old stand-up, he actually had jokes about Jonas Salk’s mother in comedy clubs in the ’70s. And then obviously if you’re going to talk about [the inventor of the polio vaccine], we wanted to talk about vaccines now. We brought in the RFK stuff, and it all just sort of fell together. But Larry’s always had historical references in his old act that, frankly, no one appreciated. This was his chance to go, “You didn’t like it before, so I’m gonna rub it in your faces now!” Gregg Perrie plays “Bobby”, Dora Salk’s vaccine-hating neighbour whom Dora (David) tells to “drop dead”. HBO Max. Were there conversations about how recent to make that history? Obama’s last sketch is the latest, set in 2014, but it’s an outlier. Was there a moment you considered, “Do we want to include the Capitol insurrection? Is there a way into 9/11?” I remember we talked about a sketch about the Charlottesville race rally [which happened in 2017]. You know, “Jews will not replace us”. We had joked around about Larry playing a Jewish guy, going, “I don’t want that. I don’t want to be a toll-booth attendant or a janitor!” But it went as far as that. We were like, “Eh, that has no legs”. But we knew we wanted to end with [former] president Obama. They were so funny together.



“I always joke that I know where the line is because I can look back and see it.” Jeff Schaffer, Larry David’s long-time collaborator How did you feel about directing a former president? You’ve directed plenty of big stars, but this is someone who directed the armed forces... Does it change the dynamic? Well, the first thing I asked, talking to our partners at Higher Ground [the production company owned by the Obamas], was, “What do I call him? How do I address him?” And they just said, “For you, I’d stick with sir.” But no, it was so good. He and Larry are so good together. It felt like a Curb sketch. It was the most amazing experience I’ve ever had, just sitting in an Oval Office with president Obama and Larry … These are his words: he said, “I really enjoy being annoyed by Larry.” Former president Barack Obama appears in a sketch based in a replica Oval Office, on criticism of him wearing a tan suit in 2014. HBO Max I can imagine that’s a special experience – though maybe less so for you, after so many years. He and I have been working together – on and off, mostly on – since I was 24. It’s literally the longest relationship I’ve ever had. I don’t know what that says about me, but I still enjoy it very much.



Larry David in the final episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm, No Lesson Learned. HBO I know this show was written in the same way you did Curb: you write an outline and work out a lot of the details through improv. Did Obama ad lib his own jokes? I mean, president Obama telling Larry that he has “old lips” and calling him “old lips” – that’s a straight-up Obama improvisation. That was all him. The first time he did it, Larry lost it. He was laughing for, like, five minutes. And then that got woven into the rest of the scene. How often does Larry break like that? Is it a real achievement? I would love to praise Obama and say that it’s a rare thing to get Larry to break, but it is not. He loved doing the show, he’s having fun and he laughs all the time. The number of takes that are ruined because of him... [Schaffer shakes his head]. He’s really having fun. Larry David in Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness. HBO Max Obama’s famously pretty funny, at least in comparison to other politicians. There was his appearance on Between Two Ferns and his bit with Keegan-Michael Key at the Correspondent’s Dinner...

World.title: ‘I don’t think that would help’: Cats coach quizzed on Kolodjashnij concussion saga
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott says he would like to give “an impassioned defence” of the people at his club who were involved in drafting the controversial agreement with Jake Kolodjashnij but would keep his counsel on the matter while an investigation was underway.

The Cats’ coach said he had not delved into the reasons why the defender was made unavailable for selection in either the VFL or AFL this weekend as the controversy continued about the agreement which contained, according to AFL chairman Craig Drummond, “a waiver”.

Geelong coach Chris Scott is being tight-lipped about the drama surrounding his defender Jake Kolodjashnij. AFL Photos

Geelong says the clause was, in fact, an “acknowledgment of risk” and have provided the AFL with the communications they shared with the league during the two-month process it took to develop the informed consent agreement with Kolodjashnij.

That agreement was reached after the player received an “amber” ruling from the league’s independent concussion panel, meaning his future was left in the club’s hands.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Court to resume at 2pm after legal issue triggers adjournment as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. I will be bringing you the latest from court today along with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete known as “J”, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. KATE GERAGHTY

Yesterday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what he had told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy. Her evidence continues today.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ASX slides in early trade after Wall Street retreats; CBA falls on slowdown warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides in early trade after Wall Street retreats; CBA falls on slowdown warning Staff writers Updated August 12, 2026 — 10:39am ,first published August 12, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket struggled in early trade on Wednesday, after Wall Street slipped further from its records overnight, with oil prices swinging on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again. Commonwealth Bank, the nation’s biggest lender and the second-biggest stock on the local market, declined after warning economic growth was slowing due to higher interest rates and inflation. The S&P/ASX 200 dropped 35.20 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 9215.40 as of 10.23am AEST, with all sectors bar utilities in the red. It added 0.2 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.67¢. Rising oil prices weighed on Wall Street, setting the scene for losses on the ASX. AP CBA’s shares dropped 1.1 per cent to $171.99 even after the banking giant notched up $11 billion in full-year cash profit, up 7 per cent, fuelled by growth across its vast loan and deposit portfolios.



Despite strong growth in the year to June, however, CBA said new applications for mortgages had fallen 15 per cent since the May budget, as the housing market slows due to higher interest rates and a tightening in tax concessions for property investors. The bank also said costs from soured loans had increased due to cost-of-living pressures and increased economic uncertainty. Related Article Breaking

Earnings season CBA posts $11b profit, but mortgage applications fell 15 per cent since May budget “Growth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing uneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity,” CBA boss Matt Comyn said. “Housing activity has softened from a high base.” The other big four banks also declined on the news, with National Australia Bank down 0.4 per cent, Westpac down 0.5 per cent and ANZ Bank down 0.7 per cent. The mining heavyweights weighed on the market in early trade, too, with iron ore and copper powerhouses BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue down 0.5 per cent, 0.8 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively.



On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for a second modest drop since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.6 per cent. The action was stronger in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly jumped above $US90 in the morning before falling back below $US87. It eventually settled at $US88.91, up 1.4 per cent from Monday. Such erratic moves have become typical since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and kept much of the world’s oil pent up in the Middle East. Last month alone, Brent’s price veered between $US72 and $US102 per barrel. Higher oil prices make inflation worse, and they’ve sent the average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to $US4.01, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US3.14 a year ago, though it’s down from last week’s nearly $US4.09. That has Wall Street’s attention focused on Wednesday [early Thursday AEST], when the US government will release the latest monthly reading on inflation. Economists expect it to show inflation remains high but that it decelerated to 3.4 per cent in July from 3.5 per cent in June.



That could help the Federal Reserve, whose members are notably split on whether they should be raising the country’s interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. While higher rates could help slow the increases of prices on store shelves, they would also slow the overall US economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Traders are betting on a coin flip’s chance that the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group. If it does, that would be the first increase in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates. Treasury yields have jumped since the war with Iran because of higher oil prices and worries about inflation, sending long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. The 10-year Treasury yield eased back on Tuesday, falling to 4.69 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday. But it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran.



On Wall Street, On Holding dropped 20.3 per cent even though the Swiss sneaker company reported a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its sales forecast though fell short of analysts’ expectations, while saying it does not want to slash prices to drum up more sales. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Companies broadly have been blowing past analysts’ forecasts, which Wall Street loves because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. Earnings per share for S&P 500 companies are on track to be 50 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet, and that’s a big reason US stocks have been setting records recently despite worries about expensive oil, high inflation and other challenges. In other international markets, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves. with AP. Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: O’Neil calls Coalition’s referral of alleged diplomatic leak a ‘political stunt’; Colombia quake death toll tops 250 as thousands remain missing
World.content:
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he has the full support of his party after a confidence vote at a three-hour emergency meeting this morning.

The showdown began at 7.30am (AEST), called by Luxon as he sought to end speculation over his leadership of the National Party ahead of the country’s November 7 election.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. AP

Luxon had faced mounting questions after a series of missteps and a slump in party support in recent opinion polls. He survived a similar leadership challenge in April.

Ahead of today’s meeting, speculation had mounted in the New Zealand media that Erica Stanford, the Auckland-based education minister, was positioning herself to replace Luxon.

World.title: Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat Iain Payten Updated August 12, 2026 — 10:09am ,first published August 12, 2026 — 8:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies backline is set for a shake-up for the rematch against Japan in Townsville, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii ruled out with another hamstring injury and Carter Gordon poised to return at five-eighth. The backline shuffle comes as the likelihood of the Wallabies naming the 1000th player also firms, with young Queensland prop Massimo De Lutiis set to win a spot against the Brave Blossoms. Loading Suaalii was scratched from the clash at Queensland Country Bank Stadium after picking up a “minor” hamstring injury in the Wallabies’ three-point win in Osaka at the weekend. His injury was revealed in a release by the Wallabies on Tuesday night and is the latest in a series of hamstring injuries for the big-money recruit. Suaalii played six games for the Waratahs this year due to hamstring complaints.



Josh Flook has joined the squad as cover and will come into contention to play a role in the Test in Townsville. With Len Ikitau (ankle) also injured, Hunter Paisami wore the No.12 in Japan and Isaac Henry debuted off the bench at outside centre, pushing Suaalii to the wing. Gordon is set for a recall to the starting No.10 jersey, replacing Declan Meredith, who had an unhappy night in Osaka. Gordon started against Ireland in July before picking up a calf injury and missing the Tests against France and Italy. When Ben Donaldson was also ruled out for the France Test, Meredith was given a debut and he held the spot through to the Japan Test, but his form waned. Carter Gordon will come into the No.10 jersey. Getty Images



Wallabies coach Les Kiss flagged changes for the second Test after the win in Osaka, saying he expected some players to be impacted by the sapping 30 degree heat. It is in this context that De Lutiis is set to make his Test debut and become Wallaby No.1000, with tighthead prop Allan Alaalatoa expected to be rested ahead of the upcoming Argentina tour. Taniela Tupou, who has been coming off the bench, is set to start at tighthead. De Lutiis would also come off the bench. Rugby Australia and Queensland successfully fended off the attention of Ireland earlier this year to re-sign De Lutiis, who is a hulking tighthead prop. Backrower Tom Hooper is also expected to return after overcoming a shoulder injury that ruled him out of the last three Tests.



Meanwhile, the Wallaroos have a new head coach after Rugby Australia announced the appointment of Sione Fukofuka through to the end of the home Rugby World Cup in 2029. But Fukofuka won’t be starting until the beginning of 2027, as part of a contract wrangle with the Scottish Rugby Union. The 47-year-old is an experienced coach who served as Wallaroos assistant coach for three years from 2021, and then served as head coach of the USA Women’s side in 2024-25. Fukofuka subsequently moved to Scotland as their women’s head coach, but two weeks ago it was announced he would be returning to Australia on compassionate grounds, due to family reasons. It was a stroke of fortune for Rugby Australia, who have been without a Wallaroos head coach since Jo Yapp departed last year and had recently had their drawn-out recruitment process knocked about when leading candidate Canadian coach Kevin Roeut backed out of a potential deal.



Fukofuka became the target but under the terms of his SRU contract exit, he will not be available until the start of 2027. World.title: The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCancer The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis Kayla Olaya Updated August 12, 2026 — 9:59am ,first published 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star of the UK version of The Office Lucy Davis has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer but is “not scared of whatever comes next”. The 53-year-old who played Dawn Tinsley, Martin Freeman’s character’s love interest in the show, shared the update on Instagram early on Wednesday (AEST) after being diagnosed with cancer a year and a half ago. She said it had now metastasised in her bones, making it too late for chemotherapy. Lucy Davis (middle right) pictured with the main cast of BBC’s The Office - Mackenzie Crook, left, Ricky Gervais, middle left, and Martin Freeman. BBC “A year and a half ago I was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer, which has metastasised to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo,” Davis said in the caption to her post. “As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.



“I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her dog, which died in 2024] sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me.” In the video post, Davis rings the bell – a ceremony for cancer patients marking the end of treatment – to applause. In the caption, she urges readers not to ignore small lumps or signs as she had. “The initial lump that I felt wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out,” Davis said. Davis, who also had roles in the Wonder Woman films and the comic zombie horror Sean of the Dead, said that as her pain intensified, tasks such as standing or walking could become difficult and told her followers to expect to see her in a wheelchair from time to time.



Lucy Davis has shared that she’s been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer. UK Press via Getty Images “If you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push,” she joked, adding that humour has been “vital” to her throughout this journey. “I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at, and most importantly of all, to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she said. In her post, Davis said that despite her pain and diagnosis, she would continue to pursue her activism for animal rights and continue to work. “I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life,” she wrote.



Jenna Fischer, who played Pam Beesly, the equivalent of Davis’s character Dawn in the US version of The Office, commented below the post supporting her decision to work with cancer. “Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let’s spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort,” Fischer said. Fischer was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023, but following treatment, she announced that she was cancer-free in late 2024. Davis signed off her post to fellow cancer battlers, sing that: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally”. “We all get to do it however we choose.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: After 30 years with Larry David, this was ‘the most amazing experience I’ve ever had’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Larry David’s new series Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness, which has just wrapped on HBO Max with a sketch featuring former US president Barack Obama, has provided plenty of talking points over the past couple of months. For fans of Curb Your Enthusiasm, it’s essentially been a reunion, featuring most of the show’s former stars as well as that sitcom’s unrelenting cringe comedy. Released as a “warts and all” celebration of America’s 250th birthday, it’s also been unafraid to take shots at the country’s current leadership including Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The sketch which was most critical of Trump also served as the last screen credit for legendary filmmaker Rob Reiner (a vocal critic of the president), filmed just a month before his tragic death. Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in August For David, however, this project has been 50 years in the making – born via niche gags in 1970s comedy clubs and fostered through a lifelong obsession with history. Deputy TV editor Meg Watson spoke with David’s long-time collaborator and series co-creator Jeff Schaffer about doing improv with a former president, the state of comedy in 2026 and why Larry David would “love” to be cancelled. MW: Congrats on the show! I can only imagine how fun it must have been to work on this project: some of the world’s best comedians playing dress up, hanging out with Larry. JS: That was the selling point for all the amazing people who came in! “Hey, come in for a day and play with Larry”. Every day was a new group of actors. Every day was new wardrobe, new hair and make-up, a new period – and I think that’s the real fun of the show. Each one had a surprise element. It was like historical Russian roulette. We knew we wanted to bring Jon Hamm in, for example. We had him earmarked for another part, but he couldn’t do it because he’s in 10 of the 12 television shows on the air right now. He said, “I really wanted to do something, but I can only do this one day”. So we were like, “Well OK then, you’re a Wright brother!”



Loading I’m really thrilled that we got to play with so many of the people not only in our Curb family, but our extended Curb family: Bill Hader and Jon Hamm and Sean Hayes and Lin-Manuel Miranda and Vince [Vaughn]. It was a blast to see everybody. [Note: Cheryl Hines, however, who played Larry’s wife on Curb and is now married to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr – who is openly mocked in the series – is a notable omission.] Editor's pick Logies ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again? How did you decide what events to include? I like that it’s as you’ve said, a “warts and all” history. There’s some dark stuff in there – from slavery to antisemitism, and suicide during the Great Depression. You wouldn’t look at that and think, “That’s going to make a great comedy sketch”. We started making a big list of events – and some are obvious, right? Like the Declaration of Independence. You do a little research and you realise, oh, everyone thinks Thomas Jefferson wrote it, but there was actually this group of five: Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Ben Franklin and also Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston. You’re like, “OK, that’s how we get in.” Larry is Robert Livingston. Larry gets his crack at it. Everyone hates it. He was ignored by history. And then there are other big hits where he’s not ignored by history. Instantly, we were like: Larry’s the guy who told Lincoln to go see that play. That’s Larry, right? Larry David, Bill Hader and Kathryn Hahn in Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness. HBO Max



And honestly, he knows so much about American history [it came very easily for him]. You can tell that this has been an obsession. If you look at his old stand-up, he actually had jokes about Jonas Salk’s mother in comedy clubs in the ’70s. And then obviously if you’re going to talk about [the inventor of the polio vaccine], we wanted to talk about vaccines now. We brought in the RFK stuff, and it all just sort of fell together. But Larry’s always had historical references in his old act that, frankly, no one appreciated. This was his chance to go, “You didn’t like it before, so I’m gonna rub it in your faces now!” Gregg Perrie plays “Bobby”, Dora Salk’s vaccine-hating neighbour whom Dora (David) tells to “drop dead”. HBO Max. Were there conversations about how recent to make that history? Obama’s last sketch is the latest, set in 2014, but it’s an outlier. Was there a moment you considered, “Do we want to include the Capitol insurrection? Is there a way into 9/11?” I remember we talked about a sketch about the Charlottesville race rally [which happened in 2017]. You know, “Jews will not replace us”. We had joked around about Larry playing a Jewish guy, going, “I don’t want that. I don’t want to be a toll-booth attendant or a janitor!” But it went as far as that. We were like, “Eh, that has no legs”. But we knew we wanted to end with [former] president Obama. They were so funny together.



“I always joke that I know where the line is because I can look back and see it.” Jeff Schaffer, Larry David’s long-time collaborator How did you feel about directing a former president? You’ve directed plenty of big stars, but this is someone who directed the armed forces... Does it change the dynamic? Well, the first thing I asked, talking to our partners at Higher Ground [the production company owned by the Obamas], was, “What do I call him? How do I address him?” And they just said, “For you, I’d stick with sir.” But no, it was so good. He and Larry are so good together. It felt like a Curb sketch. It was the most amazing experience I’ve ever had, just sitting in an Oval Office with president Obama and Larry … These are his words: he said, “I really enjoy being annoyed by Larry.” Former president Barack Obama appears in a sketch based in a replica Oval Office, on criticism of him wearing a tan suit in 2014. HBO Max I can imagine that’s a special experience – though maybe less so for you, after so many years. He and I have been working together – on and off, mostly on – since I was 24. It’s literally the longest relationship I’ve ever had. I don’t know what that says about me, but I still enjoy it very much.



Larry David in the final episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm, No Lesson Learned. HBO I know this show was written in the same way you did Curb: you write an outline and work out a lot of the details through improv. Did Obama ad lib his own jokes? I mean, president Obama telling Larry that he has “old lips” and calling him “old lips” – that’s a straight-up Obama improvisation. That was all him. The first time he did it, Larry lost it. He was laughing for, like, five minutes. And then that got woven into the rest of the scene. How often does Larry break like that? Is it a real achievement? I would love to praise Obama and say that it’s a rare thing to get Larry to break, but it is not. He loved doing the show, he’s having fun and he laughs all the time. The number of takes that are ruined because of him... [Schaffer shakes his head]. He’s really having fun. Larry David in Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness. HBO Max Obama’s famously pretty funny, at least in comparison to other politicians. There was his appearance on Between Two Ferns and his bit with Keegan-Michael Key at the Correspondent’s Dinner...
