World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott says he would like to give “an impassioned defence” of the people at his club who were involved in drafting the controversial agreement with Jake Kolodjashnij but would keep his counsel on the matter while an investigation was underway.

The Cats’ coach said he had not delved into the reasons why the defender was made unavailable for selection in either the VFL or AFL this weekend as the controversy continued about the agreement which contained, according to AFL chairman Craig Drummond, “a waiver”.

Geelong coach Chris Scott is being tight-lipped about the drama surrounding his defender Jake Kolodjashnij. AFL Photos

Geelong says the clause was, in fact, an “acknowledgment of risk” and have provided the AFL with the communications they shared with the league during the two-month process it took to develop the informed consent agreement with Kolodjashnij.

That agreement was reached after the player received an “amber” ruling from the league’s independent concussion panel, meaning his future was left in the club’s hands.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Court to resume at 2pm after legal issue triggers adjournment as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. I will be bringing you the latest from court today along with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete known as “J”, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. KATE GERAGHTY

Yesterday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what he had told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy. Her evidence continues today.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ASX slides in early trade after Wall Street retreats; CBA falls on slowdown warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides in early trade after Wall Street retreats; CBA falls on slowdown warning Staff writers Updated August 12, 2026 — 10:39am ,first published August 12, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket struggled in early trade on Wednesday, after Wall Street slipped further from its records overnight, with oil prices swinging on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again. Commonwealth Bank, the nation’s biggest lender and the second-biggest stock on the local market, declined after warning economic growth was slowing due to higher interest rates and inflation. The S&P/ASX 200 dropped 35.20 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 9215.40 as of 10.23am AEST, with all sectors bar utilities in the red. It added 0.2 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.67¢. Rising oil prices weighed on Wall Street, setting the scene for losses on the ASX. AP CBA’s shares dropped 1.1 per cent to $171.99 even after the banking giant notched up $11 billion in full-year cash profit, up 7 per cent, fuelled by growth across its vast loan and deposit portfolios.



Despite strong growth in the year to June, however, CBA said new applications for mortgages had fallen 15 per cent since the May budget, as the housing market slows due to higher interest rates and a tightening in tax concessions for property investors. The bank also said costs from soured loans had increased due to cost-of-living pressures and increased economic uncertainty. Related Article Breaking

Earnings season CBA posts $11b profit, but mortgage applications fell 15 per cent since May budget “Growth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing uneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity,” CBA boss Matt Comyn said. “Housing activity has softened from a high base.” The other big four banks also declined on the news, with National Australia Bank down 0.4 per cent, Westpac down 0.5 per cent and ANZ Bank down 0.7 per cent. The mining heavyweights weighed on the market in early trade, too, with iron ore and copper powerhouses BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue down 0.5 per cent, 0.8 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively.



On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for a second modest drop since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.6 per cent. The action was stronger in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly jumped above $US90 in the morning before falling back below $US87. It eventually settled at $US88.91, up 1.4 per cent from Monday. Such erratic moves have become typical since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and kept much of the world’s oil pent up in the Middle East. Last month alone, Brent’s price veered between $US72 and $US102 per barrel. Higher oil prices make inflation worse, and they’ve sent the average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to $US4.01, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US3.14 a year ago, though it’s down from last week’s nearly $US4.09. That has Wall Street’s attention focused on Wednesday [early Thursday AEST], when the US government will release the latest monthly reading on inflation. Economists expect it to show inflation remains high but that it decelerated to 3.4 per cent in July from 3.5 per cent in June.



That could help the Federal Reserve, whose members are notably split on whether they should be raising the country’s interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. While higher rates could help slow the increases of prices on store shelves, they would also slow the overall US economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Traders are betting on a coin flip’s chance that the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group. If it does, that would be the first increase in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates. Treasury yields have jumped since the war with Iran because of higher oil prices and worries about inflation, sending long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. The 10-year Treasury yield eased back on Tuesday, falling to 4.69 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday. But it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran.



On Wall Street, On Holding dropped 20.3 per cent even though the Swiss sneaker company reported a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its sales forecast though fell short of analysts’ expectations, while saying it does not want to slash prices to drum up more sales. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Companies broadly have been blowing past analysts’ forecasts, which Wall Street loves because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. Earnings per share for S&P 500 companies are on track to be 50 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet, and that’s a big reason US stocks have been setting records recently despite worries about expensive oil, high inflation and other challenges. In other international markets, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves. with AP. The Wallabies backline is set for a shake-up for the rematch against Japan in Townsville, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii ruled out with another hamstring injury and Carter Gordon poised to return at five-eighth. The backline shuffle comes as the likelihood of the Wallabies naming the 1000th player also firms, with young Queensland prop Massimo De Lutiis set to win a spot against the Brave Blossoms. Loading Suaalii was scratched from the clash at Queensland Country Bank Stadium after picking up a “minor” hamstring injury in the Wallabies’ three-point win in Osaka at the weekend. His injury was revealed in a release by the Wallabies on Tuesday night and is the latest in a series of hamstring injuries for the big-money recruit. Suaalii played six games for the Waratahs this year due to hamstring complaints.



Josh Flook has joined the squad as cover and will come into contention to play a role in the Test in Townsville. With Len Ikitau (ankle) also injured, Hunter Paisami wore the No.12 in Japan and Isaac Henry debuted off the bench at outside centre, pushing Suaalii to the wing. Gordon is set for a recall to the starting No.10 jersey, replacing Declan Meredith, who had an unhappy night in Osaka. Gordon started against Ireland in July before picking up a calf injury and missing the Tests against France and Italy. When Ben Donaldson was also ruled out for the France Test, Meredith was given a debut and he held the spot through to the Japan Test, but his form waned. Carter Gordon will come into the No.10 jersey. Getty Images



Wallabies coach Les Kiss flagged changes for the second Test after the win in Osaka, saying he expected some players to be impacted by the sapping 30 degree heat. It is in this context that De Lutiis is set to make his Test debut and become Wallaby No.1000, with tighthead prop Allan Alaalatoa expected to be rested ahead of the upcoming Argentina tour. Taniela Tupou, who has been coming off the bench, is set to start at tighthead. De Lutiis would also come off the bench. Rugby Australia and Queensland successfully fended off the attention of Ireland earlier this year to re-sign De Lutiis, who is a hulking tighthead prop. Backrower Tom Hooper is also expected to return after overcoming a shoulder injury that ruled him out of the last three Tests.



Meanwhile, the Wallaroos have a new head coach after Rugby Australia announced the appointment of Sione Fukofuka through to the end of the home Rugby World Cup in 2029. But Fukofuka won’t be starting until the beginning of 2027, as part of a contract wrangle with the Scottish Rugby Union. The 47-year-old is an experienced coach who served as Wallaroos assistant coach for three years from 2021, and then served as head coach of the USA Women’s side in 2024-25. Fukofuka subsequently moved to Scotland as their women’s head coach, but two weeks ago it was announced he would be returning to Australia on compassionate grounds, due to family reasons. It was a stroke of fortune for Rugby Australia, who have been without a Wallaroos head coach since Jo Yapp departed last year and had recently had their drawn-out recruitment process knocked about when leading candidate Canadian coach Kevin Roeut backed out of a potential deal.



Fukofuka became the target but under the terms of his SRU contract exit, he will not be available until the start of 2027. An interim coaching team of Waratahs head coach Mike Ruthven, Duncan Chubb, Ben Mowen, Reg Tayler and Rugby Australia’s director of women’s high performance Tim Walsh is set to coach the team for the seven Tests remaining this year. “I would like to express my gratitude to Scottish Rugby for their understanding of my family situation and desire to return home to Australia,” Fukofuka said in a statement. “Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family. I wish the players and staff all the best for the future. Australia Sevens star Maddison Levi is in line for a possible Wallaroos debut after being included in the Test squad for the upcoming 100th international against New Zealand in Auckland on August 22.



Levi is one of four uncapped players named in a new-look squad that also features NSW Waratahs player of the year Amelia Whitaker, Queensland Reds captain Jemma Bemrose and Western Force forward Pia Tapsell. UK Press via Getty Images “If you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push,” she joked, adding that humour has been “vital” to her throughout this journey. “I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at, and most importantly of all, to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she said. In her post, Davis said that despite her pain and diagnosis, she would continue to pursue her activism for animal rights and continue to work. “I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life,” she wrote.



Jenna Fischer, who played Pam Beesly, the equivalent of Davis’s character Dawn in the US version of The Office, commented below the post supporting her decision to work with cancer. “Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let’s spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort,” Fischer said. Fischer was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023, but following treatment, she announced that she was cancer-free in late 2024. Davis signed off her post to fellow cancer battlers, sing that: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally”. “We all get to do it however we choose.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Live: Christopher Luxon calls urgent caucus meeting amid leadership speculation
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon emerged after an hours-long meeting to say his caucus is united and confirm he would stay on as National Party leader:

Follow updates with our live blog below:

An "urgent in-person" National Party caucus meeting is underway in Wellington.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership following a series of missteps and clashes.

Despite speculation National MP Chris Penk had been trying to drum up support for fellow MP Erica Stanford, Penk told reporters outside Parliament he had "confidence in Christopher Luxon".

Meanwhile, the latest 1News Verian poll shows Luxon's preferred prime minister rating has dropped again to 17 percent - one percentage point from their last poll in June.

He remains ahead of Labour leader Chris Hipkins who also dropped one percentage point, to 15 percent.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

World.title: Ex-cops not guilty of obstructing justice relating to Alan Hall case
World.content:
Two former police officers accused of obstructing justice in an investigation which led to the wrongful conviction of Alan Hall in the 1980s have been found not guilty.

The men, whose names are suppressed, have been on trial in the High Court at Auckland charged with wilfully attempting to obstruct, prevent, pervert or defeat the course of justice.

A third former defendant has since died.

Justice Ian Gault delivered the decision on Wednesday morning. The men's interim name suppression is extended while the court considers an application for permanent name suppression.

Arthur Easton. Supplied / Police

Hall spent 17 years in prison after being convicted of murdering Arthur Easton, who was killed during a home invasion by a man wielding a bayonet.

The decision was quashed by the Supreme Court in 2022 after it found a substantial miscarriage of justice had occurred.

Assistant Police Commissioner Corrie Parnell acknoweldged the two families who have been seeking justice for decades - the Hall family and the Easton family.

"This decision brings an end to criminal proceedings and Police stand by our decision to put this case before the courts," Parnell said.

He said since the Supreme Court acquitted Hall in 2022, the onus has been on the entire justice system to find out how the substantial miscarriage of justice happened.

"It is our view after a thorough investigation decades later that there was an end-to-end Justice system failure, but we also recognised that individuals responsible for key steps in the case played a critical role and that needed to be answered in the courts," Parnell said.

He said police accepted that they had a part to play in the failure.

"While legislation, systems and processes in the Justice sector have advanced in the decades since this case was first prosecuted, we acknowledge the Hall family have been left waiting for answers for a long time," Parnell said.

World.title: Australian broadcaster to buy MediaWorks in $130m deal
World.content:
The Australian-listed company says the deal will create a larger trans-Tasman audio, digital and entertainment business.

Australian-listed Sports Entertainment Group Limited (SEG) has agreed to buy MediaWorks in a deal valuing the New Zealand radio and digital audio business at $130 million.

The company, listed on the Australian Securities Exchange, said it had entered a binding agreement to acquire all of MediaWorks from its current owners, including Quadrant Private Equity, Barclay Nettlefold and John O'Neill.

MediaWorks owns a stable of commercial radio brands including The Rock, More FM and The Breeze, as well as the Rova digital audio platform.

SEG described it as New Zealand's number one audio business, with about 2.4 million weekly listeners and a 59 percent audience share in the 25-to-54 demographic.

The company said the acquisition would create a leading trans-Tasman audio, digital and entertainment group, with combined weekly audiences of more than 5 million listeners across Australia and New Zealand.

SEG already has a presence in New Zealand through Sports Entertainment Network (SEN).

SEG chief executive Craig Hutchison said the acquisition was a transformational step for the company.

"It gives us immediate market leadership in New Zealand, a highly complementary content offering, and a genuine platform to extend our sport, digital and entertainment capability across the Tasman," he said.

The existing MediaWorks management team, led by chief executive Wendy Palmer, was expected to continue running the New Zealand business after completion.

The purchase price is based on an enterprise value of NZ$130m on a cash-free and debt-free basis.

SEG said MediaWorks was forecast to make NZ$25.4m in EBITDA in calendar 2026, with a pathway to more than NZ$38m by 2030.

It said the deal was expected to be accretive to earnings per share before synergies.

The company said it had already identified about A$5m (NZ$6.01m) of annual synergies.

The acquisition will be funded through existing cash, new bank borrowing, and an equity raising.

SEG has launched a placement to raise up to about A$11.7m and also plans a share purchase plan to raise up to about A$2m.

World.title: Pauline Hanna inquest: Coroner orders footage of Philip Polkinghorne interview
World.content:
A documentary company has been ordered to hand a coroner raw footage of an interview with Philip Polkinghorne.

The documentary Polk: The Trial of Philip Polkinghorne aired on ThreeNow last year and featured excerpts of an interview with Polkinghorne.

The interview was referred to on Tuesday during an inquest into the 2021 death of Polkinghorne's wife Pauline Hanna. He was found not guilty of her murder in 2024.

Coroner Tania Tehitaha has compelled the company Blonde Razor to hand over the four hours of raw footage.

She is using section 120 of the Coroner's Act to do that.

RNZ understands the raw footage is from interviews done in 2022.

RNZ / Jess Hopkins

Much of the discussion about the handing over the footage was done behind closed doors, with journalists and the public told to leave the court.

When they returned, Coroner Tehitaha said she only wanted to see aspects of the footage that related to specific aspects of the evidence.

This stage of the inquest is looking into how Pauline Hanna died and the circumstances surrounding that, including whether her death was self inflicted.

Coroner Tehitaha said it would likely take about a day to get the footage, and adjourned the hearing for the rest of Wednesday.

Polkinghorne spent most of Tuesday giving evidence, firstly his own account and then under cross examination from police counsel Alysha McClintock.

World.title: Yellow rain watches issued for Northland, Auckland and Westland
World.content:
Northern and eastern areas of Northland and Auckland north of Orewa are under a heavy rain watch on Wednesday.

The watches which also cover Great Barrier Island came into effect at 10am, MetService says.

A low-pressure system southwest of New Zealand is driving a frontal band of rain eastwards, mainly affecting the top half of the North Island and Westland today.

The forecast which applies for the upper North Island through to 1am on Thursday is for periods of rain with some heavy falls, and the amounts may approach the criteria for an upgrade to a warning.

The rain will ease from the north on Wednesday afternoon and evening, MetService says.

Meanwhile, in the South Island, there will be periods of heavy rain from 2pm today through until 6am tomorrow in Westland.

The rainfall may be especially heavy about the ranges.

The band of rain has made its way to Aotearoa from the Tasman Sea and might result in rain and showers for most of the North Island on Thursday.

World.title: Kiwi ICE detainee Everlee Wihongi on 'dehumanising conditions' in custody
World.content:
What gives you hope when you're being held in a US immigration detention facility?

For New Zealand citizen Everlee Wihongi, it was the support of her family and loved ones, but she says hope can be a bad thing in a place like that.

"Lots of times it was bad to have hope that things would go well," she said.

"It was like I can't look too far into the future because I don't know how long I'll be here."

Wihongi, who has lived in the US for decades and holds a green card, was detained by ICE in early April after coming back from New Zealand.

She was held for more than 70 days because of a 2016 cannabis conviction that was later thrown out by the courts.

Now, she's back home in Wisconsin with her family.

Speaking to RNZ, Wihongi said her time in detainment was one of the most miserable experiences of her entire existence.

Officials at the facility would refer to her as a bunk-bed number, rather than by her name, she said.

She wasn't Everlee Wihongi, she was 'Six Up'.

"It was dehumanising conditions," Wihongi said.

"Whenever you'd have an appointment or you had to go see a lawyer, anything, they would just go 'Six Up, you have an appointment'."

Wihongi said meal times at the facilities she was held in were another challenge.

"The first spot I was in, we had to get up at 6am to eat, and if you didn't get up for breakfast and you didn't eat," she said.

"When I was in Arizona, you had to get up at 3.45am to get breakfast, and if you didn't go, then you just didn't eat till lunchtime, which is around 1pm."

Wihongi was first held in an ICE facility in California, before being moved to Arizona and spending a night on the floor in a Texan holding facility along the way.

In transit, Wihongi described seeing other detainees being removed from a plane before they could board.

She and others had been woken at 1.30 that morning, shackled, and moved out, but weren't on the plane until later that evening.

"We could see the people coming off the plane, but they couldn't see into the van," she said.

"There were children in shackles, a pregnant lady, old people, everybody just being marched around like herded animals really, getting off the plane, getting into these other buses."

The conviction that saw Wihongi detained by ICE in the first place was thrown out by a court in June.

She described the moment as unbelievable.

"I didn't want to be too excited or get too ahead of myself," she said.

"I thought for sure it'd be a few more months they would try and hold me in there, I didn't think that they were going to let me out right away."

Wihongi said having hope in detention meant you'd be devastated at one point or another.

Everlee Wihongi and whanau Supplied / Courtney Wihongi

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade had been providing consular assistance during Wihongi's detainment. She said staff from the New Zealand's Los Angeles consulate were helpful, evening bringing her New Zealand chocolate on one visit.

Staff helped her recover documents like her passport, Green Card, and drivers license - something she didn't have when she was released.

Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters had said Wihongi was detained for not declaring her historic cannabis possession conviction, but that was completely false, she said.

"In all my time coming back and forth, I've never been given one of those forms."

"Even when the consulate asked, 'did you get one of those papers to mark your conviction?' I was never given one of those," Wihongi said.

She was shocked by the public response to her time in ICE custody.

"It was something else to come out of something like that to so much love and support from not only my family, but strangers and people I didn't know."

She hoped those still detained by ICE had the same love and support she experienced.

"There are just more people in there that have nothing, they don't have the family support like I did, they don't have their country supporting them like I did, I just wish more people could experience that," Wihongi said.

World.title: Pacific media figures pay tribute to Solomons legend George Atkin
World.content:
Tributes have flowed in for the renowned Solomon Islands journalist, George Atkin, who has died.

As well as being a former correspondent for the then-RNZ International, Atkin was a leading figure in journalism in Solomon Islands and in the Pacific Islands region.

He was the first President of the Media Association of Solomon Islands, serving from 1985 to 1989 and was a respected member of the country's media fraternity.

The veteran journalist worked for numerous mainstream media outlets such as the Solomon Star newspaper, Island Sun newspaper and the Solomon Islands Broadcasting Corporation.

A prominent Solomon islands media figure, Robert Iroga, said Atkin was an editor, journalist, storyteller and mentor who understood the power of the pen.

"He understood that journalism was not simply about filling pages or broadcasting news. He understood that words could change policies, challenge governments, expose wrongdoing and even force leaders to resign."

Some of the region's best known names in the news media sector have also paid tribute to Atkin on social media.

Alexander Rheeney, a former editor of both PNG's Post Courier newspaper and the Samoa Observer, said Atkin "was a legend and well respected by the media fraternity and the public".

TVNZ's long-time Pacific correspondent Barbara Dreaver said Atkin "leaves a legacy that will be remembered".

RNZ Pacific manager Moera Tuilaepa-Taylor said that Atkin "was a true professional and understood all the complex layers of politics in his country".

World.title: Litigation costs a factor as ASB net profit drops to $1.3b
World.content:
ASB's full-year profit has dipped slightly due to litigation costs, but home and commercial lending increased.

Financial results for the year ended June versus the year before.

Cash net profit after tax: NZ$1.318 billion, down 2%

Net interest income: NZ$3.14 billion, up 8%

Total operating income: NZ$3.55 billion, up 6%

Operating expenses: NZ$1.65 billion, up 16%

Home lending: NZ$84.5 billion, up 6%

Business and rural lending: NZ$36.2 billion, up 6%

ASB has reported a full-year profit of NZ$1.3 billion, down 2 percent on the previous year due to higher operating costs, including a $135 million class action settlement.

ASB, which is owned by the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, is the first of the big four Australian-owned banks to report its New Zealand result.

Operating costs were up 16 percent to NZ$1.65b.

ASB said this was due to higher staff costs, the class action settlement, spending on technology, and increased provisions for bad debts, which rose 30 percent to NZ$78m.

Its net interest margin increased by three basis points to 2.3 percent.

Home lending rose 6 percent to $84.5b, while business and rural lending increased 6 percent to $36.2b.

Commenting on the result, ASB chief executive Vittoria Shortt said it had been a challenging year given the economic disruption caused by the conflict in the Middle East and rising inflation.

"The economic recovery has been very stop-start. Although we had momentum at the beginning of the financial year, it's been a very different second half.

"The conflict in the Middle East and subsequent global oil price shock have caused significant disruption, changing the inflation outlook and pushing interest rates up faster than anticipated."

However, Shortt said ASB customers had weathered the storm well, with fewer households experiencing difficulties repaying loans.

"While we expect economic momentum to return in the coming months, uncertainty remains the new norm and we're cognisant that many New Zealanders will continue to face cost pressures.

World.title: Everything you need to know as Australia hosts Bangladesh in the Top End
World.content:
Australia is hosting Bangladesh in a rare Test series this August, as winter cricket hits the Top End.

The two teams will play two Tests, the first of which gets underway in Darwin on August 13 at Marrara Stadium.

The second starts on August 22 in Mackay, where Harrup Park will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia.

You can listen to live coverage of both Tests on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog.

'Nowhere to hide' or free swing?: ABC Cricket Podcast

It is the first time in 23 years that Bangladesh will tour Australia for a Test series.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does Australia play Bangladesh?

The first Test gets underway on Thursday, August 13, with the first session starting at 10am ACST in Darwin, NT.

That means the start time is 10:30am AEST (Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania), 10:00am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8:30am in Western Australia.

The second Test starts on Saturday, August 22, with the first ball again set to be bowled 10:00am AEST in Mackay, Queensland.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 10:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8am in Western Australia.

Each Test is scheduled for five days.

Where are the Tests being played?

Australia played South Africa at Marrara Stadium last year in a T20 international. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

August is not normally cricket season in Australia, but officials are taking advantage of the dry season in the north to take these matches to the tropics, with Darwin and Mackay hosting the Test matches.

Darwin's Marrara Oval will host just its third ever men's Test match and first since Sri Lanka visited in July 2004.

Australia have a 100 per cent winning record in Tests in Darwin, winning by an innings and 132 runs against Bangladesh in 2003, following that up with a 149-run victory against Sri Lanka the year after.

Australia has also played four ODIs in Darwin, all against Bangladesh and all resulting in emphatic victories.

In T20Is it's a slightly different story though, with South Africa sharing the spoils across two matches at the venue last year.

Mackay's Harrup Park has never hosted a men's Test match before and will become the 12th venue in Australia to do so.

Harrup Park in Mackay will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The ground did host a youth Test match last year between Australia and India's under 19 sides, a low-scoring match won by India by seven wickets.

There have been three ODIs at the ground, two of them involving Australia. Again, South Africa were the opponents in 2025 and, again, the spoils were shared.

The only other ODI took place during the 1992 Cricket World Cup between India and Sri Lanka.

Given that Mackay averages 313.2 millimetres of rain in February — the wettest month on average across the year for the city — it's perhaps not a surprise that rain meant that the match was abandoned after just two balls were bowled.

That was even after a helicopter hovered above the pitch in an attempt to dry it out.

Australia's women have played three ODIs (in 2021) and two T20Is (in 2024) at the ground, winning all but one game.

Who is playing?

Pat Cummins returns for Australia's first Test of the season. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Australia has named a strong squad, with front-line bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all returning following their injury lay offs.

Such impressive bowling depth has seen Michael Neser miss out, the luckless Queenslander then suffering a hamstring injury in any case that will keep him out of contention.

It is, essentially, a full strength team, something Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto, is pretty impressed about.

"I personally liked the fact that they have chosen their full-strength team," he said earlier this month in an interview with ESPN Cricinfo.

"They are not taking us lightly. I think our team has earned this respect."

Najmul Hossain Shanto will lead Bangladesh in Australia. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Disappointingly for Bangladesh, they come into the series missing two key weapons in lightning-fast seamer Nahid Rana, who has been ruled out due to a left-side strain, and Shoriful Islam, who has a hurt hamstring.

Then, key spin bowler Taijul Islam suffered a blow to the hand in the warm up game and did not bowl at all in the second innings.

The 23-year-old Rana is one of the form bowlers in world cricket, capable of delivering the ball at speeds in excess of 150km/h. He has already taken 44 wickets in international cricket this year — the most by any bowler — at an average of 18.31.

On a positive note, Litton Das recovered from a calf injury he picked up during the home ODI series against Australia in June.

Batting is a problem for the tourists though — chief selector Habibul Bashar said the selection of 33-year-old lefty Soumya Sarkar was as a result of "a bit of desperation". Hardly a ringing endorsement for a man who has not played Test cricket since 2021.

Australia Squad Bangladesh Squad Pat Cummins (c) Najmul Hossain Shanto (c) Scott Boland Amite Hasan (wk) Alex Carey (wk) Ebadot Hossain Cameron Green Hasan Mahmud Josh Hazlewood Jaker Ali (wk) Travis Head Khaled Ahmed Josh Inglis (wk) Litton Das (wk) Marnus Labuschagne Mehidy Hasan Miraz Nathan Lyon Mominul Haque Steven Smith Musfik Hasan Mitchell Starc Mushfiqur Rahim (wk) Jake Weatherald Shadman Islam Beau Webster Soumya Sarkar Taijul Islam Tanzid Hasan Taskin Ahmed

Jake Weatherald, the first Northern Territorian to play a Test for Australia, was watching on in the crowd the last time the Australians played in Darwin.

He is a great chance to start on his home ground after a solid spell in the County Championship with Leicestershire, where he scored 483 runs at an average of 60.37, including scoring an unbeaten 104 against Glamorgan in Cardiff.

What form are Bangladesh in?

Bangladesh have only lost one of their last five Test matches. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Bangladesh come into this Test series off the back of a pretty decent run, having lost just one of their last five matches in the format.

Two thumping victories at home against Ireland in November 2025 were backed up by a hugely impressive 2-0 series victory against Pakistan in May this year.

That wasn't bad.

Now for the things that have been pretty poor.

A one off Test against Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club resulted in a calamitous defeat by an innings and 85 runs.

If that was bad, then the absolute thrashing the Cricket Australia XI delivered last week was even worse, the tourists bowled out for just 54 in their second dig as the CA XI won by an innings and 38 runs.

If it wasn't for Mehidy Hasan Miraz's unbeaten century in the first innings, rescuing his side from 6-110, who knows how bad the score would have looked as Corey Rocchiccioli took 6-83 in that first innings and Campbell Thompson took 8-25 in the second.

What is Bangladesh's record against Australia?

Jason Gillespie's stunning double century will go down in the annals as one of the best ever night watchman displays. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Bangladesh have only ever played against Australia six times in their Test history — they've only played fewer Tests against Ireland (3) and Afghanistan (2) which, given Bangladesh have been a Test-playing nation since 2000, is a damning inditement on Australia's commitment to playing the minnows.

Somewhat surprisingly then, Bangladesh does have a Test victory against Australia to their name and, it was their most recent series in 2017.

Bangladesh claimed a stunning 20-run victory in Mirpur, with Shakib Al Hasan claiming player of the match honours after scoring a 133-ball 84 in the first innings and taking 5-85 with the ball in the final innings.

Australia got revenge in Chattogram, winning by seven wickets as Nathan Lyon took 7-94 and 6-60, while David Warner scored a brilliant, six-hour, 234-ball 123 in the first innings.

Australia's best ever batting performance in Chattogram though came 11 years before that, when night watchman Jason Gillespie scored a stunning unbeaten 201 to help Australia claim victory by an innings and 80 runs.

The first Test of that series in Fatullah had been won by the far more tense margin of three wickets, with Ricky Ponting's grinding 118 not out helping the Aussies over the line.

Bangladesh have never beaten Australia in Australia though, losing both their 2003 Tests by over an innings, in matches that took place in Darwin and Cairns.

World.title: 'Rude to say no': All Blacks icon performs solo haka against current team
World.content:
South African rugby teams love facing the haka. None have ever replied to New Zealand's traditional pre-match challenge with another haka until today.

Ma'a Nonu stepped in front of his new Sharks teammates and performed a solo haka in what will probably be the lasting memory of a tour match the New Zealanders won 54-0 at soggy Kings Park.

Nonu played 103 matches for New Zealand from 2003-15 and has continued playing around the world at age 44. The Sharks signed him a week ago to help develop their young players. Then as their injury list lengthened they drafted him onto the bench to face the All Blacks.

He was reluctant at first. He didn't want to detract from the Sharks' first match against the All Blacks in 30 years. He relented to help make up the numbers.

"I thought it would be rude to say no," Nonu told broadcaster SuperSport. "I thought I would put the boots on and try to help the team really."

For his first time facing the All Blacks, he talked to New Zealand assistant coaches Tana Umaga and Tamati Ellison on Monday about replying to the All Blacks' haka.

"Out of respect for our team and on behalf of myself and my family, I thought it was the right thing to do, to answer the boys and the All Blacks," Nonu said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

So after lining up for the anthems, then watching the haka, he stood alone with the Sharks arrayed behind him, and the All Blacks lined up on the other side of halfway. He performed the All Blacks' own haka, Kapa o Pango, to initial silence from the crowd and growing cheers.

Afterward, he nodded to the All Blacks, many of whom nodded back. Only Codie Taylor and Beauden Barrett still play for New Zealand from Nonu's last squad.

"It was such a privilege and an honour, and to do the haka, showing my respect on behalf of my family to the team I love," Nonu said.

He got into the game with a quarter to go. His first touch was to clatter into flyhalf Ruben Love, who was 2 years old when Nonu debuted for New Zealand.

"I got 20 minutes. I tried my best. It was great to see the [New Zealand] boys," he said.

"The All Blacks opened up in the last 30 minutes and I was chasing my tail. Credit to them, they're improving, and all the best to the brothers for the next game."

AP

World.title: History beckons for Phil Sami after the hard life of a Gold Coast hero
World.content:
As the weather gets warmer and the dreams of the NRL's elite become all the more real, the competition strugglers begin the march towards the end.

If South Sydney defeats Canterbury on Friday night the ninth-placed Bulldogs will be two wins outside the top eight with just three rounds remaining and their play-off hopes will feel more mathematical than truly possible.

It means, with the top eight all bust set in stone, the nine clubs who will miss out on the finals in 2026 face four matches with uncertain stakes.

Careers will begin for the young as some look to the future and end for the old as others celebrate the past on their way out the door.

Tedious debates about a potential wildcard round or expanded finals series, where games are called "content" as they transform into mere vessels for revenue, will be reheated.

Spoiling the dreams of their betters becomes the greatest prize a struggling team can hope for and incessant mentions of how one side or another is only "playing for pride" will instead merely compound their shame.

Sami has been one of Gold Coast's best during some of the club's hardest times. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It is amidst this wreckage that Phillip Sami, who has lived the hard life of a Gold Coast legend, will try and make history.

Sami is currently level with Anthony Don as the Titans all-time leading try-scorer with 85 and he has four games to land one more and leave for St George Illawarra at season's end as the top dog.

It would be a just reward for a decade spent fighting for a cause that seems to be perpetually starting over.

Counting interims, Sami has played under nine head coaches in his 10 seasons with Gold Coast.

He's played in just one semi-final, which doubles as the Titans only finals match since 2010, and has never played on a team with a winning record.

Sami debuted for Gold Coast back in 2017. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

He has been through it, as anybody who sticks around long enough to hold a Gold Coast record must, which means he knows these curious final weeks of the season very well.

Expect more of his best because if the lure of premierships was all that drove Sami he would have shot through long ago and he wouldn't be here now, on the verge of claiming the record.

A cynic might say it's a modest piece of history. Of all the clubs that have existed for as long as the Titans have or more, only Western Suburbs Magpies have a lower total for their top try-scorer.

But only a snob turns up their nose when a house record is concerned and given Gold Coast always have to fight to make themselves heard, Sami has done more for that fight than most.

He's chased this record the hard way. Given the club's point-scoring struggles and playmaker upheaval over the years, sparkling backline efforts have rarely been easy to find and there are precious few catch and fall efforts to be found here.

But every now and then, Sami goes big-game hunting and when he does he seems to have a special talent for winning battles using the weapons of his enemies.

One of the first times he showed this quality was in 2018 against the Warriors when Samis scored what remains his greatest try.

In those days, getting a hand on the light-stepping Roger Tuivasa-Sheck was like catching smoke and Sami, in just his second year of first grade, didn't so much give that year's Dally M medallist a taste of his own medicine but a lethal overdose.

Sami did the same when he flew over Clint Gutherson during the days when Parramatta really was the latter's kingdom before hitting him with his own celebration dance.

He showed he's not lost his touch earlier this season when he rounded Reece Walsh en route to a 70-metre solo effort that left the prince of Brisbane grasping at ghosts as Sami howled like a wolf.

It's not just with tries or even with football — Sami has a rare gift for being larger than life.

When he played two matches for Queensland back in 2020 a coach from his schoolboy days detailed the time Sami outran a kangaroo during a match.

It sounds like something from a folk song but rap is more Sami's speed given Goodna rapper Lisi shouted him out on a track later that same year.

At the time he was best known for the step on Tuivasa-Sheck and the moment he ran down ran down Josh Addo-Carr, which came at a time when that was like shooting Jesse James.

That try-saver, like his all-round play this year, is proof there's more to his game than just the fun stuff.

Sami has run more metres than any other player in the league, over 200 more than second place and 500 more than the next best winger. He's averaging 218 metres gained per game, the best mark of his career by miles.

He's also top when it comes to post-contact metres, a full 400 metres ahead of any other flanker, and teammate Keano Kini is the only player in the whole NRL who's run the ball more times.

Throw in that Sami only needs one more line break and one more try will match his career-best total for a single season in both categories and you can make a hipster's case he's a shot for one of the wing spots in the Dally M team of the year, making his progress towards the record an even more furious charge.

He has given his absolute best in service of one last fresh start for the Titans and perhaps this will even be the one that sticks.

Gold Coast fans have plenty to be optimistic about in the years to come. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

In Kini, Jayden Campebll, Zane Harrison and Oliver Pascoe, Gold Coast have a spine of playmakers that feels full of exciting possibilities.

Josh Hannay has shown some promising signs as coach, displaying a sharp eye for the kind of fighters the Titans will need in the years to come.

One more win will give them more victories than last year and they're a chance of finishing above Brisbane for just the sixth time in their history.

In a broader sense, after two decades the club has found a lived-in quality by sitting more comfortably with it's own history as an enticing future beckons.

Why Gold Coast has already won Magic Round One of the best parts of Magic Round is going jersey-spotting but before a ball is kicked in Brisbane the Titans have already cleaned up via their Chargers-inspired retro strip.

Sami will not be on hand to see it. He's taken up a three-year deal with St George Illawarra, one which was too good to refuse even as the Titans were open to keeping him.

So he has four games left to get one last try. The first chance is against Newcastle on Sunday and it won't be easy.

The Knights have defied their bulging casualty ward in recent weeks to keep themselves in the race for the top four and will be warm favourites at home.

But Sami has never had it easy and no Titan ever really does, so why should the moment of achievement for club and player be any different?

They've lived through dark days together, enough for both know it's how to take the shiny moments where you find them, regardless of how and when they come.

When you are in the final days of a lost year a player can either accept that fate or try and change it on the hope that this game can be better than the last just because it's a fresh start.

Sami has spent his career believing that and proving it with his actions. He wouldn't have scored these tries and lasted this long if he didn't.

Now he has a chance at a prize all his own, that he has fought for his own way and if he can break the record before leaving it will mark his ultimate reward — to live as a Gold Coast hero.

That title tells the tale of a hard footballing life but someone had to live it and Sami has lived it all the way.

World.title: Trump says FIFA would be making 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino
World.content:
Embattled FIFA leader Gianni Infantino has a powerful and vocal supporter — US President Donald Trump.

As football organisations around the world continue to call for the resignation of the FIFA president, post-World Cup, Trump blasted that idea in a message he posted to Truth Social on Monday night.

"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North America, Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) banded together earlier in the week to release an open letter, signed by the president and general secretary of each organisation, urging Infantino's resignation.

Infantino has been under fire since last month's failed plan to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would have sold part of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors to raise billions of dollars.

He apparently caused further damage by holding a crisis meeting last week in Morocco with some members of FIFA's management team.

Trump is a close ally of Infantino's after the FIFA boss awarded him the FIFA Peace Prize. (Getty Images: Kevin Dietsch)

"This recent meeting, where a select number of members of the FIFA Management Committee — not the full Committee — were summoned abroad, rather than leadership going to Zurich to address the heart of FIFA, its staff, only reinforces these concerns and represents a continuation of the very pattern of conduct that brought us to this moment," reads the letter from UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Also Monday, US Soccer and others issued their own statement backing CONCACAF.

"US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU (Caribbean Football Union) and UNCAF (Central American Football Union) stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens FIFA's governance, transparency and accountability," the statement read.

Infantino, 56, has served as FIFA president since his initial election on February 26, 2016. His current term runs through 2027, and he has announced his bid for re-election to extend his tenure to 2031.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos name new head coach as 2029 Rugby World Cup looms on horizon
World.content:
The Wallaroos have made another key appointment in the build-up to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup with Sione Fukofuka named head coach.

Fukofuka will begin the role in 2027 after the Wallaroos become a full-time program.

He will work under Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, who took on his newly created position last month.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Fukofuka was Scotland women's head coach until last week.

He was granted a release from his contract for family and personal reasons.

The 47-year-old will be returning home to Australia, having begun his coaching career while working as a teacher in the Queensland schools system.

He previously served as an assistant on the Wallaroos staff and was USA head coach between 2023-25.

"Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family," Fukofuka said in an RA statement.

"I know many of the players and coaches well from my time in the Queensland and Australian systems and, as we transition to a full-time program this year, the opportunity for growth is enormous."

The Wallaroos' on-field results will improve once the program goes full-time. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

RA is determined the Wallaroos make an impression at the next Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.

They departed last year's tournament at the quarterfinal stage and are ranked ninth in the world.

The Wallaroos went winless during April's Pacific Four Series following losses to Canada (24-0), USA (33-12) and New Zealand (40-5).

But the move to full-time status will be a game changer for the Wallaroos in terms of improving on-field results.

The alignment of the Wallaroos and Australian sevens programs, under Walsh's guidance, will also make the squad competitive with the likes of New Zealand and reigning world champions England.

Walsh said he was confident the Wallaroos would make progress under Fukofuka, whose contract runs through until the end of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"Sione is a pioneer among international coaches of Pasifika heritage and a proud product of the Australian rugby coaching system," Walsh said.

"He is highly regarded by players and staff alike for his connection, team culture and driving high standards within the daily training environment.

"He is well-positioned to lead the Wallaroos into a new era and a generational opportunity presented by the home Rugby World Cup in 2029."

The Wallaroos still have six Tests to play this year, with a return bout against New Zealand coming up in Auckland on August 22.

The clash with New Zealand has historical significance as it will be the Wallaroos' 100th Test.

They head to Europe next month to play WXV Global Series Tests against England in Salford (September 13), France in Aix-en-Provence (September 20) and Scotland in Edinburgh (September 27).

The Wallaroos will later host Scotland in Sydney (October 17) and Canberra (October 23) as part of the WXV Global Series.

Vast coaching experience

Fukofuka took charge of Scotland last December.

Under his watch, Scotland finished fifth in this year's Women's Six Nations Championship with a 1-4 win-loss record.

Former Wallabies hooker and ACT Brumbies men's coach David Nucifora, now working as Scottish Rugby performance director, said Fukofuka left with the governing body's blessings.

Fukofuka moved to Scotland after stepping down as USA head coach following the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup in England.

Sione Fukofuka coached USA at the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

USA, which drew 31-31 with the Wallaroos in the pool stage, did not advance to the quarterfinals but Fukofuka was credited with improving the level of professionalism within the Eagles program during his tenure.

"Sione is a leader with a comprehensive knowledge of Australian and international systems and a reputation for creating world-class team environments and standards," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

As Fukofuka will not take the reins until next year, Walsh will oversee the Wallaroos' coaching transition team for the remainder of the Test season.

Walsh recently guided Australia to its World Championship victory in women's sevens, ending a successful second stint as head coach.

He coached Australia to a historic victory at the 2016 Rio Olympics during his first term.

The Wallaroos' coaching transition team includes NSW head coach Mike Ruthven, who led the Waratahs to the Super Rugby Women's title last month, and ex-Wallabies captain Ben Mowen.

Mowen currently works on the Brumbies' coaching staff.

Interim coaches Sam Needs and Gill Bourke have departed the Wallaroos' set-up.

World.title: Fraser confirms intentions for Carlton coaching job after hot streak
World.content:
Carlton caretaker Josh Fraser wants the full-time coaching job.

Fraser has told Carlton hierarchy he is keen to become the permanent head coach after his stunning success as interim boss.

The former Collingwood ruckman has won 10 of 12 games since the departure of Michael Voss and is now among five candidates for the permanent job.

Fraser, 44, initially said he wasn't interested in being the full-time coach from next season.

Carlton has won 10 out of 12 games under Fraser's guidance, surging into finals contention. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

But he has changed his mind after his blistering start to coaching, and now appears the frontrunner in a field of five.

Fremantle's Jaymie Graham, St Kilda's Corey Enright, Geelong's James Kelly — all current assistant coaches — have interviewed for the role, along with Hawthorn's head of development Daniel Giansiracusa.

Fraser's about-turn comes as he revives the on-field fortunes of the Blues, who were languishing with one win and eight losses when Voss departed in mid-May.

Carlton appears set for a wildcard finals berth, sitting 10th on the ladder and two wins clear of 11th-placed St Kilda with two rounds remaining.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Blues meet the Western Bulldogs on Sunday before their last home-and-away game against ladder-leaders Fremantle.

Fraser, who played 200 games with Collingwood and 18 at Gold Coast, began his coaching career as coach of the Suns' state league side.

He then coached Carlton and Collingwood at VFL level before returning to the Blues as an assistant to Voss this season.

Two weeks ago, Carlton's football boss Chris Davies said the club wanted Fraser to apply for the full-time role.

"We think he should put his hand up," Davies said at the time.

Since those comments, Fraser has overseen a 76-point thrashing of reigning premiers Brisbane and a 44-point victory over the Saints.
